API reference

Every public module of braidpy, by what it is for.

Start here

A few questions answered in plain data, and the same offered to AI assistants.

braidpy: braids in Python — represented, worked with and analysed, and drawn and made, by hand or on a machine.

braidpy’s front door: a few questions about braids, answered in plain data — for a person at a prompt, a script, or an AI assistant (braidpy.mcp_server offers each as a tool).

Each function takes and gives only text, numbers, lists and dicts, so what goes in and comes out can be read, printed or sent as JSON as it is. None does anything of its own: each asks the module that knows, and says which.

>>> from braidpy import tools
>>> tools.describe_braid("1 -2")["permutation"]
[2, 3, 1]
>>> tools.compare_braids("1 -2", "-2 1", n_strands=3)["same_braid"]
True

A braid is given as a braid word: signed generators, 1 for σ₁, -2 for σ₂⁻¹, written as braidpy reads them (parse_word()): "1 -2", "1,-2", "s1 s2^-1" or "aB".

braidpy.tools.STUDIO = 'https://baptistelabat.github.io/braidpy/studio/'

Braid Studio, where a braid described here can be seen made.

braidpy.tools.compare_braids(a: str, b: str, n_strands: int | None = None) → dict[str, Any]

Whether two braid words make the same braid pattern, however written: alike, as braidpy’s ways of making a braid check it — by their fingerprints (braidpy.braid_pattern.BraidPattern.alike()) — and, if so, proven or not (proven()); and how unlike they are (braidpy.similarity.distance(): 0 the same, up to 6).

Parameters:

  • a – A braid word.

  • b – Another.

  • n_strands – The strands of both; as many as they need if None.

Returns:

same_braid, whether they are alike; proven, whether they are proven the same pattern — None if the proof would take too long, or they are not alike, which proves them different; and distance.

braidpy.tools.describe_braid(word: str, n_strands: int | None = None) → dict[str, Any]

What is known of a braid from its word: strands, crossings, the permutation it makes, whether it is pure and after how many repeats, what it closes up into, its Garside normal form, which of periodic, reducible or pseudo-Anosov it is, its band word where that is shorter (braidpy.braid.Braid.band_word()) — as Braid Studio’s card shows it (braidpy.web) — and a link to see it.

Parameters:

  • word – The braid word, for example "1 -2".

  • n_strands – The strands; as many as the word needs if None.

Returns:

What is known, by name.

braidpy.tools.list_braids(source: str | None = None) → dict[str, Any]

The braids braidpy knows by name, by what makes them: braid words, kumihimo disks, Ashley’s sinnets, braiding machines, lace machines (braidpy.web.catalog()).

Parameters:

source – Only this one, for example "sinnet"; all if None.

Returns:

Per source, its title and its braids — each a name and a title — and the settings it takes, with their defaults.

braidpy.tools.make_braid(spec: dict[str, Any]) → dict[str, Any]

A braid made as Braid Studio makes it (braidpy.web.build()), told in words: what is known of it and what was noted on the way — not the thousands of points of its yarns, for which build itself, or the link, is the place.

Parameters:

spec – What it is made from, for example {"source": "sinnet", "name": "abok_3042"}; see list_braids() for each source’s settings.

Returns:

title, info, notes and a studio link.

braidpy.tools.similar_braids(word: str, n_strands: int | None = None, count: int = 5) → list[dict[str, Any]]

The braids of braidpy’s catalogues most like this one, nearest first, each with every way braidpy knows of making it (braidpy.topology_catalog.related()).

Parameters:

  • word – The braid word.

  • n_strands – The strands; as many as the word needs if None.

  • count – How many to give.

Returns:

its title, distance (0 is this very braid), and made_as, each way of making it with a studio link.

Return type:

Per braid

braidpy.tools.studio_link(spec: dict[str, Any]) → str

Where Braid Studio makes a braid, from what describes it — a link to open, to see it in 3D, turn it, grow it.

Parameters:

spec – What braidpy.web.build() makes it from, for example {"source": "word", "word": "1 -2", "n_strands": 3}.

Returns:

The link.

braidpy.tools.ways_to_make(word: str, n_strands: int | None = None) → dict[str, Any]

How to make a braid by hand or on a machine (braidpy.making): a kumihimo disk’s moves, a Jacquard lace machine’s punchcard, and Ashley’s stand — a sinnet of the book’s kind if one makes it, or the braid itself one strand a space; each from the word shortened first (shortened()), fewer crossings to make.

Parameters:

  • word – The braid word, one repeat of it.

  • n_strands – The strands; as many as the word needs if None.

Returns:

its moves, from slot > to slot, and a studio link; lace: the punchcard, as punched, and where the bobbins go; ashley: its spaces, moves, whether it is a_sinnet of the book’s kind, and a studio link.

Return type:

disk

braidpy as an MCP server: braidpy.tools, each function a tool an AI assistant can call — Claude, or any client of the Model Context Protocol (https://modelcontextprotocol.io).

Installed with the mcp extra, it runs over stdio:

pip install "braidpy[mcp]"
braidpy-mcp

and is added to a client as a command, for example to Claude Code:

claude mcp add braidpy -- braidpy-mcp

The tools are braidpy.tools’s functions as they are, their docstrings what the assistant reads of them: nothing here but the wiring, so what a person reads in the library and what an assistant is told are the same words.

braidpy.mcp_server.TOOLS: list[Callable[[...], Any]] = [<function list_braids>, <function describe_braid>, <function compare_braids>, <function similar_braids>, <function ways_to_make>, <function make_braid>, <function studio_link>]

What the server offers, in the order it lists them.

braidpy.mcp_server.main() → None

Run the server over stdio: braidpy-mcp.

braidpy.mcp_server.server() → Any

The MCP server, its tools registered. The catalogue of braids by topology, a minute or so to make, is made at once in the background, so that the first question needing it is not kept waiting long.

Returns:

An mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer.

Raises:

ImportError – Without the mcp extra.

Braids and their words

Braid words, their notations, operations and properties.

The braid itself (Braid): a word in Artin’s generators on so many strands, and what can be done with it.

braidpy.braid.reduced_burau_generator(generator: int, n_strands: int, t, one, zero) → list[list]

The reduced Burau matrix of one generator, σ_i or its inverse, as rows: the identity, but for row i (from 0),

σ_i: ( …, t, −t, 1, … ) at columns i − 1, i, i + 1, σ_i⁻¹: ( …, 1, −1/t, 1/t, … ),

the columns that fall off the matrix left out. t, one and zero are of whatever ring the matrix is wanted in: a sympy symbol, an element of a polynomial field, a complex number.

Parameters:

  • generator – i for σ_i, -i for its inverse.

  • n_strands – Number of strands; the matrix is n_strands − 1 square.

  • t – The Burau variable.

  • one – The ring’s one.

  • zero – The ring’s zero.

Returns:

The rows.

class braidpy.braid.BraidWordNotation(*values)

Bases: str, Enum

How Braid.format_to_notation() writes a braid word: in Artin’s generators (s_{1}^{1.0}), in letters (aB), or as math-braid and braidlab write it (<1 : -2>).

ARTIN = 'ARTIN'
ALPHA = 'ALPHA'
DEFAULT = 'DEFAULT'
braidpy.braid.single_crossing_braiding_process(process: tuple[int | tuple[int, ...], ...]) → list[int]

Flattens a tuple of braiding steps into a list of signed crossings.

Each step may be a single crossing or multiple simultaneous crossings. To get Artin generators we need only consecutive single crossing, which is topologically equivalent

class braidpy.braid.Braid(process: int | Sequence[int | Sequence[BraidProcess]], n_strands: int = None)

Bases: object

Sometimes referred to as algebraic braids :param process: list of Artin’s generator, which may group or not by parenthesis (tuples) :type process: BraidProcess :param n_strands: number of strands. Default to the minimum number needed for process :type n_strands: Optional[int]

process: int | Sequence[int | Sequence[BraidProcess]]
n_strands: int = None
property generators: list[int]

List of Artin’s generators in the braid word.

property main_generator: int | None

A main generator of a braid word w is the generator with the lowest index.

https://pure.tue.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/67742824/630595-1.pdf page 33

format_to_notation(target: str = '') → str

Inspired from https://github.com/abhikpal/dehornoy/blob/master/braid.py

Allow to format the braidword using several classical notations.:

The Artin representation can also be used in a latex file.

The neutral element is ‘e’ for the Artin representation and ‘#’ for alpha.

Parameters:

target (str) – Among ‘alpha’: for example ‘aBa’ ‘artin’ for example ‘s_{1}^{1.0} s_{2}^{1.0} s_{1}^{-1.0} s_{2}^{-1.0}’ ‘default’ syntax used by other tools such as math-braid and braidlab

Returns:

the formatted braid word

Return type:

str

format(generator_symbols: list[str] | None = None, inverse_generator_symbols: list[str] | None = None, zero_symbol: str = 'e', separator: str = '') → str

Allow to format the braid word following different formats.

Note that the power are limited to -1/1 due to the actual braid word definition (not possible to display σ₁² for example)

See also format_to_notation for simpler predefined format

Parameters:

  • generator_symbols (Optional(list[str])) – Default to [“σ₁”, “σ₂”, …]

  • inverse_generator_symbols (Optional(list[str])) – Default to [“σ₁⁻¹”, …]

  • zero_symbol (Optional(str)) – Default to “e

  • separator (Optional(str)) – Default to “”

Returns:

the formatted braid word

Return type:

str

no_zero() → Braid

Suppress all the zero steps (multiplication by neutral element).

Returns:

A new braid with zero generators removed.

Return type:

Braid

word_length() → int

Length of the word including neutral element.

Returns:

The length of the braid word.

Return type:

int

word_eq(other: Braid) → bool

Check if two braids have identical word representations.

Parameters:

other – The braid to compare with.

Returns:

True if the braid words are identical.

Return type:

bool

word() → BraidWord

The braid’s word, compared as a word (braidpy.braid_word).

pattern() → BraidPattern

The braid made over and over, compared as a pattern (braidpy.braid_pattern).

closed() → ClosedBraid

The braid closed, each strand’s end tied to its start: a knot or a link, compared as one (braidpy.closed_braid).

inverse() → Braid

Return the inverse of the braid.

This corresponds to the image of the braid in a mirror. Both order and signs are reversed.

Returns:

The inverse braid.

Return type:

Braid

n(n_strands: int) → Braid

Compact notation to allow changing the number of strands.

Parameters:

n_strands – The new number of strands.

Returns:

A new braid with updated number of strands.

Return type:

Braid

flip() → Braid

Flip the braid This corresponds to the image of the braid in a mirror on the side of the braid reordered from left to right The strands are reversed, not the order of operations Sign is also changed. This step is often used when braiding

Example

>>> b = Braid([1], 3)
>>> basic_3_braid = (b * (b.flip())) ** 3
Returns:

The reversed braid.

Return type:

Braid

half_twist(sign: int = 1) → Braid

Twist the braid with half a turn.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twist_(differential_geometry)

Parameters:

sign – Sign of the twist. If positive the first strand is going over. Defaults to +1.

Returns:

The twisted braid.

Return type:

Braid

full_twist(sign: int = 1) → Braid

Twist the braid with a complete turn.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twist_(differential_geometry)

Parameters:

sign – Sign of the twist. If positive the first strand is going over. Defaults to +1.

Returns:

The twisted braid.

Return type:

Braid

full_twists() → int

How many whole turns of every strand together the braid contains.

The full twist Δ² commutes with every braid, so it can always be moved to the front: β = Δ^{2m} · β′. Which m is a choice, made here so that what is left sits evenly about no twist at all: the canonical factors give the least and the most twist the braid lies between (its infimum and supremum, in half twists), and m is their middle in whole turns, rounded to the nearest. Adding k full twists to any braid adds exactly k to it.

A real braid hanging free, as from a kumihimo disk, does not keep these: turning every strand together only turns the cord, which turns back. See without_full_twists().

Returns:

m, negative for turns the other way.

Return type:

int

without_full_twists() → Braid

The braid with its whole turns taken out: β · Δ^{-2m}.

What is left is the braid’s real crossings, and at most a fraction of a turn. Two braids that differ only by full twists — a word read off a kumihimo disk that was turned round, and the cord it makes — are then equal.

Returns:

the same crossings, without the full twists.

Return type:

Braid

up_side_down() → Braid

Invert up and down crossing operations.

For hair braiding this is called “inversé”.

Returns:

The mirrored braid.

Return type:

Braid

shortened() → Braid

The same braid in as few crossings as are found: crossings that cancel, brought together by the braid relations, and Dehornoy’s handle reduction where it is shorter (braidpy.shortening.shortened()).

Returns:

The braid, its word no longer than this one’s.

is_reduced() → bool

Check if a braid word is reduced.

A braid word w is reduced either if it is the null string, or the empty braid, or if the main generator of w occurs only positively or only negatively.

https://pure.tue.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/67742824/630595-1.pdf page 33

Returns:

True if the braid word is reduced.

Return type:

bool

writhe() → int

Calculate the writhe of the braid (sum of generator powers).

The writhe value.

int

get_canonical_factors() → GarsideCanonicalFactors

Get decomposition in Artin’s left normal form, Δ^k · A_1 ⋯ A_r

n_half_twist is k, the number of half twists Δ in front, and each A_i is a permutation braid — a positive braid in which any two strands cross at most once — given as the permutation it makes. See artin_left_normal_form().

Returns:

the unique decomposition of the braid according to left convention

Return type:

GarsideCanonicalFactors

get_band_canonical_factors() → GarsideCanonicalFactors

Get decomposition in Birman, Ko and Lee’s left normal form, in band generators, δ^p · A_1 ⋯ A_r (band_left_normal_form()).

Not Artin’s form: n_half_twist here counts δ, every strand a place round, a 1/n_strands turn — a full twist is n_strands of them — and each factor is strands in blocks round the circle (factor_blocks()).

the band generator decomposition.

The braid in band generators, as its band normal form spells it (band_word()): (t, s) for a_ts, strands t > s crossing in front of those between, (s, t) for its inverse. A disk braid’s is far shorter than its word.

The band letters.

Burau matrix representation is faithful for n_strands=3 or n_strands=4, but not faithful for n_strand>=5. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05283

is_trivial() → bool

Check if the braid is trivial (identity braid): no crossing at all, however its word is written (σ₁σ₁⁻¹ is trivial).

By Dehornoy’s handle reduction (braidpy.handles_reduction): a braid is trivial exactly when its Dehornoy sign is 0. It is the faster on most braids; but it can blow up on long words of many strands (ABOK #3082’s, 61 strands and 1800 crossings: minutes). So it is given HANDLE_REDUCTION_S seconds, and then the braid’s left normal form decides (artin_left_normal_form()): trivial exactly when it is no half twist and no factor (three seconds there).

Returns:

True if the braid is trivial.

Return type:

bool

permutations(plot: bool = False) → list[list[int]]

Return the permutations induced by the braid

perm() → list[int]

Compute the permutation corresponding to the braid.

This is a braid invariant.

Returns:

The final permutation due to the braid.

Return type:

list[int]

is_pure() → bool

Check if a braid is pure (permutation is identity).

Returns:

True if the braid is pure.

Return type:

bool

is_palindromic() → bool

Check if the braid word is palindromic.

Returns:

True if the braid word reads the same forwards and backwards.

bool

is_involutive() → bool

Check if braid word is involutive.

Returns true if inverse of braid word is the same as braid word. This probably works only for the neutral element.

True if braid word is involutive.

Return type:

bool

is_periodic() → bool

Check if braid is periodic: some power of it is a power of the half-twist ∆ — a rotation of the disk holding the strands, the strands riding it round.

A braid x is periodic if and only if its nth power or its (n − 1)st power is a power of the half-twist ∆ (González-Meneses, Periodic braids): that power is read in the Garside canonical form (braidpy.garside_canonical_form.artin_left_normal_form()), where a power of ∆ is the form with no permutation braid left in it. Being pure is not enough: σ₁² keeps every strand’s place and is not periodic, while σ₁σ₂ turns the three strands round and is.

https://hal.science/hal-00647035v2/file/B_nNTHClassificationv5.pdf https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~jaca2009/notes/Meneses.pdf

Returns:

True if the braid is periodic.

Return type:

bool

without_strand(strand: int) → Braid

The braid with one strand taken out, as if it had never been there.

The crossings that strand takes part in go with it; every other crossing stays, between the same two strands and the same way over, renumbered for the slot the strand no longer takes up.

Parameters:

strand – The strand to take out, numbered from 1 by where it starts, as perm() numbers them.

Returns:

The braid on one strand fewer.

Raises:

ValueError – If there is no such strand, or none would be left.

is_brunnian() → bool

Whether the braid is Brunnian: pure, and trivial once any one of its strands is taken out (without_strand()), though perhaps not before — as three strands make the Borromean rings, any two of them apart.

Brunnian braids form a subgroup of the pure braid group. On three strands or more a braid trivial with any one strand out is pure anyway; on two, purity is what rules out a single crossing. The trivial braid is Brunnian.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunnian_link#Brunnian_braids

Returns:

True if Brunnian.

Return type:

bool

is_reducible(limit: int | None = 10000) → bool

Check if the braid is reducible.

If a braid is reducible, it means that the strands can be separated into groups of strands (less groups than number of strands), such that each group is running inside one tube. The tubes themselves can form a braid. Said of curves: some round curve round consecutive strands — two of them at least, all but two at most — is brought back to itself, up to stretching. The trivial braid is reducible, every curve coming back; a periodic braid (is_periodic()) may be too, the full twist turning every curve round and back; a braid neither periodic nor reducible is pseudo-Anosov.

Reducibility goes with a braid’s conjugates, so it is asked of the super summit set (braidpy.conjugacy.super_summit_set()): a reducible braid has a conjugate there that keeps a round curve (Benardete, Gutiérrez and Nitecki 1993; Calvez, Fast Nielsen–Thurston classification of braids, theorem 10), and of that set’s braids ∆^p · A_1 ⋯ A_r the one keeps the round curve round strands i…j when every A_k carries strands i…j back to them, and ∆^p, for an odd p, when i + j is one more than the number of strands — the middle curve, which the half twist turns round and back.

Parameters:

limit – The most braids of the super summit set to find; None for no limit.

Returns:

True if reducible.

Return type:

bool

Raises:

braidpy.conjugacy.SuperSummitSetTooLarge – If it cannot tell within limit braids.

slot_history() → list[list[int]]

Which slot every strand occupies, before and after each generator.

Slots are the positions across the braid, numbered from zero. A generator names two neighbouring slots and exchanges whoever is standing in them, whichever strands those happen to be, so this is the braid word’s permutation unrolled step by step.

It says nothing about which strand passed over which: that is the sign of the generator, and it is read separately — see strand_paths().

Returns:

A list of len(generators) + 1 rows; row m holds the slot of each strand after m generators, indexed by strand.

to_parametric_strands(amplitude: float = 0.2) → list[ParametricStrand]

Convert a braid into a list of 3D parametric strand paths.

amplitude – Height of the sine wave for over/under crossings. Defaults to 0.2.

Return type:

list[ParametricStrand]

Allows to better check the different operations (with colors!).

Return type:

Braid

plot(n_samples: int = 400, line_width: float = 3.0, gap: float = 0.45, amplitude: float = 0.28, profile=None, color: str | None = None, title: str | None = None, save: str | None = None, ax=None) → Braid

Draw the braid as a 2D diagram, running down the page.

The braid hangs downward, the way it is worked, with its word written above it. Each strand is drawn in the colour draw() gives it, and the one passing behind is interrupted where they meet. The over-and-under is not re-derived: it is read from the curve strand_paths() computes.

This used to be drawn by braid-visualiser, which used its own colours, so a strand was one colour in the console and another in the plot. The arguments changed with it: “style” is gone, “gap_size” became “gap” as a fraction of the strand spacing, and “save” takes a path rather than a flag.

Parameters:

  • n_samples – Points along each strand.

  • line_width – Thickness of a strand.

  • gap – Width of the break where a strand passes behind, as a fraction of the distance between neighbouring strands.

  • amplitude – How far a strand swings out of line as it crosses.

  • profile – How a strand travels sideways; smoothstep by default, LINEAR for straight segments.

  • color – One colour for every strand; each takes its own by default.

  • title – Heading; the braid’s word by default, and “” for none.

  • save – Path to write the figure to, if wanted.

  • ax – Axes to draw on; a new figure otherwise.

Returns:

self, so the call can be chained.

Return type:

Braid

Convert an alphabetical braid word to its numerical representation.

Each lowercase letter represents a braid generator σ_i, where:

  • ‘a’ → σ₁ → 1

  • ‘b’ → σ₂ → 2

  • …

Each uppercase letter represents the inverse generator σ_i⁻¹:

  • ‘B’ → σ₂⁻¹ → -2

Special character # can be used for neutral element

Example

>>> braidword_alpha_to_numeric("abAB")

Properties and invariants of braids.

braidpy.properties.alexander_polynomial(braid: Braid) → Poly

The Alexander polynomial of the braid’s closure, in t.

From the reduced Burau matrix B of an n-strand braid (Burau, 1935):

Δ(t) ≐ det(I − B) (1 − t) / (1 − tⁿ),

up to a unit ±tᵏ, which is fixed here as most tables fix it: no negative powers, a nonzero constant term, a positive leading coefficient. A split link — loops that could be pulled apart — has Δ = 0, as can some links that are not.

It is a link invariant: it is the same for a braid read from any starting point (conjugation), and for braids on different numbers of strands that close up the same way (Markov’s theorem). It does not tell a braid from its mirror image, nor every link from every other.

Computed exactly, over the field of rational functions of t: a few hundred crossings on eight strands take a fraction of a second. For longer braids, alexander_on_circle() samples it.

Parameters:

braid – The braid.

Returns:

Δ(t), as a polynomial with integer coefficients.

References

W. Burau, “Über Zopfgruppen und gleichsinnig verdrillte Verkettungen”, Abh. Math. Sem. Hamburg 11, 179 (1935). D. Rolfsen, Knots and Links (1976), chapter 8.

braidpy.properties.alexander_on_circle(braid: Braid, angles: Sequence[float], repeats: int = 1) → tuple[float | None, ...]

log₁₀ |Δ(e^{iθ})|: the Alexander polynomial of the closure of the braid repeated repeats times, sampled on the unit circle.

On the unit circle |±tᵏ| = 1, so the modulus is exactly an invariant of the closure, with nothing to normalise; it is computed numerically, from the eigenvalues of the braid’s Burau matrix at t = e^{iθ} (_log_det_minus_power()) — milliseconds where the polynomial of a long braid takes minutes. The angles should not be rational multiples of π: at an n-th root of unity the formula divides by zero.

Parameters:

  • braid – The braid.

  • angles – The angles θ, in radians.

  • repeats – How many times the braid is repeated before it is closed.

Returns:

Per angle, log₁₀ |Δ|; None where Δ vanishes there.

braidpy.properties.burau_polynomial_on_circle(braid: Braid, angles: Sequence[float], repeats: int = 1, at: float = 2.0) → tuple[float, ...]

log₁₀ |det(x − B(e^{iθ}))| at x = at: the characteristic polynomial of the braid’s reduced Burau matrix B, the braid repeated repeats times, sampled on the unit circle.

The characteristic polynomial does not change when the braid is conjugated — read from another starting point, as a braid round a disk is wherever its circle is cut — so two braids it tells apart are not the same braid however written. It is a finer test than the Alexander polynomial of the closure (alexander_on_circle()), which is that polynomial at x = 1: where the Burau matrix has the eigenvalue 1, as for many braids with a closure of several loops, the Alexander polynomial vanishes and tells nothing apart, but this does not.

Parameters:

  • braid – The braid.

  • angles – The angles θ, in radians.

  • repeats – How many times the braid is repeated.

  • at – Where the characteristic polynomial is taken, off the unit circle so that it does not vanish there.

Returns:

Per angle, log₁₀ |det(x − B)|.

braidpy.properties.burau_polynomial_mod(braid: Braid, t: int, repeats: int = 1) → tuple[int, ...]

The characteristic polynomial det(x − Bᵏ) of the braid’s reduced Burau matrix B, the braid repeated k = repeats times, at an integer t, exactly, modulo PRIME.

burau_polynomial_on_circle() takes the same polynomial in floating point, which for a long braid loses digits: two words for the same braid can then disagree in its third. Modulo a prime nothing is rounded, so the same braid gives the same coefficients however written, and a braid read from another starting point (conjugated) too. Two different polynomials, in t and x, agree at a given t modulo the prime only by rare chance. The Alexander polynomial of the closure is in it as well: det(1 − Bᵏ) is its value at x = 1.

Parameters:

  • braid – The braid.

  • t – The Burau variable’s value; not a multiple of PRIME.

  • repeats – How many times the braid is repeated; a power taken by squaring, so millions of repeats cost a few dozen products.

Returns:

The coefficients, from xⁿ⁻¹’s (1) down, each in [0, PRIME).

braidpy.properties.conjugacy_class(braid: Braid, conjugators: list[Braid] | None = None) → list[Braid]

Generate conjugates of a braid by a list of other braids.

Parameters:

  • braid – The Braid object to conjugate.

  • conjugators – A list of Braid objects to use as conjugators. Defaults to generators and their inverses.

Returns:

List of unique conjugates a * braid * a⁻¹.

Return type:

List[Braid]

Pure braids: the ones that leave every strand where it started.

A braid is pure when its word returns every strand to the slot it set out from — when the permutation it performs is the identity. The pure braids form a subgroup, the kernel of the map from the braid group to the symmetric group, and are sometimes called the coloured braid group, since each strand can then be given a colour that survives composition.

Purity is also what decides whether a braid has a shape that repeats. A strand of a pure braid comes back to where it began, so its path closes and can be described periodically; a strand of an impure one ends somewhere else and has no period of its own until the word is repeated enough times to bring it home. closing_repeats() says how many, from the strands’ cycles().

braidpy.pure_braid.permutation(braid: Braid) → list[int]

Where each strand ends up, as a slot per strand.

Parameters:

braid – The braid.

Returns:

slot[s] — the slot strand s finishes in, having started in slot s.

braidpy.pure_braid.is_pure(braid: Braid) → bool

Whether the braid returns every strand to the slot it started in.

Parameters:

braid – The braid.

Returns:

True if its permutation is the identity.

braidpy.pure_braid.cycles(braid: Braid) → list[list[int]]

The strands’ cycles: the slots a strand passes through, braid after braid, until it is back where it started.

Parameters:

Returns:

Each cycle, as the slots in the order the strand visits them. The braid’s closure makes one separate piece per cycle.

braidpy.pure_braid.components(braid: Braid) → int

How many separate pieces the braid’s closure makes: its cycles.

Parameters:

braid – The braid.

Returns:

braidpy.pure_braid.closing_repeats(braid: Braid, limit: int | None = 1000) → int | None

How many times a braid must be repeated before it is pure.

Repeating a braid repeats its permutation, so a strand is home after a whole number of turns of its cycle: every strand, after the least common multiple of the cycles’ lengths. That is the permutation’s order, so a closing repeat always exists; the limit is there for a caller who would not repeat the braid that often.

Parameters:

  • braid – The braid.

  • limit – The most repeats worth having, or None for no limit.

Returns:

The smallest number of repeats that closes it — 1 if it is already pure — or None if that is over the limit.

braidpy.pure_braid.repeating_unit(word: Sequence[T]) → list[T]

The shortest word that, repeated, makes word.

Parameters:

word – Signed Artin generators, or any sequence: the gears a carrier track runs round, say.

Returns:

word itself if it repeats nothing shorter.

Return type:

The unit

Braids in band generators (Birman, Ko and Lee, 1998): the strands round a circle, any two crossing along the chord between them.

A band generator a_ts (t > s) crosses strands t and s directly, passing in front of every strand between them, as a band stretched across: a_ts = σ_{t-1} ⋯ σ_{s+1} σ_s σ_{s+1}⁻¹ ⋯ σ_{t-1}⁻¹, and a_{s+1,s} is σ_s. Where Artin’s generators cross neighbours on a line, these treat every place round a circle alike, as a kumihimo disk or a marudai does: a strand carried across the disk is one letter, a ring word’s crossing across the seam is a_{n,1}, and δ = a_{n,n-1} ⋯ a_{2,1}, every strand a place round, is the ring’s turn.

Every braid is δ^p A_1 ⋯ A_r in one way (Birman, Ko and Lee’s left normal form, band_left_normal_form()): each factor A_i strands in blocks round the circle, no two blocks crossing, each block’s strands a place round within it (a descending cycle), each pair of factors left-weighted. Worked out as Artin’s form is (artin_left_normal_form()): the turns kept at the word’s end, each factor made left-weighted with those before it in one pass back, a pair’s meet the blocks the two share.

Disk braids spell far shorter so: Kongo gumi on 8 strands, 81 crossings shortened, is 43 band letters (band_word()); machine braids of neighbours crossing, longer.

class braidpy.garside_canonical_form.GarsideCanonicalFactors(n_half_twist: int, n_strands: StrictlyPositiveInt, Ai: tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...])

Bases: object

Represents the Garside asymmetric canonical form of a braid. Also called greedy normal form.

Also known as Garside canonical form: https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/garside.pdf

Variables:

  • n_half_twist (int) – The exponent of the Garside element Δ (number of half-twists). From get_band_canonical_factors() it is instead the band generators’ δ, a 1/n_strands turn.

  • n_strands (int) – The number of strands in the braid.

  • Ai (Tuple[int]) – The sequence of simple elements (as indices or identifiers). Also known as Garside generators. From artin_left_normal_form(), each is a permutation: A[j] is where strand j ends.

n_half_twist: int
n_strands: StrictlyPositiveInt
Ai: tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...]
property dehornoy_floor: int

Computes the Dehornoy floor of the braid.

It is the unique integer m such that:

Δ^{2m} < β < Δ^{2m+2}

An estimate is floor(n_half_twist / 2) or floor(n_half_twist / 2) + 1 depending on the position of the braid in Dehornoy order.

For now, we return the conservative lower bound:

floor(n_half_twist / 2)

Returns:

the Dehornoy floor

Return type:

int

property garside_length: PositiveInt

Returns the Garside (canonical) length of the braid, defined as the number of simple elements A_i in the positive part.

Returns:

the Garside length

Return type:

int

braidpy.garside_canonical_form.artin_left_normal_form(generators, n_strands: int) → tuple[int, tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...]]

A braid word in Artin’s left normal form, Δ^k · A_1 ⋯ A_r.

The half twists are kept at the word’s end as it is read: there a crossing passes them by turning over (Δ σᵢ = σₙ₋ᵢ Δ), and an inverse crossing is a half twist less and a permutation braid more (σᵢ⁻¹ = (σᵢ⁻¹Δ) Δ⁻¹), so no factor read before is touched. Each factor is then made left-weighted with those before it (left_weighted()), and the half twists brought to the front, turning the factors over once.

Parameters:

  • generators – Signed Artin generators, +i for σ_i and -i for its inverse; 0 is ignored.

  • n_strands – Number of strands.

Returns:

k, the number of half twists in front — negative for half twists the other way — and the factors A_i as permutations.

braidpy.garside_canonical_form.left_weighted(k: int, factors: Sequence[tuple[int, ...]]) → tuple[int, tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...]]

Δ^k · F_1 ⋯ F_m, for any permutation braids F_i, in left normal form.

The factors are taken one at a time, each made left-weighted with the one before it, and that one with the one before it, back until a pair is left as it was: one pass back is enough for a left normal form followed by one permutation braid (Thurston; Epstein et al., Word Processing in Groups, chapter 9). Half twists the form begins with go into k, and factors left empty go.

Parameters:

  • k – Half twists in front.

  • factors – Permutation braids, Δ and the identity among them if need be.

Returns:

k and the factors, as artin_left_normal_form() gives them.

A braid word made shorter: the same braid, in fewer crossings.

Fewer crossings are fewer moves to make, by hand or on a machine. Three ways are tried, and the shortest word kept:

  • free cancellation: a crossing followed at once by its inverse, σᵢ σᵢ⁻¹, is no crossing at all (free_reduced());

  • braid relations: a crossing and its inverse kept apart by crossings that can be moved out of the way. Crossings of strands far apart commute, σᵢ σⱼ = σⱼ σᵢ when |i - j| ≥ 2, and three crossings of three strands can be made the other way round, σᵢ σᵢ₊₁ σᵢ = σᵢ₊₁ σᵢ σᵢ₊₁, signs mixed too (σᵢ σⱼ σᵢ⁻¹ = σⱼ⁻¹ σᵢ σⱼ). None of these changes the word’s length; each piece of the word, WINDOW crossings long, is rewritten every way they allow, up to SEARCH_BUDGET words, for one where two crossings cancel (shortened());

  • handle reduction (braidpy.handles_reduction): Dehornoy’s, which leaves no handle, σᵢ … σᵢ⁻¹ with only higher crossings between. Its word is often longer (the book’s #3072 goes from 114 crossings to 150), so it is kept only when it is shorter, after the search above.

A shortest word is not promised: finding one is hard in general. The word found is the same braid exactly (braidpy.braid.Braid.__eq__()), not merely one alike when repeated.

A word of moves round a ring (braidpy.annulus_braid) is shortened the same way, its relations read round the ring (shortened_ring()): crossing n, of the pair whose slots wrap, is a crossing like any other, neighbour of crossings n - 1 and 1, and a turn passes a crossing by renumbering it (turns_last()). The braid kept is the braid round the core (cored_word()), so a tube stays a tube.

Linking numbers: how many times the loops of a braid’s closure wind round each other.

Close a braid — join the top of each slot to the bottom of the same slot, round the outside — and its strands become loops, one per cycle of its permutation (braidpy.pure_braid.cycles()). Two loops have a linking number: how many times one winds round the other, counted with a sign. It does not change however the loops are bent, stretched or pulled tight, as long as neither passes through the other, so it is what is checked to know that a braid settled by physics is still the braid that was laid.

It is found two ways here, which agree:

  • from the braid word (linking_matrix()): half the signed number of crossings between the two loops’ strands, the usual combinatorial formula (Rolfsen, Knots and Links, 1976, §5.D);

  • from the yarns themselves, as curves in space (yarn_linking()): the Gauss linking integral, summed exactly over pairs of straight segments as the solid angle each pair subtends (Klenin and Langowski, Computation of writhe in modeling of supercoiled DNA, Biopolymers 54, 307, 2000), after closing the yarns up round the outside (close_yarns()).

From the word, a positive generator is a positive crossing, the usual convention: σ₁² closes into a Hopf link of linking number +1. braidpy’s own drawing of a word in space (braidpy.parametric_strand.strand_paths(), a positive generator’s lower strand passing over towards +y, the braid rising along z) is its mirror image: yarns laid that way measure the opposite sign. Either way, what is compared — a braid laid, then settled — is measured the same way.

braidpy.linking.close_yarns(yarns: Sequence[ndarray], turn: float = 0.0, pairing: Sequence[int] | None = None, bottom_turn: float = 0.0, reach: float = 40.0) → list[ndarray]

A braid’s yarns closed up into its loops, round the outside.

Each yarn’s top end is turned back by turn — the turn of the plate holding the top ends, so the top ends are where they were laid again — then taken up above the braid, out to reach from the axis, down the outside and in, under the braid, to the bottom end it joins, turned back by bottom_turn. Each yarn rises and falls at heights of its own, so no two closing paths meet.

Parameters:

  • yarns – Each yarn’s centreline, (n, 3), bottom end first, the braid rising along z round the z axis.

  • turn – How far the top ends have turned since they were laid, in radians.

  • pairing – For each yarn, the yarn whose bottom end its top end joins; by default the one whose bottom end is nearest it in angle, the top end turned back.

  • bottom_turn – How far the bottom ends have turned.

  • reach – How far out the closing paths go: well clear of the braid.

Returns:

the yarns of each, in order, with their closing paths.

Return type:

One polygon per loop

Raises:

ValueError – If the top ends do not each find a bottom end of their own.

braidpy.linking.gauss_linking_number(first: ndarray, second: ndarray) → float

The linking number of two closed polygons, from their geometry.

The Gauss linking integral, summed exactly over every pair of edges as the solid angle the pair subtends (Klenin and Langowski, 2000, eq. 15 and 16). For two closed curves that do not meet it is a whole number; any difference from one measures how near they come to touching.

Parameters:

  • first – The first polygon’s corners, (n, 3); its last corner joins its first.

  • second – The second’s, (m, 3).

Returns:

The linking number.

braidpy.linking.linking_matrix(braid, repeats: int = 1) → ndarray

The linking numbers of a braid’s closure, from its word.

Each crossing between strands of two different loops adds half its sign to their linking number; crossings of a loop with itself add nothing.

The braid may be taken repeated: each repeat makes the same crossings at the same slots, between whichever strands the repeats before have brought there, so the word is read once however many times it is repeated. A home braid of a few hundred repeats of a long unit (braidpy.similarity.home()) is millions of crossings, and reading them one by one took a minute.

Parameters:

  • braid – A Braid.

  • repeats – How many times it is repeated before it is closed.

Returns:

A symmetric matrix of whole numbers, one row and column per loop, the loops in the order of braidpy.pure_braid.cycles() (by their first strand) of the braid repeated; zero on the diagonal.

braidpy.linking.yarn_linking(yarns: Sequence[ndarray], turn: float = 0.0, pairing: Sequence[int] | None = None, bottom_turn: float = 0.0) → dict[str, object]

The linking numbers of yarns’ closure, from their geometry.

Parameters:

  • yarns – Each yarn’s centreline, bottom end first; see close_yarns(), which takes the other arguments too.

  • turn – How far the top ends have turned.

  • pairing – Which bottom end each top end joins.

  • bottom_turn – How far the bottom ends have turned.

Returns:

components, how many loops; and links, the linking number of every pair of loops, (0, 1), (0, 2), … (1, 2), …, not rounded.

Comparing and cataloguing braids

Whether braids are alike, and the braids braidpy knows.

A braid word: its crossings in order, compared as such.

One braid has many words: σ₁σ₂σ₁ and σ₂σ₁σ₂ are two words and one braid. A word is the same word only crossing for crossing; for the same braid, compare braids (BraidWord.braid()).

Braids are the same in four ways, each its own type with its own == and hash — a word (BraidWord), a braid (Braid), a pattern (BraidPattern) and a closed braid (ClosedBraid): see docs/source/comparing_braids.md, Four kinds of “the same”.

A braid made over and over, compared as such: the same pattern however often it is repeated and wherever it is read from.

σ₁σ₂ and σ₂σ₁ are two braids and one pattern, the one read from the other’s second crossing; so are w and w w. A pattern and a closed braid (braidpy.closed_braid) are both coarser than a braid, but neither than the other: w and w w close into two links.

Braids are the same in four ways, each its own type with its own == and hash — a word (BraidWord), a braid (Braid), a pattern (BraidPattern) and a closed braid (ClosedBraid): see docs/source/comparing_braids.md, Four kinds of “the same”.

Bases: object

A braid made over and over: what is the same however often it is repeated and wherever it is read from.

Two patterns are equal when their braids, brought home (home()), are conjugate (same_pattern()): proven so, or proven not. Where the search would be too long (SuperSummitSetTooLarge), as for long braids of many strands, they are equal when their fingerprints are (same_fingerprint()), which proves only that they differ; proven() says which. A pattern hashes by its fingerprint, which two equal patterns share.

A braid closed, each strand’s end tied back to its own start: a knot or a link, compared as such.

It does not matter where the braid is read from, nor how many strands it is on (Markov’s theorem): σ₁ on two strands and a single strand close into one loop, two patterns (braidpy.braid_pattern) but one closed braid. Grommets and Turk’s heads are closed braids.

Braids are the same in four ways, each its own type with its own == and hash — a word (BraidWord), a braid (Braid), a pattern (BraidPattern) and a closed braid (ClosedBraid): see docs/source/comparing_braids.md, Four kinds of “the same”.

class braidpy.closed_braid.ClosedBraid(braid: Braid)

Bases: object

A braid closed: each strand’s end tied back to its own start, a knot or a link of several loops — a grommet, a Turk’s head.

It does not matter where the braid is read from, nor how many strands it is on (Markov’s theorem): σ₁ on two strands closes into one loop, as one strand does. Telling two knots apart is hard in general, and here two closed braids are equal when nothing measured tells them apart: the number of loops, the linking numbers of every two (linking_matrix()), sorted, and the Alexander polynomial (alexander_polynomial()). Equal so is not proven the same — a knot and its mirror image are equal so — but different is proven different.

Parameters:

braid – The braid closed.

braid: Braid
property loops: int

one for a knot.

Type:

How many loops it closes into

key() → tuple[Any, ...]

What it is measured by: its loops, their linking numbers sorted, and the coefficients of its Alexander polynomial.

Braids compared by what does not depend on how they are written down.

The same braid can be written many ways: from another starting point, with far crossings swapped, made of more or fewer repeats. What does not change is its topology, and a few numbers measure it. A braid’s fingerprint() holds them; similar() ranks other braids by how far their fingerprints are from it — to suggest, for a braid of your own, the braids it is most like.

The fingerprint is of the braid’s pattern, not of its length: the word’s repeating_unit(), and that unit repeated until every strand is back where it started (home()), which closes each strand into a loop of its own. It holds:

  • n_strands;

  • loops: how the unit takes the strands round — the sizes of the loops its closure makes, largest first (braidpy.pure_braid.cycles());

  • writhe: the unit’s crossings counted with their signs. It tells a braid from its mirror image, which the others do not;

  • linking: how many times each two strands wind round each other in a repeat, as linking numbers of the home braid’s loops (braidpy.linking.linking_matrix()), sorted, so that it does not matter which strand is which;

  • alexander: the Alexander polynomial of the home braid’s closure, sampled on the unit circle (braidpy.properties.alexander_on_circle()). It tells apart braids the linking numbers cannot: a plait from strands hanging straight, both with all their linking numbers 0.

  • burau: the characteristic polynomial of the home braid’s Burau matrix, sampled on the unit circle (braidpy.properties.burau_polynomial_on_circle()). It tells apart braids whose Alexander polynomial vanishes, as it does for many braids closing into several loops: a kumihimo disk’s edo yatsu from Ashley’s 8-strand square sinnet, ABOK #3070, which agree on all the rest.

  • burau_mod: that characteristic polynomial again, exactly, modulo a prime at a few values of t (braidpy.properties.burau_polynomial_mod()). The samples above are in floating point, which a long braid rounds differently for each way it is written; they say how near two braids are (distance()), this says whether they are the same (same_fingerprint()). It holds the Alexander polynomial too, as its value at 1.

None of these changes when a braid is read from another starting point (conjugation), and the loops, linking numbers and Alexander and Burau polynomials do not change either when the strands are numbered otherwise. Equal fingerprints do not prove two braids the same — no handful of invariants can — but different ones prove them different. braidpy.conjugacy.same_pattern() proves either way, more slowly; braidpy.braid_pattern.BraidPattern is a braid compared so.

Whether two braids are the same braid however written: a proof, not a fingerprint.

Two words make the same braid, read from any starting point, when one is a conjugate of the other: b = c⁻¹ a c for some braid c. Fingerprints (braidpy.similarity) prove braids different but never the same. This decides it, by Garside’s method as Elrifai–Morton and Franco–González- Meneses made it practical:

  • every braid is written once in left normal form, Δ^p · A_1 ⋯ A_r (braidpy.garside_canonical_form.artin_left_normal_form());

  • cycling and decycling — taking A_1 round to the end, or A_r round to the front — are conjugations, and repeated they raise p and lower p + r as far as any conjugate allows: to the braid’s super summit set, the conjugates with p greatest and p + r least;

  • that set is finite, and each of its braids leads to the others by conjugating with the least permutation braids that keep it there, one for each crossing σ_i (minimal simple elements); so it is found whole by following them;

  • two braids are conjugate exactly when their super summit sets are the same, and so when one holds a braid of the other’s.

same_pattern() asks this of two braids’ patterns, their home() braids. Strands numbered from the other side, σ_i read as σ_{n-i}, need no asking: that is conjugation by Δ. The set can be large — exponential in the number of strands at worst — so the search stops at limit braids and says it could not tell.

A permutation braid is kept as in braidpy.garside_canonical_form: a tuple p, p[j] the place strand j ends at; a product is read left to right.

exception braidpy.conjugacy.SuperSummitSetTooLarge

Bases: Exception

The super summit set has more braids than the search was let find.

True if they are conjugate, False if not.

SuperSummitSetTooLarge – if it cannot tell within limit braids.

braidpy.conjugacy.same_braid(a: Braid, b: Braid, limit: int | None = 10000) → bool

Whether two braids are the same pattern, made over and over, however written: their patterns (home()) conjugate. Not whether they are the same braid, which Braid.__eq__ tells: σ₁σ₂ and σ₂σ₁ are one pattern and two braids (braidpy.braid_pattern).

Home braids repeated as often are conjugate exactly when their units are, a braid’s roots being unique up to conjugacy (González-Meneses): so then the units are compared, far shorter. And braids whose fingerprints differ (same_fingerprint()) are different already: no search is made.

Parameters:

  • a – A braid.

  • b – Another.

  • limit – The most braids of a super summit set to find.

Returns:

True if they are proven the same, False if proven not.

Raises:

SuperSummitSetTooLarge – if it cannot tell within limit braids.

Braids by their topology, and the ways each is made.

Every other catalogue lists braids by how they are made: as a braid word (braidpy.braid_catalog), on a kumihimo disk (braidpy.mobidai_catalog), as one of Ashley’s solid sinnets (braidpy.solid_sinnets_catalog), on a braiding machine (braidpy.machine_catalog). Different ways can make the same braid: the plait is a braid word, Ashley’s #2965 on his stand, and what a three-carrier flat braiding machine makes. This catalogue lists braids by what they are — their fingerprint() — each pointing to every way of making it, and each way pointing back (topology_of()). For a braid of your own, related() gives the topologies nearest it.

A way of making a braid is a Method: a source and an entry of its catalogue, with the description Braid Studio makes it from (braidpy.web.build()). Its braid word is the one braidpy reads off it, over a whole period: for a disk braid that creeps round the disk from cycle to cycle, as kongo gumi does, as many cycles as bring every strand home. A machine braiding round cores has its cores in its word, each a strand standing still (braidpy.horn_gear.word).

Building the catalogue makes every braid of every catalogue — some ten seconds — so it is built once, when first asked for (catalog()). Braid Studio has it built with the site: export() writes it as JSON, load() reads it back, and for_page() says, for the braid on the page, every other way of making it and the braids nearest it.

What every catalogue of braids in braidpy has in common.

Each catalogue — braidpy.braid_catalog (braid words), braidpy.mobidai_catalog (kumihimo disk braids), braidpy.solid_sinnets_catalog (Ashley’s solid sinnets) and braidpy.machine_catalog (braiding machines) — keeps its braids as it likes best, and lists them in a CATALOG: an Entry per braid, by the name it is known by, in the order to offer them.

A site built from braidpy can add braids of its own to a catalogue without braidpy knowing them (extended()): a package of the site’s names, in the entry point group GROUP, a CATALOG to add to one of braidpy’s, by that catalogue’s module name (docs: A site of your own).

braidpy.braid_catalog.flat3(draw: bool = True) → tuple[Braid, int]

Basic braid with 3 strands going above central braid

ABOK 2965: “FLAT, ENGLISH, ORDINARY or COMMON SINNET is the plat or braid seen in schoolgirl pigtails. It is made of three strands and is the simplest possible plat. To make: Secure three strands together and make the end fast to a hook or nail. Hold two strands in the right hand and one in the left. Bring the outer right strand down across its sister strand and lay it parallel to and below the single left strand. Now bring the upper Ie ft strand down across its sister strand and lay it parallel to and below the single right strand. Repeat alternately”

Parameters:

draw – Draw the braid as it is made (the default); False only builds it.

the braid object describing the single step to realize the braid n: the number of iterations to get back to initial order of strands

braidpy.braid_catalog.square4(draw: bool = True) → tuple[Braid, int]

Basic round braid with 4 strands

ABOK 2999. “SQUARE SINNET of four strands. Used for lanyards, whips, whiplashes, quirts and leashes. With strands of two colors, arranged as pictured, the two colors helix around the sinnet, giving a barber-pole or candy-twist effect. The sinnet is made in two movements. First, take the top left strand, bring it around to the back of the other strands and then from back to front between the opposing strands. Finally lay it beside its sister strand into the lower position at the left. Second, take the right upper strand, bring it around to the back of the other strands and then from back to front between the opposing strands. Finally lay it beside its sister strand into the lower position at the right. In this size, this sinnet, although made by the SQUARE SINNET method, is identical with ROUND SINNET of four strands.”

class braidpy.braid_catalog.AshleyPlat(shape: str, n_strands: int, n_left: int, leads: tuple[str, ...], method: Literal['plat', 'square'] = 'plat', first: Literal['left', 'right'] = 'left')

Bases: object

A sinnet plaited in the hands as The Ashley Book of Knots says, its strands held in two groups, the top strand of each led in turn.

Two ways of leading a strand, as the book’s plat sinnets have them:

  • "plat" (#2976–#2998, and Smith’s square sinnets #3017–#3019): the top strand is led to the centre, over and under its sisters as its path says, and joins the other group, lowest in it;

  • "square" (the square sinnet’s method, #2999–#3014): the top strand goes round behind its sisters and behind the opposing strands, comes forward between two of them — its path as long as the opposing strands it passed, counted from the bottom — and comes back along its path, over and under them, to lie lowest in its own group.

The strands are numbered from the left, the left group first; a strand led over its neighbour to the right is σᵢ, as everywhere in braidpy.

Parameters:

  • shape – What the book calls it: “flat”, “French”, “square”…

  • n_strands – Strands.

  • n_left – Strands held in the left hand at the start.

  • leads – Each lead’s path, the left group’s top strand first unless first says otherwise, then the right’s, in turn.

  • method – How a strand is led.

  • first – The group whose strand is led first.

shape: str
n_strands: int
n_left: int
leads: tuple[str, ...]
method: Literal['plat', 'square'] = 'plat'
first: Literal['left', 'right'] = 'left'
braid() → Braid

The braid of one round of the leads.

Returns:

The braid.

Raises:

ValueError – If a lead passes more strands than it can, or the groups are not as they started after the round.

The plat sinnets of The Ashley Book of Knots (chapter 38) made as its text says, by number. Left out: those of doubled strands (#2972, #2978, coachwhipping #3015, #3016), the “trick” sinnet #2993, #2979 (#2976 made another way, the same braid), and the round sinnets worked turning in the hand (#3021 on), which are ring words.

braidpy.braid_catalog.RECTANGULAR_14 = '2 -5 -9 7 -11 -3 13 1 -6 10 -8 4 -4 -10 -7 -12 -2 4 7 10 5 9 -7 -13 -1 11 3 -10 -4 6 8 12'

The rectangular braid of fourteen strands, as the word it repeats.

The fourteen places fall into two sets of seven that never mix: the word’s permutation is two 7-cycles, so seven repeats bring every strand home. The sets interleave across the face, one place of the first, then two of the second, then two of the first: ABBAABBAABBAAB. Thirty-two crossings a repeat, as many one way as the other, so nothing twists.

braidpy.braid_catalog.RECTANGULAR_20 = '2 19 -4 -16 1 -10 -9 -11 10 3 17 -5 -15 -6 -14 -4 -16 -8 -12 5 15 -3 -17 9 11 -2 6 14 -18 7 13 -6 -14 17 3 8 12 7 13 -12 -1 -8 -19 5 15 18'

The rectangular braid of twenty strands, as the word it repeats.

Forty-six crossings a repeat, as many one way as the other, and every one of the nineteen crossing places used. The twenty places fall into two sets of ten that never mix — the word’s permutation is two 10-cycles — so ten repeats bring every strand home. Wider than RECTANGULAR_14 and not a wider copy of it: the sets interleave as ABBABAABABBABAABABBA, in threes and pairs rather than evenly.

mobidai.py

A simulator for the traditional Japanese braiding stand (Marudai / Mobidai). Sometimes known as friendship disk and used for kumihimo braiding.

This module provides classes to model, simulate, and visualize the braiding process, based on configurations of slots, strands, and moves. It also includes topological tracking to extract the Artin Braid Group word associated with the braiding moves.

braidpy.mobidai.cycle_drift(start_slots: list[int], moves: list[Move], n_slots: int, n_shift_after_cycle: int = 0) → int

How many slots round a cycle leaves the strands from where they began.

Many braids do not bring their strands back to the slots they started in, but to the same arrangement one or more slots round — kongo gumi creeps one slot back each cycle — and the braider simply makes the same moves again from where the strands now are. That shift is a property of the cycle, so it is read off it rather than written down: one cycle is made, and the occupied slots compared with the starting ones turned round.

Parameters:

  • start_slots – The slots holding a strand at the start.

  • moves – One cycle’s moves.

  • n_slots – Slots round the disk.

  • n_shift_after_cycle – How far the disk is turned after the moves.

Returns:

The drift, the smallest turn that matches; 0 if the cycle does not bring the strands back to their arrangement at all.

mobidai_catalog.py

Kumihimo braids transcribed from Bracelets Kumihimo, technique des bracelets japonais by Agnès Delage-Calvet, and braids shared by Richard Buenger in the Kumihimo group on Facebook (each entry says which).

Each entry carries everything a Mobidai needs: how many slots the disk has, which colour starts in which slot, the moves of one cycle, and how far the disk is turned before the cycle repeats. Call CatalogedMobidai.to_config() to run one. CATALOG lists them, as every catalogue does (braidpy.catalog).

disk_animation.py

A braiding disk, animated as the braider sees it: from above.

Each strand runs from its slot on the rim in to the middle, where the braid goes down through the hole — so it is drawn as a radial line from the centre to its carrier. The carriers move continuously, step by step, along the paths disk_trajectories() gives them, so this is the same motion the braid is laid from, and what is seen here is what lay_yarns() builds on.

A strand lifted over the others passes inside the rim — over, seen from above — and is drawn on top of them while it does, so the picture says which way every crossing goes.

animate_kumihimo() and animate_mobidai() read their sources onto a disk and animate it; animate_disk() does the drawing for any disk.

class braidpy.disk_animation.BraidGrowth(start, steps, n_slots: int, yarn_diameter: float = 0.12, clockwise: bool = True, take_off_per_row: float = 1.5, window_rows: float = 12, iterations: int = 300, samples_per_row: int = 12, shown_per_row: int = 4)

Bases: object

The braid a disk is making, as it grows below it — for a side view.

The braid is laid once, from its crossings round a ring and tightened (see disk_braid()), and shown as the disk is worked: each crossing reaches the fell, just under the disk, as the strand making it passes the one it crosses on the disk, the older rows carried down by the take-off. Rows are made in the order their crossings are, so nothing shows below the disk before it is made on it. The braid hangs from the disk and turns with it. Only the last window_rows rows are shown, as a braider sees the length of braid nearest the disk.

Parameters:

  • start – Each strand’s slot, 1-based.

  • steps – Per step, the strands that move and by how many slots.

  • n_slots – Slots round the disk.

  • yarn_diameter – Yarn diameter.

  • clockwise – Whether slot numbers go round clockwise, seen from above.

  • take_off_per_row – Braid taken off per row of crossings, in diameters.

  • window_rows – Rows of braid shown below the fell.

  • iterations – Tightening steps.

  • samples_per_row – Points along each yarn per row, as tightened: fewer and the tightening can snap a yarn across its neighbour.

  • shown_per_row – Points along each yarn per row, as drawn.

Raises:

ValueError – If the moves cross no strands: there is no braid.

Ashley disk braid visualizer.

Renders an annulus partitioned into sectors. Strands in each sector lie on a common circle and are ordered counterclockwise. Each frame shows the state before a move, optional arrows for the active move path, and the final state. Optionally builds an animated GIF.

According to ABOK3036 “All odd strands, when they are moved, are led to the right, counterclockwise; all even strands are led. to the left, clock- wise. The earliest strand to occupy any space is always the next one to be moved from that space. The earliest odd-numbered strand is always the right-hand strand of its group; when it is moved it is led to the right, counterclockwise, until it reaches its destination, where it is put into the near or left-hand position of an odd-numbered space. At an even-numbered space the left strand of the group is moved to the left (clockwise) until it reaches its destination, where it is put into the right-hand position. The two ways of moving strands are indicated with arrows in diagram fIi 304 I. All strands are moved “over alL” If, however, an odd strand is led to an even-numhered space, as is sometimes the case, it passes to the right as it lea … ~s the odd space but is carried to the right side of the even-numbered space when it arrives. If a strand from an even-numbered space is led to an odd-numbered space, it is moved to the left but is placed at the left side of the odd-numbered space.”

Requirements:

matplotlib imageio (optional, for GIF)

class braidpy.ashley_solid_sinnet.AshleySolidSinnet(initial_counts_per_space: list[int], moves: list[tuple[int, int]], shape: str | None = None, all_right: bool = False)

Bases: object

Ashley-style braid pattern.

Spaces are numbered anticlockwise, seen from above, from the left of the disk as the book draws it. A strand is moved over all the strands it passes: from an odd space its right-hand strand, anticlockwise; from an even space its left-hand strand, clockwise. It goes in at the left (clockwise) end of an odd space and at the right (anticlockwise) end of an even one, so the earliest strand in a space is always the next to leave it. When all_right, as the book has it for “All strands move to the right”, the strand from an even space is led anticlockwise too, still from its left and over all.

Variables:

  • initial_counts_per_space (List[int]) – Number of strands per sector. 1-based sectors.

  • moves (List[Tuple[int, int]]) – Sequence of (from_sector, to_sector) moves, each 1-based.

  • shape (Optional[str]) – The cross-section the sinnet takes when made, as the book names it: “round”, “triangle”, “hexagon”…

  • all_right (bool) – Every strand is led to the right, anticlockwise, not only those from odd spaces. The same table makes another braid so: #3057 and #3058 differ only in this.

class braidpy.ashley_solid_sinnet.SinnetDisk(n_spaces: int, slots_per_space: int, start: dict[Hashable, int], steps: list[dict[Hashable, int]], labels: list[str])

Bases: object

A sinnet set out on a disk with a slot for every place a strand stops.

Each space has slots_per_space slots side by side, its strands kept together in the middle of them. Slots are numbered anticlockwise, as the spaces are, from the clockwise end of space 1.

Variables:

  • n_spaces (int) – Spaces round the disk.

  • slots_per_space (int) – Slots in each.

  • start (dict[collections.abc.Hashable, int]) – Each strand’s slot. Strands are numbered from 1, space by space and anticlockwise within one, as init_spaces_from_counts().

  • steps (list[dict[collections.abc.Hashable, int]]) – The strand each step moves, and by how many slots: a move, over everything it passes, or a few strands sliding along together in a space, over nothing.

  • labels (list[str]) – What each step is.

n_spaces: int
slots_per_space: int
start: dict[Hashable, int]
steps: list[dict[Hashable, int]]
labels: list[str]
property n_slots: int

The disk’s slots, every space’s.

middle_slot(space: int) → int

The slot in the middle of a space, where its number is written.

property slot_offset: float

How far round the numbering is turned to draw it as the book does: space 1 starting on the left, anticlockwise from there.

braidpy.ashley_solid_sinnet.sinnet_disk(sinnet: AshleySolidSinnet, n_cycles: int = 1) → SinnetDisk

Work a sinnet on a disk, following every strand.

Each move takes the earliest strand of its space — the right-hand one of an odd space, the left-hand one of an even space — round the disk over every strand it passes, the way AshleySolidSinnet.goes_right() says, into its place at the end of the space it goes to. The strands left behind, and those it joins, then slide along together to the middle of their spaces, so each space always has room either side of its strands.

Parameters:

  • sinnet – The sinnet.

  • n_cycles – How many times its moves are made.

Returns:

The disk, and the steps that work it.

Raises:

ValueError – If a move is from or to a space that is not there, or from a space to itself.

braidpy.ashley_solid_sinnet.sinnet_to_mobidai(sinnet: AshleySolidSinnet) → MobidaiConfig

One cycle of a sinnet as a kumihimo disk (mobidai) pattern.

The disk of sinnet_disk(), numbered as a mobidai is, every move made from slot to slot the way the sinnet goes round — anticlockwise from an odd space, clockwise from an even one, unless all go to the right — and every slide made one strand at a time, the front one first. A sinnet whose cycle brings each space back to its count brings every slot back too, so the pattern is simply repeated.

Parameters:

sinnet – The sinnet.

Returns:

The pattern.

braidpy.ashley_solid_sinnet.strand_colors(n: int) → list[str]

A colour per strand, evenly round the hue circle.

braidpy.ashley_solid_sinnet.init_spaces_from_counts(counts: list[int]) → dict[int, list[int]]

Build the mapping sector -> strand IDs from counts.

Strand IDs are assigned contiguously starting at 1, scanning sectors in ascending order.

Parameters:

counts (List[int]) – Number of strands in each sector, length = n_sectors.

Returns:

Mapping from sector index (1-based) to list of strand IDs.

Return type:

Dict[int, List[int]]

braidpy.ashley_solid_sinnet.flatten_spaces(spaces: dict[int, list[int]]) → list[int]

Flatten the strands from all spaces into a single list in order of space index.

Parameters:

spaces (Dict[int, List[int]]) – Space-to-strand mapping.

Returns:

Flattened list of strand IDs.

Return type:

List[int]

braidpy.ashley_solid_sinnet.ashley_single_move_to_artin(counts: list[int], from_space: int, to_space: int) → tuple[list[int], list[int]]

Apply one Ashley move and return updated counts and the Artin braid word segment.

The direction is determined by the parity of from_space: odd moves right (anticlockwise, increasing sector index), even moves left (clockwise). Wrap-around crosses all other strands in the appropriate Artin order.

Note

This function updates only the per-sector counts. It reconstructs strand IDs from counts at each step, so IDs are not persistent across moves. The output braid word is computed according to the provided logic but the visualizer uses counts only.

Parameters:

  • counts (List[int]) – Current number of strands per sector.

  • from_space (int) – 1-based starting sector index.

  • to_space (int) – 1-based destination sector index.

Returns:

Updated counts after the move, and the list of signed Artin σ generators produced during this move.

Return type:

Tuple[List[int], List[int]]

braidpy.ashley_solid_sinnet.ashley_to_artin_exact(counts: list[int], moves: dict[int, int] | Sequence[tuple[int, int]]) → tuple[list[int], list[int]]

Convert an Ashley-style braid (sinnet) into an exact Artin braid word.

Ashley braids are described in the Ashley book of knots

The word is read anticlockwise, and counts a strand moved over, seen from above, as a positive crossing: the mirror image, read from the other side, of AshleySolidSinnet.braid(), which reads the braid as braidpy draws one. The two are the same braid.

This function simulates each strand’s movement: - Handles wrap-around moves by crossing all other strands in reverse order. - Records crossings in correct Artin σ notation. - Handles parity-based insertion into the destination space.

Parameters:

  • counts (List[int]) – List of strand counts for each space.

  • moves – (source, destination) spaces, in order. A mapping from source to destination is also read, but cannot hold two moves from one space.

Returns:

  • List of Artin σ generators as signed int.

  • Final mapping of spaces to strands.

Return type:

Tuple[List[int], List[int]]

braidpy.ashley_solid_sinnet.visualize_sinnet(initial_counts: list[int], moves: list[tuple[int, int]], out_dir: str = 'ashley_viz', prefix: str = 'step', make_gif: bool = True, gif_name: str = 'animation.gif', show_ids: bool = True, r_strand_circle: float = 0.75, arc_pad_frac: float = 0.12) → dict[str, list[str] | str]

Render an Ashley sinnet into step images and an optional GIF.

See AshleySolidSinnet.animate() for an animation that follows every strand, and the braid growing beside it.

This function draws an initial frame, then a frame per move showing the path between sectors, then a final frame after all moves. Each strand ID gets a consistent color derived from matplotlib.cm.tab20.

Note

Colors are assigned by global strand ID computed from initial_counts. Since IDs are reconstructed from counts at each step, IDs are not persistent across moves. If persistent identity is required, use a stateful mapping and explicit crossing simulation.

Parameters:

  • initial_counts (List[int]) – Initial counts per sector.

  • moves (List[Tuple[int, int]]) – List of (from_sector, to_sector) moves, 1-based.

  • out_dir (str) – Output directory for saved frames and GIF.

  • prefix (str) – Filename prefix for step images.

  • make_gif (bool) – If True and imageio is available, save an animated GIF.

  • gif_name (str) – Filename for the GIF inside out_dir.

  • show_ids (bool) – If True, draw numeric IDs over dots.

  • r_strand_circle (float) – Radius of the strand circle inside the annulus.

  • arc_pad_frac (float) – Trim near sector borders to avoid overlaps.

Returns:

Dictionary containing:

  • ”frames”: List[str]. Paths to saved PNG frames.

  • ”final”: str. Path to the final frame.

  • ”gif”: str. Path to the saved GIF, or a message if skipped.

Return type:

Dict[str, List[str] | str]

A disk braid made as on a marudai: move by move, each moved yarn laid over the others and drawn tight, the braid turning to balance.

web/marudai.js, which Braid Studio runs in the browser, in Python: the same algorithm, step for step, in the same order (tests/test_marudai_python.py runs both and compares them). The method is braid3dmin’s, a kumihimo simulation in three.js; docs/source/marudai.md describes it as done here. The code is this project’s own. In short:

  • Each yarn is a chain of beads a unit apart, two units thick. A link pulls its beads together only when stretched, as a rope does; two beads less than two units apart push each other away.

  • Each yarn’s end is drawn towards its carrier, out on the rim and above the braid’s tip, by a constant pull: its bobbin.

  • A move lays the yarn’s end over the top of everything on its way to its new carrier, then draws the new stretch tight as a string would go: each bead to between its neighbours, or round a yarn in the way.

  • The braid then relaxes from what moved: a bead at a time, each moved by its forces, its neighbours and the beads near it then queued, with steps shrinking until the queue dies down.

  • Hanging free, the braid turns until its yarns’ ends pull it no way round.

  • Well behind a yarn’s end, the braid is made: frozen.

  • A core, if there is one, rises up the braid’s axis, past the carriers: a yarn pulled straight up, or rigid, held where it stands. A yarn’s move passes beside it, on the side it goes round — a move of more than nine tenths of a half turn is made in two — and is drawn tight round it. The braid turns about it.

Inside, lengths are in units of half a yarn diameter, y up, as the method was given; what make() returns is in yarn diameters, z up.

It follows the JavaScript step for step: JavaScript’s rounding to whole numbers (_round()), its floating-point random numbers (Machine._shuffle), and the order beads are found and woken in (the grid of cells as linked lists, and bead numbers reused as the JavaScript reuses them). Given the same numbers from the maths library, it makes the same braid bead for bead. The libraries themselves differ in the last place — Python’s math.hypot is correctly rounded, JavaScript’s Math.hypot not always — and thousands of relaxation steps make that visible, as they would any change: the two braids are alike, not identical. It is pure Python and slow — tens of times slower than in a browser — which suits checking it, not making long braids.

While the bobbins turn round the braid together: held, the yarns carried round with them rather than over each other, and not balanced; then as before again (hold in web/marudai.js).

Thread t’s end goes to the carrier at angle to: up over what lies on its way, then out to the rim, then drawn tight. Carried round with the others, not over them, it goes straight out to the rim, passing nobody.

Let the braid relax from what moved, then trim, find its tip, balance it, and forget the made braid far below.

The whole braid turned by f about the vertical through (ax, az).

The bobbins carried round by f together, the braid held: each yarn’s free part turns with them about the axis, all of it at its carrier and none of it at the braid’s tip, twisting the yarns in.

The yarns tied together where the braid begins: round a ring, as the method has it, for as many as it was made for; more, and the ring would be so wide the yarns rose from it as a tube, never drawn in to a braid. So then rings of at most RING, one under the other, the yarns taken in turn round the disk.

horn_gear/__init__.py

Horn gear braiding machine simulator.

A braiding machine is described as a graph of connected horn gears. Each gear has N slots and the bobbins (carriers) travel between gears as the gears turn.

BraidingMachine covers machines whose gears are geared together, where the carriers follow closed tracks fixed by the wiring. JacquardLaceMachine covers machines whose gears are driven one by one from a punched programme, where they do not. Both are laid out, simulated and drawn by the same code.

yarn_paths() follows the carriers through a run and lays their yarns off along the machine’s axis, with no tension yet, and visualize_yarns() draws the result in 3D standing on the machine.

horn_gear/model.py

Data model for a horn gear braiding machine.

A machine is a graph of HornGear nodes connected by Connection edges.

A connection is a fixed point in space where two gears meet. As a gear turns, a different slot arrives there; Connection.slot_a0/slot_b0 record which slot of each gear sits there at t=0.

BraidingMachine describes a machine whose gears are geared together: every gear turns one slot every step, each slot belongs to one gear, and a carrier crosses to its neighbour when its slot reaches a contact. A machine built differently says so by overriding a handful of methods — turning_gears(), rotation(), next_position() and their neighbours — and the rest of the package needs no special case. See JacquardLaceMachine.

class braidpy.horn_gear.model.Connection(gear_a: str, gear_b: str, slot_a0: int, slot_b0: int, name: str | None = None, phase: float = 0.0)

Bases: object

A transfer point between two gears.

At each simulation step the slot of gear_a that is currently at the connection angle and the slot of gear_b that is currently at the connection angle are computed. A carrier sitting in the gear_a slot transfers to gear_b (and vice-versa).

A contact hands over at the end of each step, when every gear’s slots are back on slot angles. One between two split gears, whose horns meet there once a horn’s pitch, as often as their parts in a step, hands over at phase, a fraction of the way through each step: the parts’ first pairing at 0, their second a step’s 1/k on, and so on, all at the one contact (described). A step then holds k ticks, each a pitch of the split gears, and a hand-over at each.

Parameters:

  • gear_a – Name of the first gear.

  • gear_b – Name of the second gear.

  • slot_a0 – Slot index of gear_a at the connection point at t=phase.

  • slot_b0 – Slot index of gear_b at the connection point at t=phase.

  • name – Optional label for this connection.

  • phase – How far through each step it hands over, from 0 (at the step’s end, as every contact of whole gears) to below 1.

class braidpy.horn_gear.model.Axial(name: str, anchor: tuple[str, ...])

Bases: object

A yarn fed straight down a fixed column, never carried by a gear.

Braiding carriers travel around an axial; the axial itself does not move, holds no slot, and has no track. It is therefore not a carrier and takes no part in stepping, tracks or collision detection — it is a fixed point that the braid forms around.

The column stands at the centroid of the gears it is anchored to, which covers both ways a machine carries one:

  • anchor=("B",) — one gear, so the column is that gear’s own centre, as an axial yarn fed up through a hollow horn gear spindle. This is the 0° reinforcement of a triaxial braid, and the cord of a soutache.

  • anchor=("A", "B", "C", "D") — the ring of gears around a hole, so the column is the centre of the tube they braid, as a rope core or a mandrel. tube_rings() finds these rings for you.

Parameters:

  • name – Unique identifier for this axial.

  • anchor – Names of the gears whose centroid the column stands at.

name: str
anchor: tuple[str, ...]

gear_radii() draws a gear as large as the square root of its horn count, which is a convention and no more: horn gears do not roll on one another – each is driven from below – so a radius is free where a slot count is not.
