A machine whose gears share their slots overrides this, because there the receiving gear does the sweeping: see riding_position().

A contact handing over during the step (Connection’s phase) has the carrier drawn on the neighbour from then on.

A horn gear machine written as its graph: which gears mesh with which.

A machine is gears that mesh, so it can be written as the pairs that do: A-B B-C C-D D-A is four gears in a ring, A-B two side by side. A gear’s name is any run of letters, digits and underscores (B, g2, left): no name has to come first. A gear may be given its own number of slots, A:6, anywhere it is named; the others have as many as machine_from_graph()’s n_slots, 4 unless given (Braid Studio’s Slots per gear).

A split gear — gears on one axle, turning as one, their horns taking turns round it, each meeting only its own neighbours, so that the bands they serve never exchange a carrier (multiband) — is written as its parts, each a gear in the pairs, joined on their axle: A-B1 B2-C B1+B2 is the twin plait, its middle gear of six horns split in two. A gear may be split in more parts, H1+H2+H3, its parts as many slots each; and split gears may be anywhere in the graph.

Two split gears may mesh more than once, a band to each pairing of their parts: A1-B1 A2-B2 A1+A2 B1+B2 is two bands side by side, each on its own pair of halves, and neither can reach the other. What may not happen is one part meeting one axle twice – a carrier of that band could then leave by either contact, which is the split undone – so a whole gear meshing with both parts of a split one (A-B1 A-B2 B1+B2) is refused. The two axles touch, at one contact. A horn of each comes round to it once a horn’s pitch, as often in a step as each has parts, the parts in turn: the pairing named first hands over there at the end of each step, the next a 1/k step on, and so on (a step of k ticks, a hand-over at each; Connection’s phase). The bands so share the one contact without their carriers meeting. Turning opposite ways, the two axles bring their parts round in opposite orders, which for parts in three or more the pairings named have to follow.

The rest follows from the graph:

  • Two gears that mesh turn opposite ways, so each gear’s direction is the graph’s two colours, the first gear named turning anticlockwise, a split gear’s parts all one way. A ring of an odd number of gears cannot turn at all, and is refused. Which gear is named first is all the order of the pairs says: A-B B-C and B-C A-B turn their gears opposite ways.

  • A ring is laid out clockwise, seen from above, from the gear whose name sorts first towards its neighbour whose name sorts first (compute_layout()): A-B B-C C-D D-A and A-D D-C C-B B-A are one machine, A, B, C and D clockwise round it, whichever way the pairs are written. Names that sort otherwise lay it the other way round.

  • Where the gears stand is where the layout puts them (compute_layout(), from the graph and the gears’ sizes alone, a split gear’s parts at one centre, as large as the whole); in a tree of gears, each neighbour of a split gear’s part where a horn of that part comes round.

  • Each gear’s contacts are where the layout puts them, if whole slots can say so, and otherwise as evenly spread as its slots allow, in the order the layout puts them, its first contact named at slot 0.

Where it feeds axial yarns is written as the places, B up a gear’s spindle or A-B-C-D down the hole of a ring of gears (read_axials()); the carriers it starts with, if it is not to load itself, as A:0 B:2 (read_loading()). The catalogue’s machines are written so (braidpy.horn_gear.examples).

graph_of() writes a machine back as its graph, axials_of() and loading_of() its axials and a loading. A machine written so and read again is the same machine, its slots perhaps numbered from another one round.

horn_gear/layout.py

Where everything sits: gear centres, the notches between them, the circles a carrier rides on, and the columns a braid forms around.

Gears are placed from the connection graph — BFS along the x-axis for a chain, Kamada-Kawai relaxed till every two gears that mesh touch for anything with a cycle (ring_geometry()) — unless the machine pins its own geometry, in which case preferred_layout() wins. Gear radius goes as sqrt(n_slots), which is a drawing convention and not a mechanical one — see _gear_radius().

Everything else here is derived from those centres: where two gears meet (contact_point()), how far out a carrier rides (carrier_radius()), how each gear must be turned for its slots to face its notches (slot_offsets()), by how much that fails where a line of gears bends (offset_residuals()), and how the slots are drawn so that carriers are handed on without jumping all the same (slot_angles()). It is all plain geometry with no drawing in it, so it can be measured and tested directly.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.compute_layout(machine: BraidingMachine, scale: float = 1.0, seed: int | None = 42, iterations: int = 500) → dict[str, tuple[float, float]]

Compute 2-D positions for all gears with adjacent circles exactly tangential.

For tree / path graphs (flat braid): BFS-based placement along the x-axis guarantees every pair of adjacent gear circles touches exactly.

For cyclic graphs (a tubular braider’s ring, a matrix of gears): ring_geometry(), which also sizes the gears so that they touch.

Parameters:

  • machine – The BraidingMachine whose gears to position.

  • scale – Overall scale factor for gear radii.

  • seed – Random seed for reproducibility (cyclic graphs only).

  • iterations – Spring-layout iterations (cyclic fallback only).

Returns:

Dict mapping gear name → (x, y) in layout coordinates.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.ring_geometry(machine: BraidingMachine, scale: float = 1.0, seed: int | None = 42, iterations: int = 500) → tuple[dict[str, tuple[float, float]], dict[str, float]]

Where the gears of a machine with a ring of gears stand, and how large they are drawn, so that every two that mesh touch and no two others overlap.

Kamada-Kawai lays the graph out with each mesh as long as the two radii, which it can do exactly for one ring of gears alike, as a tubular braider is. Where it cannot, as in a matrix of gears of several sizes, its compromise is relaxed (_relax()): the gears that mesh are drawn to touch, moving their centres and, within RADIUS_RANGE, their sizes; those that do not are pushed apart, past touching. Not an exact solution, but no gear runs through another, nor does a carrier through another’s path. A layout that is right already is kept as it is.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine; its graph has a cycle.

  • scale – Overall scale for the radii.

  • seed – Random seed for the spring layout, the fallback.

  • iterations – Iterations of the spring layout.

Returns:

Gear name → centre, and gear name → radius.

class braidpy.horn_gear.layout.RingContacts(first: ndarray, second: ndarray, turns: ndarray, part_first: ndarray, part_second: ndarray, weight: ndarray, timer_first: ndarray | None = None, timer_second: ndarray | None = None, n_timers: int | None = None, apart: tuple[tuple[int, int, float], ...] = ())

Bases: object

When a ring’s contacts come round, for time_ring(): one entry a contact, between gear first and gear second (indices).

A gear of n slots a part, turning d (+1 anticlockwise) and turned psi to start with, brings its part p of k to a contact at angle alpha at the times t with d n (alpha - psi) / 2 pi - d p / k = t (mod 1). Written with the gear’s start x = d n psi / 2 pi, that is turns * alpha - x - part = t.

Each start is a timer’s: by default each gear’s, its parts a fixed share of a step apart; or, with timer_first and timer_second, one of n_timers, so that the parts of a split gear, stacked on one axle, each start where they are set, as their horn plates are when the machine is assembled (part then 0).

Variables:

  • first (numpy.ndarray) – Each contact’s first gear.

  • second (numpy.ndarray) – Its second gear.

  • turns (numpy.ndarray) – d n / 2 pi of each gear, by index.

  • part_first (numpy.ndarray) – d p / k of the first gear’s part there.

  • part_second (numpy.ndarray) – The same of the second’s.

  • weight (numpy.ndarray) – A miss of one step at the contact, as a share of the gap between two horns of the first gear.

  • timer_first (numpy.ndarray | None) – The timer of the first gear’s part, by index; the gear’s own if None.

  • timer_second (numpy.ndarray | None) – The same of the second’s.

  • n_timers (int | None) – How many timers; as many as gears if None.

  • apart (tuple[tuple[int, int, float], ...]) – Timers set so far apart once fitted, as (timer, other, share of a step): the parts of a split gear, their horns taking turns round its axle. Where no contact ties the two, as two bands joined by split gears, the first’s whole band is turned so, which changes no contact of it.

second: ndarray
turns: ndarray
part_first: ndarray

weight: ndarray
timer_first: ndarray | None = None
timer_second: ndarray | None = None

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.time_ring(centers: ndarray, radii: ndarray, convention: ndarray, meshes: list[tuple[int, int]], others: list[tuple[int, int]], contacts: RingContacts) → tuple[ndarray, ndarray, ndarray, list[float]]

Move and size the gears of a ring, from ring_geometry()’s layout, so that each contact’s two horns come round to it together, and say when.

A contact between two gears asks their starts to differ by so much, mod 1 (RingContacts): one equation a contact, and one start a gear, so round each ring of gears one equation is left over, which the layout has to meet. Round a single ring of gears alike it cancels. Every two gears that mesh touch, no two others come within CLEARANCE, each radius stays within RADIUS_RANGE of its convention, and the horns arrive together: a least-squares fit of all of it, by Levenberg-Marquardt with exact derivatives.

Parameters:

  • centers – Each gear’s centre, (n, 2).

  • radii – Each gear’s radius as drawn.

  • convention – Each gear’s radius by the drawing convention (_gear_radius()), which its radius may leave by RADIUS_RANGE at most.

  • meshes – The gears that mesh, as index pairs.

  • others – Those that do not.

  • contacts – When the contacts come round.

Returns:

The centres, the radii, each gear’s start (x of RingContacts), and when each contact hands over, as a share of a step.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.axial_position(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]], axial: Axial) → tuple[float, float]

Where an axial’s column stands: the centroid of the gears it anchors to.

One gear gives that gear’s own centre; a ring of gears gives the centre of the hole they enclose.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine the axial belongs to.

  • layout – Gear centre positions from compute_layout.

  • axial – The axial to place.

Returns:

(x, y) of the column in layout coordinates.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.axial_positions(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]]) → dict[str, tuple[float, float]]

Column position for every axial on the machine, keyed by axial name.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.axial_clearance(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]], position: tuple[float, float], scale: float = 1.0) → float

Free space around a column: the distance to the nearest carrier path.

Carriers on a gear ride that gear’s rim, so the distance from a point to the nearest carrier is |distance to the centre - radius|, minimised over every gear. The one expression covers both anchors: a column at a gear’s centre clears that gear’s radius, while a column in a tube clears the gap between the hole’s centre and the surrounding rims.

A value at or below zero means carriers pass through the column in this projection. That is a genuine clash for a tube core, but expected for a flat braid, whose core rises through the convergence point where the carriers meet.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine.

  • layout – Gear centre positions from compute_layout.

  • position – The column’s (x, y).

  • scale – Scale factor (must match the one used for the layout).

Returns:

Clearance in layout units.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.contact_point(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]], gear: str, neighbor: str, scale: float = 1.0) → tuple[float, float]

The middle of the notch two gears share.

Where the circles cross, the notch is the chord between the two crossings and the bobbin sits at its middle — which lies on the line between the two centres. Where the circles merely touch, the two crossings coincide and that middle is the tangent point, so one construction serves both.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.contact_angle(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]], gear: str, neighbor: str, scale: float = 1.0) → float

Angle (rad) from a gear’s centre toward the notch it shares with a neighbour.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.carrier_radius(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]], gear: str, scale: float = 1.0) → float

How far from a gear’s centre its bobbins ride.

A bobbin sits in a notch, so it turns about the gear at the distance of that notch — the gear’s own radius when the gears merely touch, and less than that when they overlap and the notch is cut back inside the rim.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.slot_offsets(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]]) → dict[str, float]

Per-gear rotation offset phi so connection slots point toward their neighbors.

Every connection of a gear is taken into account, via the circular mean of the offsets they each ask for. When the machine’s connection slots match its layout the requests coincide and the mean reproduces them exactly; when they do not, the residual error is shared between the contacts instead of being dumped entirely onto whichever connection happened to come second.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.offset_residuals(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]]) → dict[str, float]

Worst angular error (radians) between each gear’s slots and its contacts.

Zero means every contact of that gear falls exactly on a slot. A non-zero value means its slots, turned rigidly, cannot meet every contact, as where a line of gears bends; GearAngles then draws them spread unevenly, so that carriers do not jump when they transfer there.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.FITS = 1e-09

How far (radians) a gear’s slots may miss its contacts and still be drawn turned rigidly: rounding, not a bend.

class braidpy.horn_gear.layout.GearAngles(offset: float, knots: tuple[tuple[float, float], ...] = ())

Bases: object

Where a gear’s slots are drawn on the deck, from their angle on the gear.

A gear’s slots are evenly spaced round it and turn at its rate, and are drawn turned by its offset (slot_offsets()). That puts a slot on every contact at every step only when the contacts are a whole number of slots apart round the gear, as on a straight line of gears. Where a line bends at a gear they are not, so its slots are drawn spread unevenly instead: the slot at a contact is always drawn on it, and those between two contacts evenly between their angles. A carrier rounds the outside of the bend a little faster than the inside, then, and is handed on where it is, without jumping. Which slot is where is the machine’s; only the drawing changes (see offset_residuals()).

Parameters:

  • offset – The gear’s offset, from slot_offsets().

  • knots – Each contact as (angle of its slot on the gear, angle on the deck), in order round the gear; empty where turning the slots rigidly by offset puts one on every contact.

offset: float
knots: tuple[tuple[float, float], ...] = ()

How each gear’s slots are drawn: see GearAngles.

  • layout – Gear centres, from compute_layout().

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.tube_rings(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]] | None = None) → list[list[str]]

Find the rings of gears that enclose a hole — one per tube.

Gears are tangent circles in the plane, so the connection graph is planar and the holes in the machine are exactly the bounded faces of its planar embedding. Every face is walked and the outer one — the space around the machine rather than a hole inside it — is dropped, being the largest by absolute signed area.

A flat braid has no cycle and so returns no rings; a ring braid returns one; a grid of gears returns one per opening.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine to inspect.

  • layout – Gear centre positions (computed if None).

Returns:

List of rings, each a list of gear names in the order they enclose the hole. Empty if the machine has no hole.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.tube_axials(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]] | None = None, min_clearance: float = 1e-06, prefix: str = 'core') → list[Axial]

One core Axial per tube the machine braids.

Rings too tight to hold a core — where the surrounding gears reach the centre of the hole — are skipped rather than returned, so the result is only cores that physically fit.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine to inspect.

  • layout – Gear centre positions (computed if None).

  • min_clearance – Smallest acceptable gap between core and carriers.

  • prefix – Name stem; cores are named core, core_1, … in order.

Returns:

List of Axial, empty for a machine with no tube.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.axial_spots(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]] | None = None) → list[Axial]

Every place the machine could feed an axial yarn, loaded or not.

Up each gear’s hollow spindle, at its centre — once for the parts of a split gear, which share an axle, named by its first part — and down the hole of each ring of gears that leaves room for one (tube_axials()). Which of them a machine braids round is its axials.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine to inspect.

  • layout – Gear centre positions (computed if None).

Returns:

The gears’ spots, in the machine’s order, then the rings’.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.ring_core(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]] | None = None) → Axial | None

The core a machine that is one ring of gears braids round: down the hole the ring encloses, as a tubular machine’s or a lace machine’s.

Only a ring of every gear makes a tube: a line folded round, as the multiband machine’s, encloses a hole between its gears too, but braids flat bands, not round it.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine.

  • layout – Gear centre positions (computed if None).

Returns:

The core, named centre; None if the machine is not one ring, or its hole has no room for a core.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.gear_radii(machine: BraidingMachine, scale: float = 1.0) → dict[str, float]

Return the visual radius for each gear.

Parameters:

Dict mapping gear name → radius.

braidpy.horn_gear.layout.carrier_xy(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]], angles: dict[str, GearAngles], carrier_radii: dict[str, float], position: tuple[str, int], time: int, frac: float = 0.0) → tuple[float, float]

Where in the plane a carrier is, at continuous time time + frac.

A carrier rides in a horn of its gear, so its angle is simply that slot’s angle: it turns with the gear and always sits on its slot, drawn where GearAngles draws it. It is drawn on whatever is actually moving it this step — on a machine with shared slots that is the receiving gear, see riding_position().

Transfers stay continuous without any special casing: a carrier moves to the neighbour only at the step where its slot is at the contact point, and it lands on the neighbour’s slot that is at that same contact point at that same instant, so the two coincide; where a line bends at a gear, its slots are drawn so that they still do (GearAngles).

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine definition.

  • layout – Gear centres, from compute_layout().

  • angles – How each gear’s slots are drawn, from slot_angles().

  • carrier_radii – Per-gear riding radius, from carrier_radius().

  • position – The carrier’s recorded (gear, slot) at time.

  • time – The step being taken.

  • frac – How far into that step, from 0 to 1.

Returns:

The carrier’s (x, y).

horn_gear/tracks.py

Precompute the closed carrier tracks of a braiding machine.

A track is the closed path a carrier follows when started at a given (gear, slot) position at t=0. A carrier rides in a physical horn of its gear, so at each step it either:

  1. Stays where it is — keeping its slot index while the gear turns it to a new angle.

  2. Transfers to an adjacent gear, which happens on exactly the step where its slot is the one sitting at a contact point.

Contact points are fixed in space, so a different slot index reaches them every step. The dynamics are therefore time-dependent, and a track only closes once the carrier is back at its starting slot and the contact pattern is back to its t=0 phase — usually well after one gear revolution.

Tracks normally partition the slots, but not always: two carriers may cross the same slot at different times without ever meeting, in which case their tracks overlap.

exception braidpy.horn_gear.tracks.NoFixedTracks

Bases: RuntimeError

Raised when a fixed-track calculation is asked of a programmed machine.

braidpy.horn_gear.tracks.ring_order(machine: BraidingMachine) → list[str] | None

The gears in the order they circle the machine, or None if it has no ring.

A flat braid is a chain with no way round, so there is no circulation to speak of and this returns None.

braidpy.horn_gear.tracks.circulation(machine: BraidingMachine, start: tuple[str, int], period: int | None = None) → int

Which way round the machine a carrier started at start travels.

Returns the net number of gear-to-gear steps it makes around the ring over one period: positive one way, negative the other, zero for a machine with no ring or a carrier that ends up where it began.

This counts steps around the connection graph, so it needs no layout — and it is a property of the starting position, not of the track: positions alternate in sign along a track, because a carrier placed in a slot at t=0 sits at a different phase from one that arrived there.

Only one of those two parities can be occupied at a time, though. Put carriers on both and they move towards each other and collide on the first step, so a loadable machine fills half of each track and every carrier on a given track circulates the same way. Carriers going opposite ways are on different tracks — which is what a braid is made of.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine definition.

  • start – The (gear_name, slot_index) a carrier is placed in.

  • period – Steps to follow it for; the simulation period if None.

Returns:

Signed number of places moved around the ring.

braidpy.horn_gear.tracks.walk(machine: BraidingMachine, start: tuple[str, int], period: int | None = None) → list[tuple[str, int]]

Every position a carrier passes through, in order, repeats included.

A Track lists the distinct positions on a loop, which is what you want for counting slots but not for following one: a carrier that comes back to a slot it has already used is not recorded again, so two entries that sit side by side in a track need not be a step apart in time. On a flat braid that leaves the track reading as though a carrier hopped straight from one end gear to the other, which are not even connected.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine definition.

  • start – Where the carrier begins.

  • period – Steps to follow it for; the simulation period if None.

Returns:

The positions visited, one per step, starting at start.

braidpy.horn_gear.tracks.contact_period(machine: BraidingMachine) → int

Number of steps after which every contact point shows the same slots again.

Delegates to the machine, because how fast the contacts cycle depends on how the gears are driven — see BraidingMachine.contact_period().

braidpy.horn_gear.tracks.compute_track(machine: BraidingMachine, start: tuple[str, int], max_steps: int = 100000) → list[tuple[str, int]]

Follow a single carrier from start until it returns.

Time advances for real: the contact pattern shifts every step, exactly as in simulate(). A carrier holds its slot for several steps, then transfers when that slot reaches a contact, so the track records the distinct positions visited, in order.

The track is closed only when the carrier is back at start and the machine’s contact pattern is back to its t=0 phase — otherwise the path from there onward would not repeat.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine definition.

  • start – Starting (gear_name, slot_index).

  • max_steps – Safety limit to prevent infinite loops in broken configs.

Returns:

The closed track as a list of positions (start not repeated at end).

Raises:

RuntimeError – If the track does not close within max_steps.

braidpy.horn_gear.tracks.simulation_period(machine: BraidingMachine, max_steps: int = 100000) → int

Number of steps after which every carrier is back where it started.

A carrier holds each slot for several steps and must go all the way round its track, so this is generally larger than len(track) and larger than contact_period().

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine definition.

  • max_steps – Safety limit passed to the track follower.

Returns:

The machine’s full simulation period in steps.

braidpy.horn_gear.tracks.compute_tracks(machine: BraidingMachine) → list[list[tuple[str, int]]]

Compute all distinct closed tracks for the machine.

A slot belongs to one gear and one track, so the tracks partition the slots. Following a track out of every slot instead would not improve on this: at a contact the carrier is in two slots at once, so entering the loop by the other one hands back the same track reversed, and on a flat braid entering at a different phase hands back an ordering that is neither a rotation nor a reversal of the first. Starting from the slots not yet accounted for is what keeps the result a partition.

Every (gear, slot) appears on at least one track. For most machines the tracks also partition the slots, but that is not guaranteed: two carriers may pass through the same slot at different times without ever meeting, in which case their tracks overlap and the lengths sum to more than machine.total_slots(). Callers placing carriers from tracks should therefore drop repeated positions.

Parameters:

machine – The machine definition.

Returns:

List of tracks. Each track is a list of (gear_name, slot_index) visited in order.

braidpy.horn_gear.tracks.tracks_summary(tracks: list[list[tuple[str, int]]]) → dict[str, int]

Return summary statistics for a list of tracks.

Parameters:

tracks – Output of compute_tracks.

Returns:

Dict with keys ‘n_tracks’, ‘min_length’, ‘max_length’, ‘total_positions’.

horn_gear/loading.py

Deciding where the carriers start.

Threading a machine is a search, not a convention. A placement has to survive being run: _is_collision_free() simulates a candidate and rejects it if two carriers ever share a slot or meet at a connection point. Among the placements that survive, _fullest_loading() takes the one that carries most, breaking ties on circulation balance (equal numbers going each way), crowding, and how evenly the carriers spread over the gears.

Separate from simulation because the two are different jobs and the dependency runs one way: loading calls simulate to try a candidate, while stepping never calls loading.

load_carriers() needs the machine to have fixed tracks, so it is not the whole story — a machine reaches its own threading through default_carriers(), which is a hook rather than a shortcut. A Jacquard lace machine overrides it to thread one bobbin into every notch, and must: its carriers go where the programme sends them, there are no fixed tracks, and load_carriers() raises NoFixedTracks on it.

braidpy.horn_gear.loading.load_carriers(machine: BraidingMachine) → dict[int, tuple[str, int]]

Fill the machine with as many carriers as it can hold without collisions.

A real machine is loaded with a spool in every other slot along each track, which is what this tries first, since it reproduces how a machine is threaded in practice. That has no meaning for a track whose path revisits slots — the interior gears of a flat braid are crossed once per traversal — so the machine is then filled as far as it will go instead.

Either way the candidate is validated by simulating a full period: checking occupancy at t=0 is not enough, because contact points move to a different slot every step and conflicts can surface later in the cycle.

Parameters:

machine – The machine definition.

Returns:

Dict mapping carrier_id → (gear_name, slot).

Raises:

RuntimeError – If not even one carrier can be placed.

horn_gear/simulation.py

Simulation state and stepping for a horn gear braiding machine.

Each carrier occupies exactly one (gear, slot) position. At each step every turning gear advances by one slot-pitch, carrying its slots round with it; a carrier keeps its own slot and rides with it, and crosses into a neighbour’s slot only when its own slot reaches a contact. So the slot index of a carrier riding its gear does not change from step to step — it changes when the carrier transfers.

“Turning” matters: an ordinary machine turns every gear every step, but turning_gears() enables only the gears of the current phase, and a gear that is not turning holds its carriers where they are.

This module is intentionally pure / functional: MachineState is a frozen dataclass and step() returns a new state rather than mutating in place, making it easy to replay or branch the simulation.

exception braidpy.horn_gear.simulation.CollisionError(step: int, collisions: dict[tuple[str, int], list[int]], history: list[MachineState])

  • history – Valid MachineState list up to (but not including) the colliding step — i.e. the last entry is the last safe state.

braidpy.horn_gear.simulation.carrier_places(machine: BraidingMachine, state: MachineState) → dict[int, tuple[str, int]]

Where each carrier actually is: its gear, and the angle it has reached.

A slot index is a label painted on a turning gear, not a place. Every step turns a gear by one slot, so its notches land back on notch angles and the gear is indistinguishable from the gear a step earlier — which means a carrier sitting in a different notch may be at exactly the point in space it started from, and one back in “its own” notch may be on the far side of the gear. What the eye sees, and what the machine does next, follow from the angle.

Angles are returned as whole millionths of a turn, so they compare exactly and 0 and a full turn are the same place.

  • state – The snapshot to read.

(gear, angle in millionths of a turn)}.

braidpy.horn_gear.simulation.state_period(machine: BraidingMachine, carrier_positions: dict[int, tuple[str, int]] | None = None, max_steps: int = 10000) → int | None

Steps after which the machine is exactly as it started, or None.

“Exactly” means every carrier back at the point it set off from — see carrier_places() for why that is not the same as back in its own slot — and the drive back to its starting phase, so the step that follows is the step that followed then. Run the machine for this many steps and the last frame hands straight back to the first.

This is a property of the machine and of how it is loaded, and it varies a lot: eight steps for a square braid, eighteen for a flat braid on nine carriers. It is not how long a carrier takes to walk its whole track — that flat braid’s track is ninety steps round — because the machine is back where it started long before any one carrier has been everywhere.

A machine driven by a programme need not ever come back — a carrier goes where the programme sends it — so this returns None rather than pretend.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine definition.

  • carrier_positions – The carriers to follow; the machine’s own if None.

  • max_steps – How far to look before giving up.

Returns:

The cycle length in steps, or None if there is none within reach.

horn_gear/word.py

The braid word a machine and its loading make.

A braid word is not a property of a machine alone. It is a property of the machine, how it is threaded, and a direction to look from — a braid is a set of curves in space, and a word records which strand passed in front of which when they are projected onto a plane. Two projections of the same braid give different words.

Two projections are offered, because braiding machines come in two shapes:

  • flat_word() looks along the deck’s y axis, so the carriers are ordered left to right and the word is an ordinary Artin word. This is the right reading for a flat braider, whose carriers stay strung out along a line.

  • ring_word() reads round an axis — a core, or a spot one could be fed at — and writes the braid as moves round a ring (RingWord), turns and all: with the core kept as a strand it is the braid the machine makes round it, and it can be shortened (RingWord.shortened()).

  • annular_word() looks outward from a point you choose, so the carriers are ordered by angle around it and the word is an annular one — the vocabulary of braidpy.annulus_braid, where index n is the pair whose numbering wraps. This is the right reading for a tubular braider, and the point to choose is normally the axis of the tube.

Both read the word from where the carriers actually are, computed exactly from the machine at each instant by carrier_xy() — not sampled off the yarn geometry. A crossing is therefore found wherever two carriers exchange order, with no dependence on how finely a shape was drawn.

braid_word() reads a word off drawn curves instead, and the two should agree for a flat machine. The tests check that they do, which is worth more than either on its own: one works from the machine’s motion, the other from the shape that motion lays down.

braidpy.horn_gear.word.annular_word(machine: BraidingMachine, around: tuple[float, float] | None = None, carriers: dict[int, tuple[str, int]] | None = None, n_steps: int | None = None, n_substeps: int = 64, scale: float = 1.0) → AnnularWord

The braid this machine makes, read as it winds round a point.

Carriers are ordered by their angle about around, and two of them cross exactly when their angles coincide — when their unwrapped angles differ by a whole turn. The generator’s index is where the pair sits in that cyclic order, so index n is the pair straddling the point where the numbering wraps, and its sign says which passed outside.

Nothing distinguishes that wrapping pair physically: it is an artefact of having to start numbering somewhere, exactly as in braidpy.annulus_braid.

  • around – The point to look out from; deck_center() if None.

  • n_steps – How many steps to read; one full cycle if None.

  • n_substeps – Samples per step.

  • scale – Layout scale.

Returns:

The crossings, and how far each carrier wound round the centre.

In this order: an axial the machine feeds down a ring’s hole; the hole a ring of gears encloses, which a tubular braider braids round (tube_axials()); an axial the machine feeds up a gear, as a soutache’s cord; the gear nearest the deck’s centre (deck_center()).

braidpy.horn_gear.word.flat_word(machine: BraidingMachine, carriers: dict[int, tuple[str, int]] | None = None, n_steps: int | None = None, n_substeps: int = 64, scale: float = 1.0) → list[int]

The Artin word of the braid this machine makes, seen from the front.

Carriers are ordered left to right across the deck and a crossing is recorded whenever two neighbours exchange places. Its sign says which passed in front: positive when the one arriving from the left passes on the near side, the convention braid_word() and to_parametric_strands() both use.

This suits a machine whose carriers stay strung out along a line. On a tubular braider the left-to-right order is meaningless — the carriers go round — and the word comes out as noise; use annular_word() there.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine definition.

  • carriers – The loading; the machine’s own if None.

  • n_steps – How many steps to read; one full cycle if None.

  • n_substeps – Samples per step. Two carriers exchanging and exchanging back within one sample are missed, so this is generous by default.

  • scale – Layout scale.

Returns:

The word, as signed generator indices.

braidpy.horn_gear.word.ring_unit(machine: BraidingMachine, axis: Axial | None = None, carriers: dict[int, tuple[str, int]] | None = None) → tuple[RingWord, int]

The shortest stretch of a machine’s cycle that, repeated, makes it: as few steps as bring the carriers back to where carriers stood, each perhaps where another was, read as a ring word (ring_word()).

A tube comes round long before its carriers are home: a tubular braider of 16 does in 2 steps what its 16-step cycle does 8 times. The stretch need not bring a strand home, nor make a pure braid; made over and over, it makes the machine’s braid round its core, exactly.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine.

  • axis – As ring_word() takes it.

  • carriers – The loading; the machine’s own if None.

Returns:

The stretch’s ring word, shortened (RingWord.shortened()), and how many times a cycle makes it.

braidpy.horn_gear.word.ring_word(machine: BraidingMachine, axis: Axial | None = None, carriers: dict[int, tuple[str, int]] | None = None, n_steps: int | None = None, n_substeps: int = 64) → RingWord

The braid a machine makes as moves round a ring, read round an axis.

Seen from the axis, the strands are in a ring: in order round it, clockwise from a seam put in the widest gap between them. Two strands neighbours round it cross when they come in line with the axis, the one further from it outside; a strand passing the seam, crossing nobody, turns the ring by a slot. Where annular_word() keeps only the order round the axis, this keeps the seam, and so the turns: the braid round the axis, its core kept (RingWord.cored()), is the braid the machine makes round a yarn fed there, exactly.

The axis matters: round another point the same machine makes another braid round its core, the same once the core is taken away (RingWord.braid()).

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine.

  • axis – What to read the braid round, an axial or a spot one could be fed at (axial_spots()); default_axis() if None. An axial the machine feeds there is the core, not a strand.

  • carriers – The loading; the machine’s own if None.

  • n_steps – How many steps to read: one cycle of the machine if None (state_period()), or for a machine driven by a programme, one pass of it.

  • n_substeps – Samples per step.

Returns:

The moves, and which strand began where.

Raises:

ValueError – If a strand passes through the axis.

horn_gear/jacquard.py

Jacquard lace machine: a braiding machine whose gears are driven one by one from a punched programme instead of being geared together.

An ordinary braiding machine turns every gear on every step, so its braid is fixed by the wiring of the machine. A Jacquard machine reads, at each step of its programme, a two-line binary mask over the gears:

  • the first line says which gears take a half turn trigonometrically (CCW),

  • the second line says which take a half turn clockwise.

A gear’s direction belongs to the gear and never changes; the mask only says whether it is allowed to turn this step.

What makes this machine different is its geometry. Its gear circles interpenetrate rather than merely touching, and a slot is the notch cut where two of them overlap — so a slot belongs to both gears at once, and a bobbin sitting in one is swept out by whichever of the pair turns. That is what lets a gear turn while its neighbour stands still, which a machine of tangent gears cannot do.

It also means two neighbouring gears must never turn together: they would both reach for the bobbin in the notch they share. Hence the two lines, driven one after the other — neighbours alternate direction round a ring, so each line on its own only ever turns gears that do not touch. A programme that breaks this is rejected when the machine is built.

Because the programme decides where every bobbin goes, a bobbin’s path need not come back on itself: there are no closed tracks here and no period, and compute_tracks() and its relatives say so rather than inventing one. Thread the machine with notch_positions() and simulate the programme instead.

Layout, drawing and collision detection are shared with any other machine and need no special case: the only things that differ are how far each gear has turned by a given step and where a bobbin goes next, both of which the base class already asks itself through rotation() and next_position().

exception braidpy.horn_gear.jacquard.JacquardProgramError

One bobbin in every notch — the usual way a lace machine is threaded.

A notch is shared by the two gears whose circles cut it, so there is one bobbin position per contact, not per slot. Filling them all is safe by construction: no two bobbins can land in the same notch.

machine – The machine to thread.

Parameters:

  • gears – The horn gears. Lace machines use 2-slot gears, but any slot count works.

  • connections – Contacts between gears, as for any machine.

  • program – One entry per programmed step, each a (trigonometric_line, clockwise_line) pair. A line is a bit per gear, in the order the gears were given — "1010", (1, 0, 1, 0) or a tuple of bools.

  • axials – Optional cords the braid forms around.

Raises:

The circles overlap, and a slot is the notch they cut between them.

Carriers go where the programme sends them, so their paths need not close and the machine has no tracks or period to compute.

The notches threaded, by contact; every one if None.

turning_gears(step: int) → frozenset[str]

Gears enabled for the phase running from step to step + 1.

program_rows() → list[tuple[str, tuple[bool, ...]]]

The programme as punchcard rows, two per punched step.

preferred_layout(scale: float = 1.0) → dict[str, tuple[float, float]] | None

Place a ring so every notch lands exactly on a slot.

The generic layout sets gear circles tangent, which is right for a braiding machine but wrong here: these circles have to overlap for there to be a notch at all. For a ring of n gears of 2 slots the geometry is forced, and worth deriving rather than approximating.

A gear’s two notches are cut where its circle crosses each neighbour’s, and being 2-slot they must come out diametrically opposite — so the gear’s centre is the midpoint of the two notches. Putting the centres on a circle of radius R and working that condition through gives:

r = R * tan(pi / n)

which is larger than the R * sin(pi / n) half-spacing that would make them touch, so the circles interpenetrate exactly as they should.

Returns None — deferring to the generic layout — for anything that is not a ring of equal 2-slot gears.

Parameters:

scale – Overall scale factor for gear radii.

Returns:

Gear name → (x, y), or None.

riding_position(pos: tuple[str, int], time: int, frac: float = 0.0) → tuple[str, int]

Which gear sweeps a bobbin through this step — which may not be its own.

A bobbin in a notch is swept by whichever of the two gears turns, so the gear that moves it is the one it ends the step on. Drawing it on its own idle gear instead would leave it still for the whole step and then jump it across to the neighbour.

All three cases fall out of next_position(): the bobbin’s own gear when that turns, the receiving gear when the neighbour takes it, and where it already is when nothing moves.

default_carriers() → dict[int, tuple[str, int]]

Thread one bobbin into every notch, or into those threaded.

next_position(pos: tuple[str, int], time: int) → tuple[str, int]

Where a carrier goes during the step from time to time + 1.

The gear circles interpenetrate, so a slot is the notch cut where two of them overlap and belongs to both gears at once. A bobbin sitting in that notch is swept out by whichever of the two turns:

  • its own gear turns → it stays on that gear, carried round to the gear’s other notch;

  • its own gear is idle and the gear across the notch turns → that gear takes it, and it rides on round to that gear’s other notch;

  • neither turns → it stays where it is.

Both turning at once would have the two gears fighting over the same bobbin, which is why the mask is split into two lines and applied one after the other; the constructor rejects a line that enables neighbouring gears together.

Parameters:

  • pos – Current (gear_name, slot_index).

  • time – Step being taken.

Returns:

The (gear_name, slot_index) the carrier occupies afterwards.

rotation(gear_name: str, time: int) → int

Signed slots turned through after time simulation steps.

contact_period() → int

Steps until the programme restarts and every gear is back square.

The programme repeats every steps_per_pass steps, but a gear only looks the same again once its accumulated turns are a whole number of revolutions, so the true period is a multiple of the programme length.

property steps_per_pass: int

Simulation steps in one pass of the programme — two per punched step.

The two mask lines are driven one after the other, so a punched step takes two simulation steps.

braidpy.horn_gear.jacquard.jacquard_lace_ring(n_gears: int = 6, program: Sequence[tuple[str | Sequence[int | bool], str | Sequence[int | bool]]] | None = None, n_slots: int = 2, threaded: Sequence[int] | None = None) → JacquardLaceMachine

A tubular Jacquard lace machine: 2-slot gears in a ring.

Layout:

[A] - [B] - [C] - [D] - [E] - [F] - back to [A]

Each gear carries two slots, one at each of its two contacts, so a half turn swaps which neighbour each of its carriers faces. Gears alternate direction round the ring, which is why n_gears must be even — meshing gears have to turn opposite ways.

With no programme given, every gear is enabled on every step, which drives the machine exactly like an ordinary tubular braider and is the useful baseline to compare a real programme against.

Parameters:

  • n_gears – Number of gears in the ring; must be even and at least 4.

  • program – Punched steps; defaults to one step with everything enabled.

  • n_slots – Slots per gear. Lace machines use 2.

  • threaded – The notches a bobbin is put in, notch k between gears k and k + 1; every notch if None.

Returns:

JacquardLaceMachine for a ring of gears.

Raises:

ValueError – If n_gears is odd or smaller than 4.

A braiding machine worked by hand: carriers placed, the handle turned a step at a time, forwards or back.

load_carriers() loads a machine outright, but when the loading wanted collides it says nothing of where or why. Turning the handle and watching is often quicker.

What is turned is always the loading at step 0 — the carriers the machine braids with — so there is one thing to keep: going back a step is running one step fewer, and a carrier put on a slot at step t goes onto the slot at step 0 that brings it there (origin()), changing the loading itself. Every step is the machine’s own (simulate()), and so is every collision: two carriers in one slot, two crossing at a contact, or a carrier either side of one.

Handle keeps a loading and a step, for Python and plotly; Braid Studio keeps them in the page and asks turn() for each step.

A line of horn gears that braids several bands at once.

A line of gears braids one band however long it is: every interior gear has two contacts, so a carrier entering by one leaves by the other and walks the whole line. A band needs a gear at each end that turns its carriers back, and that gear needs an odd number of slots: an even one returns a carrier to the strand it came in on and breaks the band into short tracks that fill only part of it (see flat_braid_9()).

Where two bands meet, one gear turns the carriers of both back. It is a split gear: two gears on one axis, turning together, one for each band, with their horns between each other’s. A six-horn split gear gives each band three: an odd turning gear for each, and the two never share a horn. Each half meets only its own band’s neighbour, so a carrier can never cross into the other band, and the half that is not at a contact is always a third of a pitch away from it.

It is modelled as two HornGear of three slots at the same centre, drawn as large as the six-horn gear they make. Each turns one of its own slots a step, as every gear does, which is two horns of the whole gear: the bands see three-slot turning gears, which is what the machine needs.

multiband_10_15_10() is the three-band machine of the Atelier de Tressage’s circuit drawing (see the references page), sixteen gears:

5  4  4  8  6  8  4  4  4  4  8  6  8  4  4  5
            ^                    ^
         split                 split

The two six-horn gears are split, cutting the line into bands of 24, 38 and 24 slots. Each band holds at most half its slots, 12, 19 and 12 carriers, as a flat braid does; the drawing runs 10, 15 and 10 (MULTIBAND_10_15_10_LOADING).

twin_plait() is the smallest such machine: three gears, 3 6 3, and two plaits braided side by side.

an end gear of three slots, a six-slot gear split three and three, and another end gear. Each band is three slots of end gear and three of split gear, the smallest flat braid there is: two plaits side by side.

Type:

The smallest line that braids two bands

braidpy.horn_gear.multiband.MULTIBAND_10_15_10_LOADING = ((('G0', 0), ('G0', 2), ('G0', 4), ('G1', 2), ('G1', 3), ('G2', 1), ('G2', 2), ('G3', 2), ('G3', 5), ('G4a', 1)), (('G4b', 0), ('G4b', 2), ('G5', 2), ('G5', 5), ('G6', 1), ('G6', 2), ('G7', 2), ('G7', 3), ('G8', 1), ('G8', 2), ('G9', 2), ('G9', 3), ('G10', 1), ('G10', 4), ('G11a', 2)), (('G11b', 0), ('G11b', 1), ('G12', 1), ('G12', 4), ('G13', 2), ('G13', 3), ('G14', 1), ('G14', 2), ('G15', 2), ('G15', 4)))

10, 15 and 10, the 10-15-10 of its name. Not the most it holds (the exact loading search gives 12, 19 and 12): as the drawing loads it, gear by gear, each carrier going the way the drawing’s arrows send it. Every gear but the eight-horn ones takes its carriers on the only slots that do; an eight-horn gear carries one each way, as drawn, on one of the four pairs of slots that run (the drawing does not say which). The tests run it over the whole machine’s period, 2280 steps.

horn_gear/take_off.py

The braid coming off a horn gear machine.

The machine says where each carrier is at every instant (carrier_trajectories()); from there the braid is laid, drawn in to a fell and tightened exactly as any other source of strands is — see braidpy.take_off, which holds the model. This module only adds what a machine knows: its gears to stand the braid on, the middle of them for an axis, the axial cores the braid is laid round, and a take-off rate in proportion to its gears.

Bases: StrandTrajectories

Where every carrier went, sampled through a run of the machine.

StrandTrajectories with times in steps, and the machine’s layout kept alongside.

Parameters:

  • layout – Gear centres the positions are measured against.

  • radii – Gear radii at the same scale.

layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]]
radii: dict[str, float]
class braidpy.horn_gear.take_off.Clearance(distance: float, gap: float, met: TooCloseError | None)

Bases: object

How close a machine’s carriers come to each other, and so how large the machine has to be for its bobbins.

Scaled up, a machine keeps its carriers further apart in proportion: bobbins of diameter b pass if it is drawn b / distance times as large (scale_for()), in whatever unit b is given. Only two carriers at one point (met) can pass on no machine.

Variables:

  • distance (float) – The closest two carriers come.

  • gap (float) – The smallest gap between two neighbouring horns of a gear; round a split gear, all its parts’ horns count.

  • met (braidpy.horn_gear.take_off.TooCloseError | None) – Where two carriers first came to one point, if they did.

distance: float
gap: float
met: TooCloseError | None
property share: float

The closest two carriers come, as a share of gap.

scale_for(bobbin_diameter: float) → float

How large the machine must be drawn for bobbins of bobbin_diameter to pass each other: so many of the bobbin’s units to one unit of the drawing (mm to a unit, for a diameter in mm).

exception braidpy.horn_gear.take_off.TooCloseError(step: int, carriers: tuple[int, int], distance: float, limit: float, history: list)

Bases: CollisionError

Raised for two carriers that come to one point (MEET), in different slots: the simulation sees no collision, but they would hit on a machine of any size.

Variables:

  • step – The step during which they came that close.

  • collisions – The first carrier’s place as the step began, and the two carriers, as CollisionError gives them.

  • history – The states before that step.

  • distance – How close they came.

  • limit – How close they could have come.

braidpy.horn_gear.take_off.carrier_trajectories(machine: BraidingMachine, n_steps: int, carrier_positions: dict[int, tuple[str, int]] | None = None, n_substeps: int = 12, scale: float = 1.0) → CarrierTrajectories

Follow every carrier through n_steps steps of the machine.

Each step is split into n_substeps samples, at the same positions the animation draws (carrier_xy()), so what is laid here is exactly what is seen turning there.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine definition.

  • n_steps – How many steps to run.

  • carrier_positions – The loading; the machine’s own if None.

  • n_substeps – Samples per step.

  • scale – Layout scale.

Returns:

The sampled trajectories, n_steps * n_substeps + 1 samples long.

Raises:

CollisionError – If the loading collides within the run — a braid that cannot be made has no shape to give.

braidpy.horn_gear.take_off.clearance(machine: BraidingMachine, n_steps: int, carrier_positions: dict[int, tuple[str, int]] | None = None, scale: float = 1.0) → Clearance | None

How close the carriers come in n_steps, following them as they are drawn (carrier_trajectories()).

The simulation stops a machine where two carriers would take one slot (CollisionError). Two carriers in different slots can come to one point all the same, as on gears laid out too close together.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine definition.

  • n_steps – How many steps to look over.

  • carrier_positions – The loading; the machine’s own if None.

  • scale – Layout scale.

A machine driven by a card, as a lace machine is, swaps two bobbins by passing one by the other in a notch: it is not looked at.

Returns:

How close they come, and where two first came to one point if they did; None for fewer than two carriers, or a machine driven by a card.

braidpy.horn_gear.take_off.default_take_off(machine: BraidingMachine, scale: float = 1.0) → float

A take-off rate that draws a machine’s braid in sensible proportions.

Half the mean gear radius per step: a carrier then moves across the deck about as far as the braid moves up, so its yarn leaves at roughly 45°, near the angle a braid is usually made at. It sets only how stretched the picture is — nothing about which yarn crosses which depends on it.

braidpy.horn_gear.take_off.jammed_contraction(rel: ndarray, spacing: float, diameter: float) → float

How far a braid can be drawn in before two yarns touch.

Drawing the plane in by k shrinks the sideways part of every distance by k and leaves the height part alone, so a pair of samples a height dz apart and s apart sideways touches when k = sqrt(d² - dz²) / s. The braid jams at the largest of these — an exact answer over the samples, with no search.

Parameters:

  • rel – Per yarn, its samples relative to the axis; shape (yarns, n, 2), every yarn at the same heights.

  • spacing – Height between successive samples.

  • diameter – Yarn diameter.

Returns:

The contraction k; above 1 if the yarns do not fit even undrawn.

Raises:

ValueError – If two yarns pass through the same place too close in height for any drawing-in to separate them — the take-off is too slow for yarns this thick.

braidpy.horn_gear.take_off.tighten_yarns(paths: YarnPaths, yarn_diameter: float, iterations: int = 400, step: float = 20.0, core_radius: float | None = None, tolerance: float = 0.001, hold_top: bool = True, rigid: Collection[Hashable] = (), periodic: Periodic | None = None) → tuple[YarnPaths, dict[str, list[float]]]

Pull the yarns taut above the fell, without letting them overlap.

Each iteration shortens every yarn, sideways only, so every sample keeps its height; then it pushes apart any two samples of different yarns closer than a diameter, until none are. The yarn is held where it arrives at the fell from its carrier, and at its oldest end, where the take-off holds it. Between the two, far enough from the fell, the braid takes the shape its yarns pull it into, whatever shape the fell started it in.

Shortening at fixed height is the length objective of Solving a braid’s shape numerically in its small-slope form — tension pulls a yarn toward the middle of its neighbours — and the push is its non-interpenetration constraint. The tension is taken implicitly, as a backward-Euler step of step along that flow, which settles a whole yarn in a few dozen iterations where moving each sample toward its neighbours would take thousands. No sample moves more than a fifth of a diameter in one go, though, so a yarn cannot jump through another and the braid the machine made is the braid that comes out.

Parameters:

  • paths – The braid to tighten.

  • yarn_diameter – Yarn diameter.

  • iterations – Shortening steps.

  • step – How far along the tension flow each step goes, in units where 1 moves a sample half way to its neighbours’ middle.

  • core_radius – Keep the yarns outside a core of this radius round the axis, for a braid laid over one.

  • tolerance – Overlap, as a fraction of the diameter, that the contact push accepts.

  • hold_top – Hold the oldest end where it is, as the take-off does. Left free, the end can turn about the axis and untwist the braid. Ignored when periodic is given, which holds neither end.

  • rigid – Yarns held where they are all along, as stiff cores: the others are pushed off them, and they never move.

  • periodic – Join the fell end of the braid to its top, so that what is tightened is one window of an endless braid rather than a short piece of a held one. See Periodic: the window must be a whole number of periods.

Returns:

"length", the total yarn length above the fell, and "closest", the closest approach, after each iteration.

Return type:

The tightened braid, and its history

Warns:

UserWarning – If the braid is laid too coarsely for contact between samples to keep its yarns apart (warn_if_too_coarse()).

braidpy.horn_gear.take_off.too_close(machine: BraidingMachine, n_steps: int, carrier_positions: dict[int, tuple[str, int]] | None = None, scale: float = 1.0) → TooCloseError | None

The first time two carriers come to one point in n_steps, if they do (clearance()): they would hit on a machine of any size.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine definition.

  • n_steps – How many steps to look over.

  • carrier_positions – The loading; the machine’s own if None.

  • scale – Layout scale.

Returns:

The first two carriers at one point, as an error to raise or report; None if no two are, or the machine is driven by a card.

braidpy.horn_gear.take_off.visualize_yarns(machine: BraidingMachine, paths: YarnPaths | None = None, output_html: str | None = None, title: str | None = None, tube_diameter: float | None = None, n_around: int = 12, show_deck: bool = True, **kwargs) → Figure

The yarns in 3D, standing on the machine that laid them.

visualize_yarns(), with the gears outlined on the deck and any axial core standing as a column through the braid. Each yarn is drawn in its carrier’s colour — the same colours as animate().

  • paths – Yarns to draw; computed by yarn_paths() if None, which kwargs are then passed to.

  • output_html – If given, write the figure to this HTML file.

  • title – Figure title; says which model the yarns follow if None.

  • tube_diameter – Draw the yarns as tubes this thick. Defaults to the yarn diameter the braid was made for, if any; 0 draws lines.

braidpy.horn_gear.take_off.yarn_paths(machine: BraidingMachine, n_steps: int | None = None, carrier_positions: dict[int, tuple[str, int]] | None = None, take_off: float | None = None, n_substeps: int = 12, scale: float = 1.0, n_cycles: int = 3, axials: bool = False, **lay) → YarnPaths

The braid a machine has made after n_steps steps.

Follows the carriers (carrier_trajectories()) and lays their yarns with lay_yarns(), which lay is passed to: fell_radius, yarn_diameter, fell_height, axis, n_converge and settle_length. The axis defaults to the middle of the gears.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine definition.

  • n_steps – How long to braid for. If None, n_cycles full cycles of the machine (state_period()), so the braid shows its repeat that many times over; a programmed machine with no cycle runs its drive round that many times.

  • carrier_positions – The loading; the machine’s own if None.

  • take_off – Length of braid drawn off per step. Defaults to default_take_off().

  • n_substeps – Samples per step. With a yarn_diameter, keep take_off / n_substeps below it, or contacts go unseen.

  • scale – Layout scale.

  • n_cycles – Cycles to braid for when n_steps is None.

  • axials – Lay the axial cores too, each a yarn that stays where it enters the braid, named after the axial: drawn in to the fell and tightened with the others, it ends up inside the braid, held there by the yarns crossing round it, as a core is.

Returns:

The yarns, one per carrier, and one per axial if asked for.

horn_gear/visualization.py

Interactive Plotly visualizations for horn gear braiding machines.

Three entry points:

  • visualize_machine: Static diagram of gear layout and connections.

  • visualize_tracks: Tracks drawn as circular arcs connecting physical

    gear-contact points (no straight-line jumps).

  • animate: Smooth sub-step animation showing continuous

    gear rotation (e.g. quarter-turns for 4-slot gears), one full cycle of the machine, played round and round.

Key geometric conventions

Each gear G has a layout position (cx, cy) and radius r. Two connected gears meet at a notch: for tangent gears that is the single point where they touch, and for gears that interpenetrate it is the middle of the chord between the two places their circles cross. Either way it lies on the line between the two centres, and a carrier rides at that distance from its gear’s centre — on the rim when the gears merely touch, inside it when they overlap.

The rotation offset phi_G turns each gear so its connection slots point at its notches, fitted across all of them (slot_offsets()); where a line of gears bends, so that turned rigidly they cannot all meet them, the slots are drawn spread unevenly instead, so that carriers are handed on without jumping (slot_angles()).

Nothing here decides how far a gear has turned, where a carrier goes next, or which gear is carrying it — those belong to the machine, so that an ordinary braider and a programme-driven lace machine can both be drawn by this code without it knowing the difference.

braidpy.horn_gear.visualization.track_curves(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]], tracks: list[list[tuple[str, int]]] | None = None, scale: float = 1.0) → list[tuple[str, ndarray]]

Each carrier track as a closed run of arcs, seen from above.

A run of positions on the same gear is drawn as a single arc from the notch the carrier came in by to the one it leaves by, following the gear’s rotation, at the radius the carriers actually ride at — so the tracks lie under the carriers rather than beside them.

Tracks belong to the wiring, so they are the same at every step. A machine driven by a programme has none.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine.

  • layout – Where its gears are (compute_layout()).

  • tracks – Its tracks, if already worked out.

  • scale – The layout’s scale.

Returns:

Per distinct closed curve, a name — the loop of gears it runs round — and its points, shape (n, 2), the first repeated at the end.

braidpy.horn_gear.visualization.colored_tracks(machine: BraidingMachine, layout: dict[str, tuple[float, float]], tracks: list[list[tuple[str, int]]] | None = None, scale: float = 1.0) → list[tuple[str, str, ndarray]]

Each carrier track (track_curves()) in its colour: the palette’s, one after another, wherever the tracks are drawn.

Returns:

Per track, its name, its colour and its points.

braidpy.horn_gear.visualization.visualize_machine(machine: BraidingMachine, scale: float = 1.0, output_html: str | None = None, title: str = 'Horn Gear Braiding Machine') → Figure

Static diagram of the machine layout with oriented slot tick marks.

braidpy.horn_gear.visualization.visualize_tracks(machine: BraidingMachine, tracks: list[list[tuple[str, int]]] | None = None, scale: float = 1.0, output_html: str | None = None, title: str = 'Carrier Tracks') → Figure

Draw carrier tracks as circular arcs that meet at physical contact points.

For each run of consecutive positions on the same gear, the arc runs from the physical contact point with the incoming gear to the physical contact point with the outgoing gear, following the gear’s rotation direction. Gear transfers happen exactly at the tangent point between gear circumferences – no jump lines.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine to visualise.

  • tracks – Precomputed tracks (computed if None).

  • scale – Layout scale.

  • output_html – If given, write figure to this HTML file path.

  • title – Figure title.

Returns:

Plotly Figure.

braidpy.horn_gear.visualization.animate(machine: BraidingMachine, n_steps: int | None = None, carrier_positions: dict | None = None, scale: float = 1.0, output_html: str | None = None, title: str = 'Carrier Animation', frame_duration_ms: int = 40, n_substeps: int = 9, max_frames: int = 900) → Figure

Animate carriers with smooth gear rotation between simulation steps.

By default the animation runs for exactly one cycle of the machine — the point at which every carrier is back at the place it set off from, with the drive in its starting phase (state_period()) — so the last frame hands straight back to the first and the page written by output_html plays it round and round. That is a good deal shorter than a carrier’s whole journey: the machine comes back long before any one carrier has been everywhere its track goes.

Each simulation step is split into n_substeps intermediate frames. Carrier and tick-mark positions are interpolated so a 4-slot gear shows a smooth 90° (quarter-turn) rotation per step.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine definition.

  • n_steps – Number of simulation steps to animate. One full cycle if None, falling back to the drive’s own period for a programmed machine, whose carriers need never come back at all.

  • carrier_positions – Optional initial carrier placement.

  • scale – Layout scale.

  • output_html – If given, write figure to this HTML file path.

  • title – Figure title.

  • frame_duration_ms – Duration of each sub-frame in ms.

  • n_substeps – Intermediate frames per simulation step.

  • max_frames – Frame budget. A long cycle gets fewer sub-frames per step rather than a page too big to open.

Returns:

Plotly Figure with animation frames.

horn_gear/examples.py

Classic braiding machine configurations as factory functions.

Each function returns a ready-to-use BraidingMachine, written as its graph (machine_from_graph()): the gears that mesh and where it feeds axial yarns. Each loads itself. braidpy.machine_catalog lists the braids they make.

References

  • Brunnschweiler, D. (1953). “Horn Gear Mechanism of Braiding Machines.”

  • Kyosev, Y. (2014). “Braiding Technology for Textiles.”

braidpy.horn_gear.examples.flat_braid_3() → BraidingMachine

The simplest machine there is: 2 gears of 3 slots, 3 carriers.

Layout:

[A(3)] -- [B(3)]

This is the smallest configuration that still braids, and the easiest one to read in the animation. Six slots hold three carriers; each rides its gear for three steps, hands over at the single contact, rides the other gear for three steps and comes back, so the whole machine repeats every 6 steps. Three strands shuttling between two points is the ordinary three-strand plait.

Both gears have a single connection, so their one contact can always be placed exactly on a slot — the layout is exact.

Returns:

BraidingMachine for a 2-gear, 3-carrier flat braid.

braidpy.horn_gear.examples.flat_braid_4(n_slots: int = 4) → BraidingMachine

Flat braid: 2 gears in a row, turning in opposite directions.

Layout:

[A] -- [B]

Carriers shuttle between the two gears through the single contact. Half the slots can be loaded, so the machine carries n_slots carriers. See flat_braid_3() for the smallest useful case.

Parameters:

n_slots – Number of slots per gear (= number of carriers).

Returns:

BraidingMachine for a 2-gear flat braid.

braidpy.horn_gear.examples.soutache_braid(n_slots: int = 5) → BraidingMachine

Soutache: the narrow flat braid used for trimming and in jewellery.

Layout:

[A(5)] -- [B(5)]

Two gears carrying the same odd number of slots, loaded every other slot, which gives n_slots carriers. The odd count is what makes the braid narrow and even: a carrier returning from one gear comes back on the opposite strand, so every slot lies on its own two-position track and the whole machine repeats in 2 x n_slots steps.

Both gears have a single connection, so their slots sit exactly on their one contact whatever the count — the layout is always exact.

Soutache carries two cords, one fed up the spindle of each gear, and the carriers braid around both as they pass between them. They are Axial columns: they never ride a horn, and each stands clear of the carriers by its gear’s radius. The two cords are what make soutache soutache — the braid closes over them and is held flat, rather than rounding up as an uncored braid would.

Parameters:

n_slots – Slots per gear. Odd values give the classic soutache.

Returns:

BraidingMachine for a 2-gear soutache braid with two cords.

braidpy.horn_gear.examples.princess_braid() → BraidingMachine

Princess braid: 3 gears, 5/6/5 slots, 8 carriers over a cord.

Layout:

           cord
            ↓
[A(5)] -- [B(6)] -- [C(5)]

The classic princess arrangement: two 5-slot end gears either side of a 6-slot centre gear, sixteen slots carrying eight carriers on a single track, so every carrier eventually occupies every slot and the braid is fully interlinked.

Unlike soutache_braid(), this machine has a gear in the middle, so its cord can be fed up that gear’s spindle and stands clear of the carriers by a full gear radius. The cord is an Axial: it never rides a horn, and the carriers braid around it as they pass between the end gears.

The end gears have one connection each, so their 5 slots sit exactly on their contacts; the centre gear’s two contacts are 180° apart, which is three of its six slots. The layout is exact.

Returns:

BraidingMachine for a 3-gear princess braid with a cord core.

braidpy.horn_gear.examples.flat_braid_9(n_end: int = 5) → BraidingMachine

9-carrier flat braid: 4 gears in a row, turnaround gears at each end.

Layout:

[A(5)] -- [B(4)] -- [C(4)] -- [D(5)]

The end gears have only one connection each, so their slot count is free: that single contact can always be put exactly on a slot whatever it is. The interior gears sit between two neighbours on a straight line, 180° apart, which is a whole number of slots for a 4-slot gear. Every variant is therefore geometrically exact.

What n_end changes is how the carrier paths join up. A carrier entering an end gear rides round it and leaves by the same contact it arrived through, so an odd n_end brings it back on the opposite strand and fuses the machine into one closed track over every slot, while an even n_end returns it to its own strand and leaves separate tracks that never exchange carriers:

Odd values always reach 50% loading — the ceiling, since only one of the two slots meeting at a contact may be occupied — at the cost of a much longer period. Even values can fall short: 4 and 8 share a factor with the 4-slot interior gears, which fragments the machine into many short tracks and strands slots that cannot be filled. These are true maxima, not the best a search happened to find: load_carriers solves loading exactly.

Parameters:

n_end – Slot count of the two end gears. Odd gives one combined track, even gives several separate ones.

Returns:

BraidingMachine for a 4-gear flat braid.

braidpy.horn_gear.examples.tubular_braid_8() → BraidingMachine

Classic 8-carrier tubular braid: 4 gears in a ring.

Layout:

   [A]

[D]   [B]
  \   /
   [C]

All gears have 4 slots; rotations alternate around the ring.

Four equal circles in a ring meet at contacts 90° apart on each gear, which is exactly one 4-slot pitch, so each gear’s two contact slots are side by side: carriers then sweep in step with the gear instead of drifting against it.

Returns:

BraidingMachine for a 4-gear ring braid.

braidpy.horn_gear.examples.tubular_braid_12() → BraidingMachine

12-carrier tubular braid: 6 gears in a hexagonal ring.

Each gear has 4 slots; gears alternate direction around the ring. Produces the classic 12-carrier tubular braid.

Returns:

BraidingMachine for a 6-gear hexagonal ring braid.

braidpy.horn_gear.examples.tubular_braid_16() → BraidingMachine

16-carrier tubular braid: 8 gears in a ring.

Each gear has 4 slots; gears alternate direction around the ring. This produces the classic tubular braid with 16 carriers.

Returns:

BraidingMachine for an 8-gear ring braid.

braidpy.horn_gear.examples.triaxial_braid_16() → BraidingMachine

16-carrier triaxial braid: the tubular braid of 16, round 8 axial yarns.

A triaxial braid lays a third set of yarns along the braid, at 0°, between the two sets braided at ±θ: they stiffen it along its length and hold its diameter, which is why braided composites are made so. On a maypole braider each axial yarn is fed up through a hollow horn gear spindle (van Ravenhorst’s thesis, see the references page): it stands still at that gear’s centre while the gear’s carriers go round it, those of one set passing it on the inside of the braid and those of the other on the outside, so that it lies between them.

So this is tubular_braid_16(), unchanged, with an Axial up each of its eight gears.

Returns:

BraidingMachine for an 8-gear ring braid with an axial yarn up each gear.

braidpy.horn_gear.examples.diamond_braid() → BraidingMachine

Diamond / square braid — the same machine as tubular_braid_8().

Drawing the four gears as a 2×2 grid rather than a ring suggests a different machine, but it is not one. Both are a 4-cycle of 4-slot gears with alternating rotations, and they are isomorphic with slot counts and directions respected (A→A, C→B, D→C, B→D): 16 slots, 8 carriers, four 4-position tracks, period 8. So this delegates rather than restating the same gears and connections in a different order.

The braiding terms diamond (1/1 intersection) and square or regular (2/2) name different interlacings of this one machine, not different machines. Telling them apart needs which yarn crosses over which, which the simulator does not compute yet — see the axial/interlacing note in Axial.

Returns:

BraidingMachine for a 4-gear ring braid.

braidpy.horn_gear.examples.mixed_gear_machine() → BraidingMachine

Example machine mixing 4-slot and 6-slot gears.

Layout:

[A(6)] -- [B(4)] -- [C(6)]

Demonstrates heterogeneous gear support.

Returns:

BraidingMachine with mixed slot counts.

The braids horn gear braiding machines make, and the Jacquard lace machines (braidpy.horn_gear.jacquard), as every catalogue lists its braids (braidpy.catalog).

A horn gear machine is one of braidpy.horn_gear.examples, written there as its graph, as a machine of your own is (machine_from_graph()). The machines that braid several bands at once are built by braidpy.horn_gear.multiband, as their line folds round and their bands’ colours are more than a graph says yet.

Listing them loads nothing: a machine is only made, and the simulator and networkx with it, when it is asked for.

machine() → BraidingMachine

The machine, its gears driven by the card.

A braid as neighbours swapping places round a ring: the step between a braid and the ways of making it.

A braid word, a kumihimo disk, a lace machine: each makes a braid by moving strands round a ring of places, two neighbours at a time. A RingProgram says so once, for all of them: the places, which strand starts where — a place may be empty — and rows of swaps, each two neighbouring places exchanging what they hold, the swaps of a row sharing no place so that they are made at once. A braid becomes a ring program (from_braid()), and a ring program becomes each way of making it; read back as a braid (RingProgram.braid()), each must be the braid it was made from, as braidpy compares braids: by their topology, their patterns alike (braidpy.braid_pattern.alike()).

Conventions. The ring is seen from above, from the side the braider works from on a kumihimo disk, and the braid is made downwards, away from the eye, as it hangs below a disk. Places are numbered 0 to n - 1 clockwise, the seam between the last and place 0. A swap of place p exchanges what places p and p + 1 hold:

  • two strands make a crossing. At a positive swap, +1, the strand at p + 1 goes first, anticlockwise, lifted over the one at p — over as seen from above, so passing inside it, nearer the braid’s axis — and the strand at p then moves clockwise into the place it left. At a negative swap, -1, the strand at p goes first, clockwise, over the one at p + 1. With the strands at places 1 to n, counted from the seam, the positive swap of place i - 1 is σᵢ, the negative one σᵢ⁻¹: the disk’s own reading (disk_annular_word()) reads them back so;

  • a strand and an empty place make no crossing: the strand moves on by one place, to the empty one, and the swap’s sign changes nothing;

  • two empty places: nothing moves.

The ring has a seam, between its last place and its first. Strands carried across it twist the braid below them, as carriers going round a tubular braiding machine do: every strand once round the ring is a full twist. That is still a braid, and often a shorter way to make one; but a braid word has its strands in a row from the seam, so the ways made from a word keep them off it for now, and make that very word. Shorter programs, going over the seam, are for later.
