A braid as moves on a kumihimo disk (a mobidai).

A mobidai’s move takes one strand from a slot to another, the short way round, lifted over every strand it passes (braidpy.mobidai). The strands are kept two slots apart — strand k from slot 2k + 3 — so that every strand has an empty slot either side of it, and each crossing is three moves:

  • one of the two strands crossing is lifted over the other, and over every strand between them, into the empty slot beyond it;

  • the other moves into the place it left;

  • the lifted strand settles into the other’s old place.

Every strand is then back two slots from the next, and the disk ready for the next crossing. The two strands need not be neighbours: a band letter a_ts (braidpy.band_canonical_form), strands t and s crossing in front of those between, is three moves however far apart they are, where in crossings of neighbours it is 2(t - s) - 1 of them. The braid is made in band letters where that takes fewer — a disk braid, its strands carried across the disk: Kongo gumi’s 81 crossings, 243 moves so, are 43 letters, 129 moves — and as its ring program’s crossings of neighbours (braidpy.ring_program) where not, as a machine’s braid. A 32-slot disk takes up to 15 strands this way. None passes the seam between the last slot and the first: that would twist the braid, which is still a braid and can be shorter to make, but from a braid word the strands are in a row, and keeping them so makes the word itself. Shorter moves, over the seam, are for later.

disk_braid() reads the braid back as braidpy reads any mobidai’s (mobidai_steps()).

A braid as a punchcard for the Jacquard lace machine.

braidpy’s lace machine (jacquard_lace_ring()) is a ring of 2-slot gears. A bobbin sits in a notch, cut where two neighbouring gears overlap — notch k between gears k and k + 1 — and a gear’s half turn swaps the bobbins of its two notches: gear g, notches g - 1 and g. The notches are a ring of places, and a half turn a swap of neighbours (RingProgram).

A gear always turns the same way, and neighbours turn opposite ways, so which bobbin passes over is fixed by where the crossing is made: a gear turning anticlockwise (an even one) makes a positive crossing, one turning clockwise a negative one. A braid word does not care: its crossings may come with any signs, anywhere. So the ring has notches to spare, and before each crossing its two strands are brought, through the empty notches between and beside them, to two notches whose gear turns the way of the crossing’s sign, crossing nobody; only those two move, and only if they must. Where both are hemmed in, the strands beside are pushed along towards the nearest empty notch. The strands keep their order and keep off the ring’s seam, as the strands of a word do (braidpy.ring_program); and they end in the notches they began in, since a punchcard is run round and round.

Spare notches cost gears but save steps: with one, every strand between a pair and the spare notch must move for each sign that does not suit; with one beside each strand, only the pair does. Where the strands begin matters as much: begun a notch along, the plait’s crossings all fall on gears of their signs. So the strands are tried packed together from every notch, spread a notch apart and spread evenly (_starts()), on as many gears as are given or on each number from the fewest to MOST_GEARS_PER_STRAND a strand; then searched, a few hundred tries seeded: the crossings in other orders where they commute (_reordered()), the strands begun anywhere, a crossing at times at the next nearest gear of its sign. The card of fewest steps is kept, of fewest gears if two tie. A word shortened first (braidpy.braid.Braid.shortened()) has fewer crossings to make, and so fewer moves: Braid Studio shortens it so.

A step of the card is two lines over the gears, as the machine reads it: the gears to turn anticlockwise, then those to turn clockwise. The swaps of a ring program’s row share no notch, so their gears never touch, and a row is a step: each swap is made in the first step after the last that used either of its notches, so that moves of strands apart are made at once.

lace_braid() reads the braid back off the machine: the punchcard is run (simulate()), after each step each bobbin is found in its notch, and each gear that turned swapped the two — the machine’s own motion, with each crossing the sign of the gear’s turn.

braidpy.making.lace.card_conjugate(braid: Braid, search: ConjugateSearch = ConjugateSearch(tries=3000, crossings=300000, warm=1.0, cooling=0.999, cold=0.05, seed=0)) → Braid

A conjugate of a braid whose repeats a lace card makes in fewer steps: the same braid, once repeated, seen another way.

The word is read round, as a card runs it, and rewritten by the braid relations (braidpy.shortening), wherever the word is cut: crossings of strands apart swapped, three crossings of three strands made the other way round. Reading it from elsewhere conjugates it, and a relation keeps it, so each word met is a conjugate. A rewrite that lowers the floor a repeat (repeat_floor()) is kept, one that raises it now and then, less and less often, so as to cross what does not change it. Seeded, so a braid always has the same conjugate. The book’s sinnets, written as cascades of one strand crossing many, come out with a floor a third of theirs or less.

Parameters:

  • braid – The braid.

  • search – How the conjugate is searched for.

Returns:

the braid if none is lower.

The conjugate of lowest floor found

A braid round a core, as a ring word, as a lace machine’s punchcard: a tube made as a tube.

lace_card() keeps its strands off the ring’s seam, as a braid word’s are in a row, and so makes a flat braid curled up; here they go round, across the seam as a tube’s do. A ring word’s moves (braidpy.annulus_braid) say which two neighbours round the ring cross, with which sign, and how far round each strand ends; the crossings are made as lace_card() makes them — the two strands brought through the empty notches between and beside them to a gear turning the way of the sign, the strands beside pushed along if hemmed in — but round the ring, and every strand then walks to where it ends, as many times round the ring as the word takes it. A pass of the card need not bring a strand home: the notches threaded are the same, each perhaps holding another strand, so the card runs round and round.

The same starts and the same seeded search are tried as for lace_card(), a crossing always at the nearest gear of its sign.

Parameters:

  • moves – Crossings ±1 to ±n_strands, turns ±(n_strands + 1).

  • n_strands – The strands round the ring.

  • n_gears – Gears round the ring, even and at least FEWEST_GEARS; each number from the fewest that hold the strands to MOST_GEARS_PER_STRAND a strand if None.

  • search – How the card is searched for.

Returns:

made, its braid round the ring’s core is the word’s (cored_word()).

Return type:

The card

Raises:

ValueError – If no card is found: the strands fill the ring, and its gears do not turn the ways the crossings want.

braidpy.making.lace.step_floor(word: Sequence[int], n_strands: int) → int

The fewest steps any card for a word can take, on any lace ring: no fewer than its longest chain of crossings each waiting for the last, a crossing waiting a step more when a strand of it crossed last the same way with the same sign. Neighbouring gears turn opposite ways, so its two gears are of the same way, a notch apart: it must move a notch between. On the small braids of the catalogue, the fewest steps there are, found by trying every turn of every gear, are this or a few more.

Parameters:

  • word – The crossings, i for σᵢ and -i for σᵢ⁻¹.

  • n_strands – The strands.

Returns:

The floor, in steps.

A braid as a sinnet on Ashley’s stand, found by searching.

On Ashley’s stand (braidpy.ashley_solid_sinnet) the strands lie in spaces round the rim, and a move carries a strand from one space to another, over every strand it passes. A move is not a swap of neighbours, so a braid cannot be turned into moves crossing by crossing as for a disk or a lace machine: a sinnet that makes it is searched for instead.

The sinnets searched are made as the book’s are: every space gives a strand and receives one in each cycle, so a cycle’s moves follow a derangement of the spaces — no space to itself — and every space has its strands back after a cycle. Each candidate is the strands shared out among the spaces, the derangement, and the order of its moves. A cycle read from another move is the same braid, so the first move is taken from space 1.

A sinnet is found when its braid is the braid wanted, compared as every way of making a braid compares them: by their topology (alike()) — the braid repeated, read from any strand, however written. Fewer spaces are tried first, so the simplest sinnet is found first; the search stops at a time limit, and says whether it tried everything it could. Not every braid is a sinnet: when none is found, the nearest is given, and how far it is (distance()).

Every braid can be made on the stand, though, once its moves need not be a sinnet’s (ashley_moves()): one strand per space, with an empty space after each, and each crossing made in three or four moves through the empty spaces, every space holding what it held before. It is the braid itself, exactly, but no longer a sinnet of the book’s kind: spaces give and take strands unevenly, and a space can sit empty.

A sinnet can also be made from the shape it is to take, as the book draws it (sinnet_from_shape()): straight lines across the shape, parallel to its sides, each turning at the outline in a bight into the next. The bights are the spaces, the lines the moves, made in the book’s order. And the other way: a sinnet’s moves, grouped by the direction of their lines (move_groups()), are the same at any size for shapes drawn on one principle, and make its shape (shapes_from_moves()).

braidpy.making.ashley.ashley_moves(braid: Braid) → AshleySolidSinnet

Any braid on Ashley’s stand, crossing by crossing; see the module.

The strands lie one per odd space, from space 1, each followed by an empty even space: 2n spaces for n strands. A strand moved from an odd space goes anticlockwise, from an even one clockwise, over every strand it passes. The two strands of σᵢ are in spaces a = 2(n - i) - 1 and b = a + 2, as the stand reads its strands the other way round, and the crossing is made through the empty spaces after them:

  • σᵢ: b to b + 1, b + 1 to a + 1, over the strand in a; then a to b and a + 1 back to a;

  • σᵢ⁻¹: a to b, over the strand there; then b (its earlier strand) to b + 1, and on to a.

Parameters:

braid – The braid.

Returns:

The strands and moves, as a sinnet whose one cycle is the braid, exactly.

braidpy.making.ashley.move_groups(moves: Sequence[tuple[int, int]]) → MoveGroups

A sinnet’s moves grouped by the direction of their lines (see MoveGroups).

Lines of one direction never cross. Where joining every two moves whose lines do not cross leaves sets in which none do, as across an oblong, those sets are the directions, taken as evenly spread (at right angles for two). Otherwise, as across a triangle, whose lines of different directions miss each other near its corners, the directions are found from the spaces’ numbers: round a stand of n spaces evenly spaced, the line from space a to space b runs at (a + b) π / n and a half turn, so moves whose spaces add up to the same number, modulo n, are parallel. Wherever the numbering starts, or whichever way it runs, the directions only turn together, and are kept turned as little as can be.

Parameters:

moves – The moves, each space giving and receiving once.

Returns:

The groups.

The shapes drawn on the principle of a sinnet’s moves, at its size.

On a grid (grid_shape()): the shapes with as many lines as there are moves, on the grids their groups (move_groups()) say, each kept if its own sinnet joins the same spaces. Off a grid, made from the groups: each direction of lines is a side, or a pair of parallel sides, of the shape, as far across as its moves need, a regular polygon of an odd number of sides (regular_polygon()) where the directions are evenly spread with as many moves each, and the shape with sides parallel in pairs; each kept if its own sinnet’s moves group alike.

braidpy.making.ashley.sinnet_from_shape(outline: Sequence[tuple[float, float]], extra: Sequence[int] | None = None, turned: Sequence[int] = (), order: str = 'book', holes: Sequence[Sequence[tuple[float, float]]] = (), across: Sequence[float] | None = None, halfway: float | None = None) → AshleySolidSinnet

The sinnet the book’s method makes of a shape.

Lines cross the shape parallel to its sides (shape_lines()), and at the outline each turns, in a bight, into the next: two lines meeting the outline at one point into each other, others into their neighbour on the same side. The bights are the spaces, numbered anticlockwise from the one nearest the first corner, and each line is a move between the two it joins.

The moves are made in the book’s order: from space 1, along the line across the first side if one starts there; then each from the space beside where the last ended, one back, then one on, and so on, along the line parallel to the last while there is one there, across the shape and back; a space that has given its strand gives none again, and its line is taken towards it. The moves of any track (shape_tracks()) may be made the other way round: every space still gives once and receives once. Each space starts with the fewest strands the order lets it (least_counts()), and any extra: the book adds strands at the corners of a shape to sharpen its edges.

Parameters:

  • outline – The shape’s corners, anticlockwise, in spacings between lines; the first is where the numbering starts, the book’s bottom left.

  • extra – Strands to add to each space, space 1 first; none if None.

  • turned – The tracks made the other way round, numbered from 1 as shape_tracks() lists them.

  • order – “book”, the book’s order; or “spaces”, space by space, as the book makes the moves where it cannot alternate them.

  • holes – The corners of each hole in the shape, clockwise: its bights are numbered with the outline’s, by the way they lie from the middle (shape_diagram()).

  • across – The lines’ directions, if not the sides’, as on the diagonal grid (shape_lines()).

  • halfway – The direction of lines halfway between the others’ crossings, as on the skewed grid (shape_lines()).

Returns:

The sinnet.

Raises:

ValueError – If the lines cannot be made into moves in that order.

braidpy.making.ashley.triangle(lines_per_side: int) → list[tuple[float, float]]

A triangle standing on its base, as the book draws #3045, #3047 and #3051 (2, 4 and 6 lines a side): see regular_polygon().

A braid designed in braid3d, the 3D braid designer of craftdesignonline.com (see the references page), read from its file as a mobidai braid: the disk’s slots, where each yarn starts, and the moves of a cycle (CatalogedMobidai).

The file (.b3d) is URL-encoded JSON: each yarn’s colour, and the steps the braid was designed by, each a group of moves of yarns from one angle round the disk to another, or a repeat of earlier steps. web/b3d.js writes one for a braid made on the marudai here (write_b3d() writes any design’s JSON so, read_b3d() reads it). This needs only the standard library, so that Braid Studio can read a design in the browser too.

How a file is read:

  • Where the yarns start: the first list of where the yarns are that names each yarn once. braid3d, and braidpy after it, write with each step where the yarns are before it, the first step’s list left as it was by braid3d and where they start by braidpy: either way, that list is the start.

  • A step moves the yarns standing at its moves’ first angles, as braid3d does, each to its second angle, the short way round, one after another in the order given, but for a yarn going where another of the step is leaving, which waits for it to go, as a braider makes room.

  • A repeat first moves the yarns back to where the repeated steps found them, then plays those steps again, so many times. Moving them back must pass no yarn over another, which is checked: the yarns keep their order round the disk, only spaced otherwise. Its rotate turns the whole braid, which moves nothing against anything else and changes nothing here.

  • The disk: angles become the slots of a disk of as few slots as hold them all exactly; a design whose angles fall on no such disk is given as few as keep every yarn in its order round the disk and every move going the same way round. The braid is the same; only the spacing differs. A move of exactly half a turn, which the file cannot say the way round of, goes round as a mobidai’s does. braidpy writes a move of half a turn or more as two steps, each less than half a turn, so it is read going round as it went.

  • The cycle: a design that is one cycle and a repeat of it is that cycle, made as many times; any other is all its moves, made once.

class braidpy.parametric_strand.StrandPath(slots: tuple[int, ...], signs: tuple[int, ...], spacing: float = 1.0, amplitude: float = 0.2, profile: tuple[float, ...] = (0.0, 1.0))

Bases: object

One strand’s path through a braid, segment by segment.

Unlike ParametricStrand, which is a closure, this keeps the braid’s own description of the strand — where it is and what it passed — so that exact things can be computed from it. One unit of z per generator, and it repeats.

Parameters:

  • signs – Per segment, +1 if it crosses over, -1 if under, 0 if it holds its slot.

  • spacing – Distance between neighbouring slots.

  • amplitude – How far off the axis a crossing strand rides.

  • profile – How it travels sideways; see LINEAR and SMOOTHSTEP.

braidpy.parametric_strand.strand_paths(braid, spacing: float = 1.0, amplitude: float = 0.2, profile: tuple[float, ...] = (0.0, 1.0)) → list[StrandPath]

The path of every strand of a braid.

Which strand of a crossing goes over is read from the generator’s sign, not from the direction it moves: a positive generator sends the strand coming from the lower slot over the top, and its inverse sends the one from the upper slot over instead. Both exchange the same pair, so a model that watched only the slots would make a braid and its inverse identical.

Parameters:

  • spacing – Distance between neighbouring slots.

  • amplitude – How far off the axis a crossing strand rides.

  • profile – How a strand travels sideways within a segment.

braidpy.parametric_strand.transported_frame(points)

A frame carried along a centreline without spinning about it.

Two vectors square to the curve and to each other at every point, got by rolling the previous pair onto the new tangent — parallel transport. The obvious alternatives both misbehave:

  • the Frenet frame flips at an inflection, where the curve straightens and the normal is undefined, which creases a tube drawn on it;

  • recomputing a frame at each point from a fixed world axis, as the Cosserat animation’s create_circle does, leaves consecutive rings unaligned, so a tube built segment by segment does not join up — and it degenerates when the curve runs along that axis, which np.allclose(direction, [0, 0, 1]) catches going up and misses coming down.

The carried frame need not close up after a loop. For a tube of circular section in one colour that is invisible; for anything painted round the tube it is not.

Parameters:

points – The centreline, as a sequence of (x, y, z).

Returns:

(centre, normal, binormal) as arrays of one row per point.

Sweeps a circle of radius along a sampled centreline, so a picture of a braid shows its strands at their real thickness — and therefore shows them touching, which is the whole of what sets a braid’s size. A line drawing cannot show that and has to be believed instead.

Takes the points rather than a strand, so it serves anything that can be sampled: a ParametricStrand via sample(), a StrandPath, a helix, or a rod simulation’s output.

braidpy.parametric_braid.closest_approach(strands: Sequence, n_samples: int = 600, span: float = 1.0, against: Sequence[int] | None = None) → float

The nearest the centres of two different strands come to each other.

Strands of diameter d may not come closer than d. Nothing in a drawing enforces that, so it has to be measured — and a shape that fails here is not a braid however pretty. Works on anything that answers position(z) over a known length, whoever produced it.

Every pair of heights is compared, not only equal ones. Comparing strands at the same height is much cheaper and is wrong: two strands that wind round each other pass closest at different heights, and on a three-strand rope laid one turn per period the equal-height figure overstates the clearance by a third. A strand is followed over span periods either side of the other’s, which is ample — the distance between two points is at least their difference in height, so a neighbour further away than that in z cannot be the nearest.

Parameters:

  • strands – The strands to compare.

  • n_samples – Points sampled along a period. The measurement is a minimum over samples, so it converges from above.

  • span – Periods to follow one strand either side of the other’s. The distance between two points is at least their difference in height, so a fraction of a period is enough whenever the strands are thin against the period — and much cheaper.

  • against – Compare only these strands against all the others, rather than every pair. For a braid with a symmetry that carries one strand onto another, most pairs are repeats of a few, and naming the few is the difference between a search that finishes and one that does not. Comparing everything if left out.

Returns:

The smallest distance found; infinity if there are fewer than two strands.

The 2D braid diagram, drawn by braidpy rather than by a library.

braidpy used to hand this picture to braid-visualiser, which drew a perfectly good diagram in its own colours — so a strand was one colour in the console and another in the plot, and the two could not be read together. Drawing it here fixes that: the diagram uses terminal_colors, the same palette draw() uses, so strand 3 is the same colour wherever you look at it.

The braid runs down the page, the way a braid hangs and the way a braider works, with the word written above it. Strands swing across on the smoothstep profile of parametric_strand, so a crossing is a curve rather than a corner; pass profile=LINEAR for straight segments.

Nothing about the braid is re-derived here. strand_paths() gives each strand as a curve in three coordinates — across the braid, depth (positive where a strand passes in front), and along — so the diagram is that curve seen from the front, with the strand passing behind interrupted where the two meet.

Each strand as the pieces of it that are visible from the front.

A strand is hidden where it passes behind another — where the two are at the same place across the braid and this one has the lesser depth. Breaking the line there is what makes a diagram readable as a braid rather than as a tangle.

  • paths – StrandPath objects, as strand_paths() returns.

  • n_samples – Points along each strand. A crossing narrower than the spacing between samples would be drawn unbroken.

  • gap – How wide the break is, as a fraction of the distance between neighbouring strands.

Returns:

Per strand, a list of (n, 2) arrays of (across, along) to draw as separate lines.

Asked for the very last point of one period it therefore answers with the first, and a diagram drawn from that has every strand jumping back to where it started. The colour of a strand, matching the one the console draws it in.

index – Which strand, from 0. Wraps round when there are more strands than colours, exactly as the console does.

Returns:

A colour matplotlib understands.

Braids on a ring of slots, and the shape a laid rope takes.

References on the annular braid group:

  • https://people.math.wisc.edu/~aekent2/annular.pdf

  • https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228456153_Cohomology_of_Artin_groups_of_type_zAn_Bn_and_applications

  • https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4504420/braid-groups-for-ropes

A flat braid lays its slots out on a line, so a strand that wants to get from one end to the other has to climb over everyone in between. An annulus lays them round a circle, and that changes what a word can ask for:

A crossing puts two neighbouring strands past each other. On a line one of them goes over; on a ring the depth direction is radial, so one of them goes outside — further from the axis — and the other inside. A positive move sends the strand in the lower-numbered slot of the pair outside, which is the same rule as the flat braid’s positive generator sending the lower strand over.

Slot numbers run 0 to N-1, so the pairs run (0,1) up to (N-2,N-1) — indices 1 to N-1 — and then (N-1,0), index N, which is the pair a flat braid has no room for. Nothing distinguishes that pair on the ring: it is the pair whose slot numbers wrap, and the wrap exists only because the numbering has to start somewhere. Rotate the labels and a different pair becomes index N. The annular braid literature writes this generator as \(\sigma_0\) or \(\sigma_N\) and says the indices are read modulo N; wrap_crossing() is just a name for crossing(N) so a word reads without the reader counting slots.

A turn carries every strand round one slot together. Nobody passes anybody and nobody goes outside anybody; the cross-section simply rotates. On a line there is no such move. On a ring it is what a rope is. Index N + 1 names it.

Everything up to tubular_paths() is bookkeeping — which strand is where, and which passed outside which — and is exact combinatorics, checkable against a drawing of the braid.

rope_helices() is the one piece of geometry in braidpy that is both closed-form and physical, and it is worth being clear about why it can be. Laying up a rope asks nothing of the strands beyond winding on together, so their shape is a one-parameter family — helices of radius R — and symmetry says where they touch without anyone having to search for it. Minimising length then drives R down until they do, at lay_radius(). Take away either the symmetry or the absence of crossings and neither step survives; see docs/source/why_no_closed_form.md.

braidpy.annulus_braid.crossing(index: int) → int

The move that puts slots index - 1 and index past each other.

Used positive, the strand in slot index - 1 passes outside — at the greater radius — and ends up in slot index; the other passes inside. Negate the move to swap who goes outside.

Parameters:

index – Which neighbouring pair, from 1 to n_strands. The last value names the pair (n_strands - 1, 0), whose slot numbers wrap; wrap_crossing() names it without counting.

Returns:

The move, which is the index itself.

braidpy.annulus_braid.wrap_crossing(n_strands: int) → int

The move that crosses the pair whose slot numbers wrap round to zero.

This is crossing(n_strands): the pair made of the last slot and slot zero. It is a crossing like any other — the ring has no privileged place, and which pair wraps depends only on where the numbering starts. What makes it worth a name is that a flat braid has no such pair, so this is the one crossing that needs the ring.

Used positive, the strand in the last slot passes outside, and carries on round rather than turning back: its winding goes up by one while the other strand’s goes down.

Parameters:

n_strands – How many slots the ring has.

Returns:

The move, which is n_strands.

braidpy.annulus_braid.turn(n_strands: int) → int

The move that carries every strand round one slot, passing nobody.

Nobody is outside or inside anybody — the whole cross-section rotates. Used positive it turns towards increasing slot numbers.

Parameters:

n_strands – How many slots the ring has.

Returns:

The move, which is n_strands + 1.

braidpy.annulus_braid.rope(n_strands: int) → list[int]

The word for a rope: every strand round together, once round the tube.

Laying up a rope is not a sequence of crossings — no strand climbs over another — it is the cross-section turning.

Parameters:

n_strands – How many strands are laid up.

Returns:

The word, one turn per slot, which brings every strand home.

braidpy.annulus_braid.solid_word(moves: Sequence[int], n_strands: int) → list[int]

The flat braid word of a ring braid with nothing in the middle.

A solid braid — a kumihimo cord, a solid sinnet — has no core for its strands to go round: they meet in the middle. Filling the hole of the annulus that way sends each crossing to the flat braid’s generator of the same index, and the two moves a flat braid has no room for to what they become once the middle is solid:

  • the turn, every strand carried round one slot towards increasing numbers, is σₙ₋₁…σ₂σ₁: the last strand passes outside every other to the front, a 1/n turn of the whole braid; n of them are a full twist. A strand that goes once round inside all the others, crossing them and then the seam, so comes back unlinked;

  • the crossing whose slots wrap is what the first crossing becomes once the numbering is turned back by one: the turn, σ₁, the turn undone.

This respects every relation of the ring’s moves, so the flat word does not depend on where the ring’s numbering starts, up to conjugation.

Parameters:

  • moves – Crossings ±1 to ±n_strands, turns ±(n_strands + 1).

  • n_strands – How many slots the ring has.

Returns:

The word, as signed generator indices from 1 to n_strands - 1, with any generator next to its own inverse cancelled.

Raises:

ValueError – If a move is not one of the ring’s.

braidpy.annulus_braid.ring_moves(word: Sequence[int], n_strands: int) → tuple[list[int], bool]

A flat braid word as moves on a ring: what solid_word() undoes.

A full run of crossings round the ring — σₙ₋₁…σ₁, or its inverse σ₁⁻¹…σₙ₋₁⁻¹ — is the bobbins all turning one place round (turn()), as a braider lays up a rope; carried out as crossings, one strand would go all the way round under the others. Every other crossing stays a crossing of neighbours. The ring is numbered whichever way round finds the more turns: the other way is a half turn of the whole braid about its axis, σᵢ read as σₙ₋ᵢ.

Parameters:

  • word – Signed generator indices, from 1 to n_strands - 1.

  • n_strands – How many slots the ring has.

Returns:

The moves — crossings ±1 to ±(n_strands - 1), turns ±(n_strands + 1) — and whether the ring is numbered the other way round. solid_word() of the moves is the word, or read the other way round if so, with any generator next to its own inverse cancelled.

braidpy.annulus_braid.cored_word(moves: Sequence[int], n_strands: int) → list[int]

The flat braid word of a ring braid round a core: the core kept, as a strand of its own that the others go round.

solid_word() fills the middle, and a braid round a core and the same braid lifted off it are then one; a strand going once round the core comes back unlinked. Kept as a strand, the core tells them apart: a tube is not a flat braid curled up. The core is strand 1, standing still, and the ring’s slots are strands 2 to n_strands + 1:

  • a crossing of slots i - 1 and i is σᵢ₊₁, of the same sign;

  • the turn is σₙ₊₁…σ₃σ₂σ₁²: the last strand passes outside every other to the front, as in solid_word(), and goes round the core;

  • the crossing whose slots wrap is the turn, σ₂, the turn undone.

Forgetting the core (strand 1) gives solid_word() back.

Parameters:

  • moves – Crossings ±1 to ±n_strands, turns ±(n_strands + 1).

  • n_strands – How many slots the ring has.

Returns:

The word on n_strands + 1 strands.

Raises:

ValueError – If a move is not one of the ring’s.

braidpy.annulus_braid.turns_last(moves: Sequence[int], n_strands: int) → list[int]

The same ring braid with its turns all at the end, as few as there are.

A turn renumbers the slots by one, so a crossing made after it is the crossing of the pair one slot back before it: a turn followed by crossing i is crossing i - 1 followed by the turn, indices read round the ring. Moved to the end so, the turns one way and the other cancel, and what is left is the cross-section’s net rotation.

Parameters:

  • moves – Crossings ±1 to ±n_strands, turns ±(n_strands + 1).

  • n_strands – How many slots the ring has.

Returns:

The crossings, then the turns, all one way.

Raises:

ValueError – If a move is not one of the ring’s.

class braidpy.annulus_braid.TubularStrandPath(slots: tuple[int, ...], signs: tuple[int, ...], n_slots: int)

Bases: object

Where one strand goes round a tubular braid, and what it passed.

This records the braid’s combinatorics, not a shape: which slot the strand occupies at each step and which side of each crossing it took. Turning that into a curve is the part that has no general answer.

Parameters:

  • slots – Its unwrapped slot number at each of len(signs) + 1 instants — it counts on past the last slot rather than resetting to zero, so that going round reads as carrying on.

  • signs – Per move, +1 if it passed outside — further from the axis — -1 if inside, 0 if it passed nobody. The two strands of a crossing always get +1 and -1; a turn gives everyone 0.

  • n_slots – How many slots the ring has.

slots: tuple[int, ...]
signs: tuple[int, ...]
n_slots: int
property length: int

The braid’s period along its axis, one unit per move.

property turns: float

How many times round the tube the strand goes in one period.

braidpy.annulus_braid.tubular_paths(moves: Sequence[int], n_strands: int) → list[TubularStrandPath]

Follow every strand round a tubular braid word.

Parameters:

  • moves – The word. ±i for i in 1..``n_strands - 1`` crosses slots i-1 and i; ±n_strands crosses the wrapping pair (n_strands - 1, 0); ±(n_strands + 1) turns the whole ring; 0 does nothing. A positive crossing sends the strand in the lower-numbered slot outside, at the greater radius.

  • n_strands – How many strands, which is how many slots the ring has.

Returns:

One path per strand, in strand order.

Raises:

ValueError – If a move names something the ring does not have.

braidpy.annulus_braid.packing_radius(n_strands: int, diameter: float) → float

The radius n parallel strands sit at when they touch their neighbours.

Evenly spaced round a circle, strands touch when the chord between two neighbours is one diameter:

\[R = \frac{d}{2 \sin(\pi / n)}\]

This is the cross-section packing answer, and it is exact only for strands that run straight — a rope with no lay at all. Twist them and they come closer than this says, because a strand’s neighbour is nearer at a different height than alongside it: at the tightest lay they can be made at, three strands at this radius clear 0.76 of a diameter, and the shortfall barely eases with more strands — 0.71 at twelve. For a rope with an actual lay use lay_radius(), which solves for it.

Parameters:

  • n_strands – How many strands are laid up.

  • diameter – How thick they are.

Returns:

The radius at which parallel neighbours just touch.

Raises:

ValueError – If there are fewer than two strands to touch.

braidpy.annulus_braid.minimum_lay(n_strands: int, diameter: float) → float

The shortest lay an evenly laid rope of this thickness can have.

Strand k of an evenly laid rope is strand 0 slid along the axis by k n-ths of a lay — the strands are one helix, repeated at n phases. So take a point on one and the matching point on another: they are at the same place across the rope and differ only by lay / n of height. Widening the rope does not separate them, because they are the same point of the same curve. Hence

\[\lambda \ge n \, d\]

Below that no radius keeps the strands apart and the rope cannot be made.

What this needs is the evenness, not ropes in general: it follows from the strands being one curve repeated, which is what “evenly laid” means here. A rope whose strands differ from one another is outside it.

The bound is not attained — clearing a diameter at it would take an infinite radius — and it is rarely what bites first; crowding round the circle usually does. It is cheap to check and exact, which is its use.

Parameters:

  • n_strands – How many strands are laid up.

  • diameter – How thick they are.

Returns:

The shortest workable lay length.

braidpy.annulus_braid.helix_clearance(n_strands: int, radius: float, lay: float, n_samples: int = 2000) → float

How close two strands of a laid rope come, exactly.

Because the strands are one helix repeated — strand k slid along by k n-ths of a lay — the distance between two of them depends only on how far along one is slid relative to the other:

\[D(w)^2 = 4R^2\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi w}{\lambda}\right) + \left(\frac{k\lambda}{n} - w\right)^2\]

so the clearance is that minimised over w — one variable, no surface to search. At w = k\lambda/n it is the chord between neighbours, which is the packing answer; at w = 0 it is k\lambda/n, which is why minimum_lay() exists. The true minimum is generally at neither.

Parameters:

  • n_strands – How many strands are laid up.

  • radius – The radius they sit at.

  • lay – The lay length — the axial distance for one full turn.

  • n_samples – Points in the coarse scan, before it is refined.

Returns:

The smallest distance between the centres of two strands.

braidpy.annulus_braid.lay_radius(n_strands: int, diameter: float = 0.4, lay: float | None = None, tolerance: float = 1e-09) → float

The radius a rope of a given lay settles at, found by squeezing it.

Nothing holds strands out at a radius: a helix of smaller radius is shorter, so tension pulls them in and what stops them is each other. Where they stop depends on the lay, and not in a way packing_radius() can express — the tighter the lay, the further out they must sit for the same clearance, because winding brings a strand nearer to its neighbour’s other turns.

There is no closed form, only a well-posed search: helix_clearance() rises with the radius, so bisection finds where it equals a diameter. That it is a search rather than a formula is the point — see docs/source/why_no_closed_form.md.

Parameters:

  • n_strands – How many strands are laid up.

  • diameter – How thick they are.

  • lay – The lay length. Defaults to the shortest that can be made, minimum_lay(), which needs an infinite radius — so give a longer one for a rope that exists.

  • tolerance – How closely to pin the radius down, relative to the diameter.

Returns:

The radius at which the strands just touch.

Raises:

ValueError – If the lay is too short for the strands to fit past one another at any radius at all.

A strand winding uniformly at a constant radius.

braidpy.annulus_braid.rope_helices(n_strands: int, diameter: float = 0.4, length: int = 1, turns: float = 1.0, radius: float | None = None) → list[Helix]

The shape a laid rope takes: helices, touching, evenly spaced.

The only braid shape in this package that is both closed-form and physical. It is available because a rope asks nothing of its strands beyond winding on together, which leaves a one-parameter family; because symmetry says which strands touch, so the contact set needs no searching; and because minimising length within that family is then a single inequality. Where that inequality bites has no closed form once the rope has any lay to it, so lay_radius() searches for it.

Parameters:

  • n_strands – How many strands are laid up.

  • diameter – How thick they are.

  • length – The period along the axis.

  • turns – Laps per period.

  • radius – Override the radius. Left out, it is the one the lay settles at — see lay_radius() — since nothing holds the strands out at any other. Anything smaller makes them overlap, which closest_approach() reports.

Returns:

One helix per strand, evenly spaced in phase.

class braidpy.annulus_braid.TubularBraidStrand(n_strands: int, radius: float, braid_angle: float, bulge: float, direction: int, phase: float)

Bases: object

A strand of a braided tube, after Brunnschweiler’s geometric model.

The strand winds round the tube at a constant angle to the axis while its distance from the axis swings in and out — out where it passes over a strand coming the other way, in where it passes under. That swing is the whole of the braid: take it away and the strands are helices that would have to pass through one another.

From “The geometry of tubular braided structures”, page 19: https://scispace.com/pdf/the-geometry-of-tubular-braided-structures-32b4yiwio2.pdf

Parameters:

  • n_strands – How many strands the tube has, half going each way.

  • radius – The mean distance from the axis.

  • braid_angle – The angle the mean helix makes with the axis, in radians — zero is straight up the tube, a right angle is round it. The swing makes the local angle wander either side of it, and biases it upward, since swinging out and in adds path across the tube but none along it.

  • bulge – How far the strand swings out and in. Two strands crossing are 2 * bulge apart radially, so half a diameter makes them touch there.

  • direction – +1 or -1, which way round the tube it goes.

  • phase – Where on the circle it starts, in radians.

n_strands: int
radius: float
braid_angle: float
bulge: float
direction: int
phase: float
property length: float

The axial distance in which the strand goes once round the tube.

position(z: float) → tuple[float, float, float]

Where the strand is at z along the axis.

braidpy.annulus_braid.tubular_braid(n_strands: int, radius: float = 1.0, braid_angle: float = 0.7853981633974483, diameter: float = 0.4, bulge: float | None = None) → list[TubularBraidStrand]

A braided tube: half the strands each way, interlacing.

Two things the bare formula does not say, and without which it does not braid:

The strands alternate direction round the tube. Spaced evenly and alternating, two that cross meet where the radial swing is at its extreme, so one is fully out and the other fully in. Space them any other way and they meet mid-swing, or — in the worst case — where the swing is zero and they are in the same place.

The swing follows the direction. A strand going one way bulges out where one going the other way tucks in; give them a common sign and both strands of a crossing take the same radius, which is a collision rather than a braid.

Parameters:

  • n_strands – How many strands, which must be even — half go each way.

  • radius – The mean distance from the axis.

  • braid_angle – The angle the strands make with the axis, in radians.

  • diameter – How thick the strands are. Only used to pick a default bulge; the geometry itself does not depend on it.

  • bulge – How far the strands swing. Half a diameter if left out, which sets two crossing strands exactly a diameter apart at the crossing — the clearance everywhere only while the crossings are the tightest spot, which closest_approach() will tell you.

Returns:

One strand per place round the tube, alternating direction.

Raises:

ValueError – If the strand count is odd, or the braid angle leaves the strands running straight up the tube without braiding.

braidpy.annulus_braid.tubular_braid_clearance(strands: Sequence, n_samples: int = 500) → float

How close two strands of a braided tube come, using its symmetry.

Turning the tube by two places and relabelling the strands to match carries the braid onto itself, so the pair (0, j) is the same distance apart as the pair (2, j + 2). Every pair is therefore a repeat of one involving strand 0 or strand 1, and comparing those two against the rest answers the question at a fraction of the cost — which matters, because finding a tube’s radius asks it a few dozen times.

The strands are also thin against the length in which they go once round, so only a fraction of a period either side need be searched.

Parameters:

  • strands – The strands of one braided tube, as tubular_braid() returns them.

  • n_samples – Points per period.

Returns:

The smallest distance between the centres of two strands.

braidpy.annulus_braid.crossing_binds_above(n_strands: int, braid_angle: float) → bool

Which of the two conditions on the radius is the binding one.

See tubular_braid_radius(). Below the crossover angle the tube’s width is set by the strands’ own swing; above it, by how fast they climb. The crossover is at

\[\tan q^{*} = \sqrt{1 + 4/n^{2}}\]

which tends to 45 degrees as the strands are added, so any braid of more than a few strands changes character near 45.

Parameters:

  • n_strands – How many strands, half each way.

  • braid_angle – The angle they make with the axis, in radians.

Returns:

True if the climbing condition binds, False if the swing does.

braidpy.annulus_braid.tubular_braid_radius(n_strands: int, diameter: float = 0.4, braid_angle: float = 0.7853981633974483, bulge: float | None = None) → float

The narrowest tube on which these strands braid without crowding.

In closed form, from the geometry, rather than by squeezing and measuring.

Take the two strands of a crossing and let s and t measure how far each has gone past it. At the crossing itself the swing holds them 2b apart. Just beside it the swing has decayed — as \(\cos(ns/2)\), so by \(b n^{2} s^{2}/8\) to second order — while the angle between them has opened by s + t and their heights have parted by \(R\cot q\,(s - t)\). Writing p = s + t and m = s - t, the squared distance comes out as

\[D^{2} \simeq 4b^{2} + p^{2}\left[(R^{2} - b^{2}) - \tfrac{1}{4}b^{2}n^{2}\right] + m^{2}\left[R^{2}\cot^{2}q - \tfrac{1}{4}b^{2}n^{2}\right]\]

— no cross term, the two motions being independent. So the crossing is the tightest spot exactly when both brackets are non-negative, and the narrowest tube is where the first of them reaches zero:

\[R = b \max\!\left(\sqrt{1 + \tfrac{n^{2}}{4}},\; \tfrac{n}{2}\tan q\right)\]

Two conditions, and which one binds says what is holding the tube open: the strands’ own swing, or the rate at which they climb past one another. crossing_binds_above() says which.

The rope has no such formula (lay_radius() searches), and the reason is visible here: this works because a crossing is a point of symmetry for both strands, so it is automatically a critical point of the distance and only the second-order terms matter. Two helices of a rope have no such point — their nearest approach is not where the chord between them is.

Parameters:

  • n_strands – How many strands, half each way.

  • diameter – How thick they are.

  • braid_angle – The angle they make with the axis, in radians.

  • bulge – The radial swing; half a diameter if left out.

Returns:

The smallest mean radius at which the strands are no closer together than they are at their crossings.

braidpy.annulus_braid.cover_factor(n_strands: int, radius: float, braid_angle: float, diameter: float) → float

How much of the tube’s surface the strands hide, as a fraction.

The measure of a braid’s tightness, and the one a braider cares about: a sleeve at 0.4 is visibly open, one at 1 is closed. Half the strands run each way, so one direction covers the surface when its n/2 strands, each crossing a circumferential cut in a segment of d / cos(q), together span the circumference:

\[\text{cover} = \frac{n}{2}\, \frac{d / \cos q}{2 \pi R}\]

Above 1 the strands of one direction would have to overlap each other, which round ones cannot.

Parameters:

  • n_strands – How many strands, half each way.

  • radius – The mean distance from the axis.

  • braid_angle – The angle the strands make with the axis, in radians.

  • diameter – How thick they are.

Returns:

The covered fraction, counting one direction.

braidpy.annulus_braid.radius_for_cover(n_strands: int, diameter: float, braid_angle: float, cover: float = 1.0) → float

The radius at which the strands cover that fraction of the tube.

cover_factor() rearranged, which is worth having because the radius that avoids crowding and the radius that looks like a braid are not the same number, and the gap between them is the model’s main limitation — see below.

\[R = \frac{n \, d}{4 \pi \, \text{cover} \, \cos q}\]

This will not clear. At its own non-crowding radius (tubular_braid_radius()) the model covers about 0.4 whatever the strand count, the braid angle or the swing depth — measured across 4 to 16 strands and 45 to 80 degrees. Tightening past that makes the strands overlap: at a cover of 0.9 they are a third of a diameter into one another.

The reason is the sinusoidal swing. Two strands are nearest not at their crossing, where the swing holds them a full 2b apart, but just beside it, where the swing has decayed while the angle between them is still small — and at a smaller radius a given angle buys less arc to separate them with. A real braid escapes this because its strands are not round: yarn flattens where it crosses and stays proud for longer, which is a squarer swing than a sine.

So use this to draw a braid that looks like one, and tubular_braid_radius() for the tightest the round-strand model honestly allows.

Parameters:

  • n_strands – How many strands, half each way.

  • diameter – How thick they are.

  • braid_angle – The angle they make with the axis, in radians.

  • cover – The fraction of the surface to hide.

Returns:

The mean radius giving that cover.

Closed-form shapes for braids symmetric enough to have one.

No formula takes a braid word to the shape its strands settle into — see docs/source/why_no_closed_form.md. But some braids are regular enough that a family of shapes can be written down and the choosing left to a handful of numbers, and then the question becomes a small search instead of an open problem.

The classic three-strand flat braid is one. Every strand does the same thing a third of a period later, so one curve and three phases describe the whole braid:

\[x_k(z) = A \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi z}{P} - \frac{2\pi k}{3}\right), \qquad y_k(z) = H \sin\!\left(\frac{4\pi z}{P} - \frac{4\pi k}{3}\right)\]

The over-and-under runs at exactly twice the frequency of the side-to-side, which is what makes each strand a figure eight in cross-section, and what makes the three of them braid rather than merely weave past one another. braid_word() reads the braid straight off the curves and confirms it is the flat braid, six crossings to the period.

Two amplitudes and a period are all that is left to choose, so the shape can be optimised — shortest strands that still keep a diameter apart — which is a search in two variables rather than over a space of curves. That is the honest sense in which a braid like this has an analytic geometry: the family is closed-form, the choice within it is not.

Two facts about the family worth having, both exact:

  • The period cannot be shorter than ``n`` diameters. Strand k is strand 0 slid along the axis by k thirds of a period, so a point on one and the matching point on another are at the same place across the braid and differ only by P/3 of height — which widening the braid does not change, since they are the same point of the same curve. This follows from the strands being one curve repeated and says nothing about braids that are not.

  • Across the cross-section alone, two strands pass closest at a crossing, where they sit at ±H√3/2, so they clear H√3 there — provided A >= 2H. Below that the tightest spot moves off the crossing. Neither statement is the whole clearance, which also counts the axial offset: that is figure_eight_clearance().

braidpy.symmetric_braid.minimum_period(n_strands: int, diameter: float) → float

The shortest period this family can have, n diameters.

Strand k is strand 0 slid along the axis by k n-ths of a period, so a point on one and the matching point on another sit at the same place across the braid and differ only by P/n of height. Widening the braid does not separate them — they are the same point of the same curve — so below n diameters no amplitudes will do.

The bound belongs to braids whose strands are one curve repeated, which this family is by construction; it is not a fact about braids in general.

In practice the family needs a good deal more than this — crowding across the cross-section bites first, and it runs out between six and seven diameters of period — but this bound is exact and costs nothing to check.

Parameters:

  • n_strands – How many strands.

  • diameter – How thick they are.

Returns:

The shortest conceivable period.

braidpy.symmetric_braid.crossing_clearance(amplitude: float, height: float) → float

How far apart two strands pass, counting the cross-section only.

At a crossing the two strands sit at angles of pi/6 and 5pi/6, so their heights are ±H√3/2 and they clear H√3. Writing the pair separation as (A√3 cos u, H√3 cos 2u), the squared distance 3(A²c² + H²(2c² - 1)²) is smallest at c = 0 — the crossing — exactly when A >= 2H; below that the tightest spot slides off the crossing and the clearance is smaller.

This ignores the axial offset between strands, so it is an upper bound on the real clearance, not the real clearance. Use figure_eight_clearance() for that.

Parameters:

  • amplitude – A.

  • height – H.

Returns:

The smallest separation within a cross-section.

braidpy.symmetric_braid.symmetric_contact_needs(amplitude: float, height: float) → bool

Whether the strands pass closest where they cross, as the tube’s do.

A braided tube’s tightest spot is its crossing, which is a point of symmetry for both strands and therefore a critical point of the distance whatever the parameters — which is what lets its radius be written down (tubular_braid_radius()).

This family has a candidate for the same role: w = P/4, where the two strands sit either side of the widest part of the swing and so are at the same place across the braid. There the sideways term drops out entirely and the distance depends on H alone. But it is only a minimum in w while

\[A \ge 4H\]

and below that it is a saddle: the tightest spot slides off it, picks up a dependence on A, and stops being anywhere symmetry can name. The shapes worth having sit below it — the tightest three-strand plait comes out at A/H near 1.2 to 1.7 — so the flat braid does not close the way the tube does, and tightest_figure_eight() searches.

Parameters:

  • amplitude – A.

  • height – H.

Returns:

True if the crossing is the tightest spot.

Minimises _pair_distance_squared() — two variables in closed form, rather than a grid over two sampled curves. A coarse sweep then a local descent, because the minimum is not at any point symmetry can name (see symmetric_contact_needs()) and so there is nothing to solve for.

The shortest strands of this family that still clear a diameter.

Length falls as the amplitudes shrink and clearance falls with them, so the answer sits on the boundary where the strands just touch. Finding it is a search in two variables — coarse grid, then refined about the best — which is cheap and reliable, and is the sense in which this shape is “solved”.

(amplitude, height), or None if no shape of this family fits that period — which happens long before minimum_period().

braidpy.symmetric_braid.braid_word(strands: Sequence, n_samples: int = 200000) → list[int]

Read the braid word off a set of curves.

Which slots a crossing exchanges is read from the order of the strands across the braid, and its sign from which of the two was higher as they passed — the same convention to_parametric_strands() draws with.

This is how a shape is checked against the braid it claims to be, rather than taken on trust. It needs the strands to be ordered across the braid at every height, so it suits a flat braid and not a tubular one.

Parameters:

  • strands – Anything answering position(z) over a common length.

  • n_samples – Heights to look at. A crossing narrower than the spacing between samples is missed, so this wants to be generous.

Returns:

The word, as signed generator indices.

take_off

A braid as it comes off whatever made it: laid, drawn in, and tightened.

Everything here works from one thing only — where each strand’s carrier was, in a plane, over time (StrandTrajectories). A horn gear machine, a braid word, a kumihimo disk: each says where its strands go, and from then on the braid is made the same way.

  • carrier_trajectories() follows the bobbins of a horn gear machine.

  • parametric_trajectories() reads a ParametricBraid, and braid_word_trajectories() a braid word through it — so anything that produces a word, kumihimo included, can be laid.

  • disk_trajectories() moves strands between the slots of a disk, and mobidai_trajectories() and kumihimo_trajectories() read a mobidai or a kumihimo sequence into it — the motion, for animating. For the braid itself, mobidai_braid() and kumihimo_braid() keep only the crossings the moves make and lay them round a ring (disk_braid()): where a disk’s strands wait is not where a braid holds them.

Laying

The braid is drawn off along the axis square to that plane at a steady rate, and a yarn is taken to stay where its carrier put it. The piece laid at time t sits over the point the carrier occupied then, carried up by the braid taken off since:

yarn(t) = (x(t), y(t), take_off * (T - t))

for a braid observed at time T. That gets the topology exactly: which yarn passes which, and on which side.

The fell

Real yarns run straight from their carriers up to the fell, where the braid forms, at fell_height: a ring about the size of the braid itself, yarns being as thick as they are. Above it each level of the braid is the carriers’ footprint drawn in toward the axis by a factor k: the fell’s own size at the fell — by default the braid’s own, as tight as the yarn allows (jammed_contraction()); k = 0 is the idealised braiding point, every yarn meeting at one point — and away from it as tight as the yarn allows. Any positive k at each level keeps which yarn passes over which, so the braid made is the braid kept.

Tightening

tighten_yarns() then shortens every yarn under tension, keeping every point at its height and no two yarns closer than a diameter — the problem of Solving a braid’s shape numerically. Far from the fell the braid settles to the shape its yarns pull it into, whatever the fell started it as.

Its parts

Each name is imported from here; it is kept in one of

  • braidpy.take_off.paths: the trajectories a braid is laid from, and the yarns laid;

  • braidpy.take_off.laying: laying them, drawn in to the fell;

  • braidpy.take_off.contact: contact between yarns, and how fast and how tight they allow;

  • braidpy.take_off.tighten: tightening;

  • braidpy.take_off.drawing: drawing the yarns;

  • braidpy.take_off.sources: where strands go, from a braid word, a disk, a mobidai or a kumihimo;

  • braidpy.take_off.ring: a disk’s braid, laid round a ring.

class braidpy.take_off.Periodic(partner: tuple[int, ...])

Bases: object

How the bottom of a tightened braid continues into its top.

A braid off a machine repeats, so a length of it is a window on something endless. Holding both ends still is a boundary the real braid does not have, and it is felt for a few periods in from each end. Saying instead that the yarn leaving the bottom of the window arrives at the top of it removes the boundary altogether: what is solved is one window of an endless braid rather than a short piece of a held one.

The window must be a whole number of periods, and the pattern must come back to itself over it – same positions, possibly a different yarn in each. partner says which: the yarn that leaves the fell end of yarn a arrives at the top end of yarn partner[a]. For a braid whose period permutes its strands this is that permutation; where the window is a whole number of full cycles it is the identity.

A window over which the pattern also turns about the axis is not handled: choose a whole number of turns, where there is nothing to undo.

Parameters:

partner – Yarn index to yarn index, a permutation. Yarns are numbered in the order of YarnPaths.points.

partner: tuple[int, ...]

check(n_yarns: int) → None

Raise if the wrap does not cover n_yarns yarns.

loops(n_yarns: int, n_levels: int, tied: bool = False) → list[ndarray]

The closed loops the wrap makes, as sample indices in order.

Following a yarn down to the fell and on into its partner comes back to where it started after one cycle of the permutation, so the samples fall into one loop per cycle.

Parameters:

  • n_yarns – Number of yarns.

  • n_levels – Samples per yarn.

  • tied – The last level repeats the first, so it is not a sample of its own and is left out of the loop.

Returns:

One array of sample indices per loop, each in the order the yarn runs.

class braidpy.take_off.StrandTrajectories(times: ndarray, xy: dict[Hashable, ndarray], outlines: tuple[ndarray, ...] = (), axis: tuple[float, float] | None = None, label: str = 'Yarn ', outline_name: str = 'Deck', slots: tuple[tuple[float, float, str], ...] = ())

Where every strand’s carrier went, sampled over time.

This is all the rest of the module needs: a braid is laid from it, drawn in and tightened without knowing what made it.

  • xy – Per strand, its position in the plane at each of those times; shape (n, 2).

  • label – Prefix naming a strand in a drawing, followed by its key.

  • outline_name – What the outlines are, in a drawing’s legend.

  • slots – Named places in the plane to mark in a drawing — a disk’s slots — as (x, y, name).
