braidpy.take_off.braid_word_trajectories(braid, samples_per_crossing: int = 24, spacing: float = 1.0, lift: float = 0.5) → StrandTrajectories

A braid word’s strands, as trajectories to lay.

The strands stand in a row spacing apart, and a crossing swaps two neighbours, the one going over lifted lift * spacing to one side and the one going under to the other — the drawing of to_parametric_strands(). Anything that makes a braid word can therefore be laid, tightened and drawn: a kumihimo sequence, a catalogue braid, or a word read off a machine.

Parameters:

  • braid – A Braid, or its generators as signed integers.

  • samples_per_crossing – Samples per generator.

  • spacing – Distance between neighbouring strands.

  • lift – How far a crossing strand moves off the row, as a fraction of spacing.

Returns:

The trajectories, over times 0 to 1.

braidpy.take_off.crossing_rows(order: Sequence[Hashable], crossings: Sequence[tuple[Hashable, Hashable]], in_turn: bool = False) → list[int]

The row of the ring each crossing is made in — see ring_trajectories().

Each crossing goes in the first row after both its strands’ last ones, so crossings of different strands are made side by side and each strand’s crossings stay in order.

Parameters:

  • order – The strands round the ring.

  • crossings – (over, under) in the order they are made.

  • in_turn – Never put a crossing in a row before an earlier crossing’s, so the rows are made in the order the crossings are, as a braid grows below a disk.

Returns:

One row index per crossing.

braidpy.take_off.default_take_off(trajectories: StrandTrajectories) → float

A take-off rate that draws a braid in sensible proportions.

The strands’ mean speed across the plane: a yarn then rises about as fast as it travels sideways, so it leaves at roughly 45°, near the angle a braid is usually made at. It sets only how stretched the picture is — nothing about which yarn crosses which depends on it.

braidpy.take_off.disk_annular_word(start: Mapping[Hashable, int], steps: Sequence[Mapping[Hashable, int]], n_slots: int, clockwise: bool = True) → tuple[list[int], int]

The annular braid a disk’s moves make — see braidpy.annulus_braid.

The strands are numbered in order round the disk, seen from above and read clockwise from the seam between the last slot and slot 1, so an anticlockwise disk is read from its last slot back. A strand lifted over another — over, seen from above — passes inside it, nearer the braid’s axis, and the annulus counts a crossing by who is outside: a move clockwise over a strand is a negative crossing, anticlockwise a positive one.

A strand passing between the last slot and slot 1, crossing nobody, changes nothing on the disk, but every strand’s number then moves on one: a turn (turn()), as the disk turning by one strand would be. Which strands are numbered from where depends only on where slot 1 is; another starting point gives the same braid, conjugated.

Parameters:

  • start – Each strand’s slot, 1-based.

  • steps – Per step, the strands that move and by how many slots, as disk_crossings() takes them.

  • n_slots – Slots round the disk.

  • clockwise – Whether slot numbers go round clockwise, seen from above.

Returns:

The word, crossings ±1 to ±n and turns ±(n + 1), and the number of strands n.

Raises:

ValueError – As disk_crossings().

braidpy.take_off.disk_braid(start: Mapping[Hashable, int], steps: Sequence[Mapping[Hashable, int]], n_slots: int, yarn_diameter: float, take_off_per_row: float = 1.5, iterations: int = 300, clockwise: bool = True) → YarnPaths

The braid a disk’s moves make: laid on a ring, drawn in and tightened.

The crossings are read off the moves (disk_crossings()), the strands set evenly round a ring and crossed there (ring_trajectories()), and the braid laid and tightened as any other (lay_yarns(), tighten_yarns()).

Parameters:

  • start – Each strand’s slot, 1-based.

  • steps – Per step, the strands that move and by how many slots.

  • n_slots – Slots round the disk.

  • yarn_diameter – Yarn diameter.

  • take_off_per_row – Braid taken off per row of crossings, in yarn diameters. Above one: two strands often cross back over each other a row later, along the same path, and need that much room.

  • iterations – Tightening steps.

  • clockwise – Whether slot numbers go round clockwise, seen from above.

Returns:

The tightened braid.

braidpy.take_off.disk_crossing_steps(start: Mapping[Hashable, int], steps: Sequence[Mapping[Hashable, int]], n_slots: int) → tuple[list[Hashable], list[tuple[Hashable, Hashable]], list[float]]

The crossings a disk’s moves make, and when each is made.

A strand that moves while the others stay passes over each strand between its slot and its new one, one after another, nearest first — the rule disk_trajectories() draws and the mobidai’s own word records. A step that moves every strand alike turns the disk and crosses nothing; so does one that slides a few strands along together, as long as no strand that stays is in their way.

Parameters:

  • start – Each strand’s slot, 1-based.

  • steps – Per step, the strands that move and by how many slots, as mobidai_steps() and kumihimo_steps() give them.

  • n_slots – Slots round the disk.

Returns:

The strands in slot order from slot 1 at the start, each crossing as (over, under), and when each is made, in steps: a strand moving n slots passes the slot j along at j / n of its step, as disk_trajectories() moves it.

Raises:

ValueError – If two strands move at once other than by turning the disk or sliding along together, which this cannot order into crossings.

braidpy.take_off.disk_crossings(start: Mapping[Hashable, int], steps: Sequence[Mapping[Hashable, int]], n_slots: int) → tuple[list[Hashable], list[tuple[Hashable, Hashable]]]

The crossings a disk’s moves make, in the order they are made.

See disk_crossing_steps(), which also says which step made each.

Returns:

The strands in slot order from slot 1 at the start, and each crossing as (over, under).

braidpy.take_off.disk_trajectories(start: Mapping[Hashable, int], steps: Sequence[Mapping[Hashable, int]], n_slots: int, radius: float = 1.0, lift: float = 0.15, samples_per_step: int = 12, clockwise: bool = True, label: str = 'Strand ', slot_offset: float = 0.0, slot_names: Mapping[int, str] | None = None) → StrandTrajectories

Strands moved between the slots round a disk, as trajectories to lay.

This is how a kumihimo disk or a mobidai is worked: each step moves some strands round the rim by a number of slots — positive toward higher slot numbers — and a step that moves every strand alike is the disk itself turning.

A strand that moves while others stay is lifted over the ones it passes — over as seen from above the disk, the side the braider works from, with the braid going down through the middle. Over is therefore inside: the moving strand travels round inside the rim, a lift fraction of the radius in, and comes back out to its new slot. Read in slot order with inside as over, that gives the crossings the mobidai’s own braid word records on a clockwise disk — a move toward higher slots crosses over, positively.

That is the opposite way round from braidpy.annulus_braid, which looks at a tube from outside, where over is outside.

Parameters:

  • start – Each strand’s slot, 1-based.

  • steps – Per step, the strands that move and by how many slots.

  • n_slots – Slots round the disk.

  • radius – The disk’s radius.

  • lift – How far in a moving strand travels, as a fraction of the radius.

  • samples_per_step – Samples per step.

  • clockwise – Whether slot numbers go round clockwise, seen from above.

  • label – Prefix naming a strand in a drawing.

  • slot_offset – Slots the numbering is turned by, so slot 1 sits that far round from the top. A kumihimo disk marks the top between its last slot and slot 1: half a slot.

  • slot_names – What to call each slot that is marked, by slot number; every slot by its number if None.

Returns:

The trajectories, one unit of time per step.

Raises:

ValueError – If a strand is not on a slot, or a step leaves two strands in one slot.

braidpy.take_off.jammed_contraction(rel: ndarray, spacing: float, diameter: float) → float

How far a braid can be drawn in before two yarns touch.

Drawing the plane in by k shrinks the sideways part of every distance by k and leaves the height part alone, so a pair of samples a height dz apart and s apart sideways touches when k = sqrt(d² - dz²) / s. The braid jams at the largest of these — an exact answer over the samples, with no search.

Parameters:

  • rel – Per yarn, its samples relative to the axis; shape (yarns, n, 2), every yarn at the same heights.

  • spacing – Height between successive samples.

  • diameter – Yarn diameter.

Returns:

The contraction k; above 1 if the yarns do not fit even undrawn.

Raises:

ValueError – If two yarns pass through the same place too close in height for any drawing-in to separate them — the take-off is too slow for yarns this thick.

braidpy.take_off.kumihimo_braid(kumihimo, yarn_diameter: float, n_strands: int | None = None, **kwargs) → YarnPaths

The braid a kumihimo sequence makes — see disk_braid().

Parameters:

  • kumihimo – A Kumihimo, or a pattern of S and R.

  • yarn_diameter – Yarn diameter.

  • n_strands – Strands, when given a pattern.

  • **kwargs – Passed on to disk_braid().

Returns:

The tightened braid.

braidpy.take_off.kumihimo_steps(kumihimo, n_strands: int | None = None) → tuple[int, dict[Hashable, int], list[dict[Hashable, int]]]

A kumihimo sequence, as the disk and steps disk_trajectories() takes.

Reads a Kumihimo — its strand count and the S and R moves it has recorded — or a pattern string such as "SRSR" for n_strands strands, without running anything.

The disk is given twice as many slots as there are strands, so that a swap has somewhere to pass: position p is slot 2p + 1. A swap of the top and bottom strands is then the move swap_top_bottom() writes down — the top strand goes over every strand on its way to just past the bottom one, the bottom one comes back over the others to the top, and the first settles into its place. A rotation turns the whole disk, a quarter turn clockwise per R.

Parameters:

  • kumihimo – A Kumihimo, or a pattern of S and R.

  • n_strands – Strands, when given a pattern.

Returns:

The number of slots, each strand’s starting slot, and the steps.

Raises:

ValueError – If the pattern is empty or has other moves, or the strands are not a multiple of four.

braidpy.take_off.kumihimo_trajectories(kumihimo, n_strands: int | None = None, radius: float = 1.0, lift: float = 0.15, samples_per_step: int = 12) → StrandTrajectories

A kumihimo sequence worked on its disk, as trajectories to lay.

Positions are numbered anticlockwise from the top, as plot_timeline() draws them.

Parameters:

  • kumihimo – A Kumihimo, or a pattern of S and R.

  • n_strands – Strands, when given a pattern.

  • radius – The disk’s radius.

  • lift – How far in a moving strand travels, as a fraction of the radius.

  • samples_per_step – Samples per step.

Returns:

The trajectories, one unit of time per step.

braidpy.take_off.lay_yarns(trajectories: StrandTrajectories, take_off: float | None = None, fell_radius: float | None = None, yarn_diameter: float | None = None, fell_height: float | None = None, axis: tuple[float, float] | None = None, n_converge: int = 16, settle_length: float | None = None) → YarnPaths

The braid laid from these trajectories, as it stands at their last sample.

With neither fell_radius nor yarn_diameter each yarn lies over the path its carrier traced, lifted along the axis by the braid taken off since. With either, the yarns converge on a fell and the braid above it is drawn in toward the axis. With both, the fell is only where the braid starts: it opens out — or closes in — to as tight as the yarn allows over settle_length of take-off, and tighten_yarns() takes it from there.

Parameters:

  • trajectories – Where the strands went.

  • take_off – Length of braid drawn off per unit of time. Defaults to default_take_off() — or, with yarn_diameter, faster if need be, so that two yarns passing the same point are a diameter apart in height there; see least_take_off().

  • fell_radius – Radius of the fell circle the braid is formed on; 0 for a braiding point.

  • yarn_diameter – Draw the braid in as far as yarns this thick allow — see jammed_contraction() — away from the fell, and at the fell too if fell_radius is not given. The samples should then be closer than a diameter apart along the axis, or contacts between them go unseen.

  • fell_height – Height of the fell over the plane. Defaults to as far above it as the braid is drawn in, so the yarns converge at about 45°.

  • axis – The braid’s axis, in the plane. Defaults to the trajectories’.

  • n_converge – Points along each yarn from the fell down to its carrier.

  • settle_length – Take-off over which the braid goes from the fell’s size to its own, when both fell_radius and yarn_diameter are given. Defaults to twice the difference in radius.

Returns:

The yarns, one per strand.

braidpy.take_off.least_take_off(trajectories: StrandTrajectories, yarn_diameter: float, take_off: float) → float

The slowest take-off that lifts yarns passing the same point, or nearly, far enough apart to fit, at least take_off.

Where one strand leaves a place and another comes to the very same point later — as each crossing of a braid word does, one strand arriving where the other left — no drawing-in can separate them (jammed_contraction()): only the height the take-off puts between them can. The fewer strands move at a time, the slower the default take-off, and the closer in height they come.

Nearly the same point is as bad: two yarns a sideways distance s apart touch, dz apart in height, unless the braid is drawn out by sqrt(d² − dz²) / s, a hundredfold for carriers on one split axle that pass a hundredth of a diameter apart between two samples. So the take-off is raised until every pair fits undrawn, dz at least sqrt(d² − s²); a braid whose yarns already do is left as it was.

Parameters:

  • trajectories – Where the strands went, sampled evenly in time.

  • yarn_diameter – Yarn diameter.

  • take_off – The take-off to start from.

Returns:

take_off, or a little faster than the least take-off that lets the closest such pair fit.

braidpy.take_off.longest_step(paths: YarnPaths) → float

The furthest any yarn moves sideways between two levels of the braid above the fell.

braidpy.take_off.mobidai_braid(mobidai, yarn_diameter: float, n_cycles: int = 8, **kwargs) → YarnPaths

The braid a mobidai makes in n_cycles cycles — see disk_braid().

Parameters:

  • mobidai – A Mobidai or MobidaiConfig (see braidpy.mobidai).

  • yarn_diameter – Yarn diameter.

  • n_cycles – Cycles to work.

  • **kwargs – Passed on to disk_braid().

Returns:

The tightened braid, one yarn per strand, keyed as the mobidai’s.

braidpy.take_off.mobidai_steps(mobidai, n_cycles: int = 1, drift: int | None = None) → tuple[dict[Hashable, int], list[dict[Hashable, int]]]

A mobidai’s cycles, as the start and steps disk_trajectories() takes.

Reads either a Mobidai or its MobidaiConfig (see braidpy.mobidai) without running it, and follows its rules: a move goes the short way round unless forced, a move from an empty slot does nothing, and the disk turns n_shift_after_cycle slots after each cycle.

Some braids do not come back to the slots they started in after a cycle but one or more slots round from them — kongo gumi creeps one slot back each time — and the braider simply repeats the same moves from where the strands now are: cycle c makes every move c * drift slots round from the first cycle’s. The drift is read off the cycle itself, as Mobidai does (see cycle_drift()).

Parameters:

  • mobidai – The mobidai, or its configuration.

  • n_cycles – Cycles to work.

  • drift – Slots each cycle’s moves are shifted from the one before; read off the cycle if None.

Returns:

Each strand’s starting slot, keyed by strand id, and the steps.

braidpy.take_off.mobidai_trajectories(mobidai, n_cycles: int = 3, drift: int | None = None, radius: float = 1.0, lift: float = 0.15, samples_per_step: int = 12, slot_offset: float = 0.0) → StrandTrajectories

A mobidai worked for n_cycles cycles, as trajectories to lay.

Parameters:

  • mobidai – A Mobidai or MobidaiConfig (see braidpy.mobidai).

  • n_cycles – Cycles to work.

  • drift – Slots each cycle’s moves are shifted from the one before; read off the cycle if None — see mobidai_steps().

  • radius – The disk’s radius.

  • lift – How far in a moving strand travels, as a fraction of the radius.

  • samples_per_step – Samples per move.

  • slot_offset – Slots the numbering is turned by — see disk_trajectories().

Returns:

The trajectories, one unit of time per move.

braidpy.take_off.parametric_trajectories(braid, n_samples: int = 400, label: str = 'Strand ') → StrandTrajectories

The strands of a parametric braid, as trajectories to lay.

A ParametricStrand is a curve γ(t) = (x, y, z) for t from 0 to 1. Its (x, y) is taken as where its carrier was at time t, so the strand drawn first is laid first and ends up highest, as ParametricBraid.plot draws it — over and under come from y, as they do there.

Parameters:

  • braid – A ParametricBraid, or a sequence of strands.

  • n_samples – Samples along each strand.

  • label – Prefix naming a strand in a drawing.

Returns:

The trajectories, over times 0 to 1.

braidpy.take_off.ring_trajectories(order: Sequence[Hashable], crossings: Sequence[tuple[Hashable, Hashable]], diameter: float = 1.0, samples_per_row: int = 12, clockwise: bool = True, label: str = 'Strand ', rows: Sequence[int] | None = None) → StrandTrajectories

Strands standing evenly round a ring, swapping neighbours as they cross.

Every crossing is made by two strands next to each other round the ring: they change places, the one going over passing inside, the other outside, a diameter apart where they meet. Crossings of different strands are made side by side, in rows, as long as each strand’s crossings stay in order; each row takes one unit of time.

Nothing about which strand passes which, or on which side, is lost — inside is over, as on a disk seen from above — so a braid laid from this is the braid the moves made, with the strands where a braid holds them rather than where a disk does.

Parameters:

  • order – The strands round the ring, in slot order.

  • crossings – (over, under) in the order they are made; each pair must be neighbours on the ring when its turn comes.

  • diameter – Yarn diameter, setting the ring’s size and how far apart the two strands of a crossing pass.

  • samples_per_row – Samples per row of crossings.

  • clockwise – Whether the order runs clockwise, seen from above.

  • label – Prefix naming a strand in a drawing.

  • rows – The row of each crossing; crossing_rows() if None.

Returns:

The trajectories, one unit of time per row.

Raises:

ValueError – If a crossing’s strands are not neighbours on the ring.

braidpy.take_off.tighten_yarns(paths: YarnPaths, yarn_diameter: float, iterations: int = 400, step: float = 20.0, core_radius: float | None = None, tolerance: float = 0.001, hold_top: bool = True, rigid: Collection[Hashable] = (), periodic: Periodic | None = None) → tuple[YarnPaths, dict[str, list[float]]]

Pull the yarns taut above the fell, without letting them overlap.

Each iteration shortens every yarn, sideways only, so every sample keeps its height; then it pushes apart any two samples of different yarns closer than a diameter, until none are. The yarn is held where it arrives at the fell from its carrier, and at its oldest end, where the take-off holds it. Between the two, far enough from the fell, the braid takes the shape its yarns pull it into, whatever shape the fell started it in.

Shortening at fixed height is the length objective of Solving a braid’s shape numerically in its small-slope form — tension pulls a yarn toward the middle of its neighbours — and the push is its non-interpenetration constraint. The tension is taken implicitly, as a backward-Euler step of step along that flow, which settles a whole yarn in a few dozen iterations where moving each sample toward its neighbours would take thousands. No sample moves more than a fifth of a diameter in one go, though, so a yarn cannot jump through another and the braid the machine made is the braid that comes out.

Parameters:

  • paths – The braid to tighten.

  • yarn_diameter – Yarn diameter.

  • iterations – Shortening steps.

  • step – How far along the tension flow each step goes, in units where 1 moves a sample half way to its neighbours’ middle.

  • core_radius – Keep the yarns outside a core of this radius round the axis, for a braid laid over one.

  • tolerance – Overlap, as a fraction of the diameter, that the contact push accepts.

  • hold_top – Hold the oldest end where it is, as the take-off does. Left free, the end can turn about the axis and untwist the braid. Ignored when periodic is given, which holds neither end.

  • rigid – Yarns held where they are all along, as stiff cores: the others are pushed off them, and they never move.

  • periodic – Join the fell end of the braid to its top, so that what is tightened is one window of an endless braid rather than a short piece of a held one. See Periodic: the window must be a whole number of periods.

Returns:

"length", the total yarn length above the fell, and "closest", the closest approach, after each iteration.

Return type:

The tightened braid, and its history

Warns:

UserWarning – If the braid is laid too coarsely for contact between samples to keep its yarns apart (warn_if_too_coarse()).

braidpy.take_off.visualize_yarns(paths: YarnPaths, output_html: str | None = None, title: str | None = None, tube_diameter: float | None = None, n_around: int = 12, show_deck: bool = True, colors: Sequence[str] | None = None, extra_traces: Sequence[go.BaseTraceType] = ()) → go.Figure

The yarns in 3D, standing on whatever laid them.

Each yarn ends in a marker at the plane, where its carrier is now; the source’s outlines are drawn there, and the fell or braiding point where the yarns meet.

Parameters:

  • paths – The yarns to draw.

  • output_html – If given, write the figure to this HTML file.

  • title – Figure title; says which model the yarns follow if None.

braidpy.take_off.warn_if_too_coarse(paths: YarnPaths, yarn_diameter: float) → None

Warn when the braid is laid too coarsely for tighten_yarns() to keep its yarns apart: see SAFE_STEP.

Parameters:

  • paths – The braid about to be tightened.

  • yarn_diameter – Its yarns’ diameter.

braidpy.take_off.tighten.SAFE_STEP = 1.0

How far, in diameters, a yarn may move sideways between two levels and tightening still keep yarns from passing through each other. It looks for contact between samples only, and two yarns can cross between two levels without a sample of either coming within a diameter of the other only if their steps there add up to two diameters or more.

Yarns as elastic rods, settled by their own physics: web/rope.js, in Python.

The same algorithm, step for step, in the same order (tests/test_rope_python.py runs both and compares them); the model is rope.js’s, and docs/source/rope_physics.md describes it. In short, each yarn is a chain of beads, and its energy is the sum of

  • stretching: k_s/2 (|x_{i+1} - x_i| - s)² per link — stiff, so yarn barely stretches;

  • bending: k_b/2 |x_{i-1} - 2 x_i + x_{i+1}|² / s² per bead — slight;

  • contact, for any two segments of different yarns (or of one yarn, far apart along it): a yarn is a firm core inside a soft surface. Closer than a diameter d, the surfaces press together, k_r/2 (d - r)²; closer than d - w, the cores too, k_c/2 (d - w - r)², much stiffer;

and the ends’ work. The yarns’ bottom ends are clamped; their top ends are fixed to an end plate, drawn up by a force, which may turn about the axis. The yarns may also be fed through the plate from bobbins pulling them back with a tension T, their links’ rest length then one more unknown. The minimum of that energy, the braid at rest, is found by FIRE (Bitzek et al., 2006). Lengths are in yarn diameters.

The mechanics (near_pairs() to move_beads(), and relay()) are shared with braidpy.form, as rope.js shares them with form.js.

It follows the JavaScript step for step: given the same numbers from the maths library, it settles the same yarns, bead for bead. The libraries differ in the last place (Python’s math.hypot is correctly rounded, JavaScript’s not always), and thousands of steps make that visible: the two settle alike, not identically. It is pure Python and slow — tens of times slower than in a browser — which suits checking it, not settling long braids.

References:

  • FIRE: E. Bitzek, P. Koskinen, F. Gähler, M. Moseler, P. Gumbsch, “Structural relaxation made simple”, Phys. Rev. Lett. 97, 170201 (2006).

  • Closest points of two segments: C. Ericson, Real-Time Collision Detection (Morgan Kaufmann, 2005), §5.1.9.

  • The grid of cells: M. Teschner, B. Heidelberger, M. Müller, D. Pomeranets, M. Gross, “Optimized spatial hashing for collision detection of deformable objects”, Vision, Modeling, and Visualization (2003). rope.js hashes the cells with three large primes; here a cell is its own key, which finds the same pairs in the same order.

braidpy.rope.relay(yarn: Sequence[float], spacing: float) → list[float]

A yarn’s beads again, evenly spaced about spacing apart, its two ends kept.

braidpy.rope.settle(yarns: Sequence[Sequence[float]], spacing: float | None = None, force: float = 1.0, turns: bool = False, feed: float | None = None, stretch: float = 400.0, bend: float = 0.5, contact: float = 400.0, soft: float = 5.0, shell: float = 0.1, steps: int = 20000, tolerance: float = 0.001, dt_max: float = 0.05, progress: Callable[[dict[str, Any]], None] | None = None) → dict[str, Any]

Parameters:

  • yarns – Each yarn’s beads, x y z after x y z, bottom end first.

  • spacing – Rest length of a link; by default each yarn’s first link’s.

  • force – Drawing the end plate up.

  • turns – Whether the end plate may turn.

  • feed – T: feed the yarns through the plate at this tension. Without it, each yarn keeps its length.

  • stretch – k_s.

  • bend – k_b.

  • soft – k_r, the soft surfaces’.

  • shell – w, how thick the soft surface is, of a diameter; 0 for a yarn hard all through.

Making a braid crossing by crossing — beaten up, row by row, with friction: web/form.js, in Python.

The same algorithm, step for step, in the same order (tests/test_rope_python.py runs both and compares them). braidpy.rope.settle() beats a whole laid braid up at once. Here the braid is made from its oldest row up, as a braid is made: its yarns as laid by braidpy, in the order their crossings are made, so the crossings are the right ones.

The yarns are in three parts:

  • made: below a working window, the braid already beaten up, frozen;

  • working: the window, a row or two, where the yarns move — the same stretching, bending and contact as braidpy.rope, plus friction;

  • to come: above it, the rest of the braid as laid, moving as one block. The yarns’ tension draws it down onto the window, a weight draws it up: while the yarns pull harder, the newest row is beaten up against the made braid, until its crossings jam.

Each yarn slides into the window from the block at its tension, as from a bobbin. Once a row is beaten up, the lower part of the window is frozen into the made braid, and the window takes in the next row from the block.

Friction: two yarns in contact hold each other along their surfaces with a spring from where they first touched, until its pull reaches mu times the push between them, when they slip (Coulomb’s law, as the discrete element method has it). It is what keeps a beaten crossing where it was beaten.

The window is settled by FIRE, with braidpy.rope’s own mechanics, as form.js uses rope.js’s. Lengths are in yarn diameters. Pure Python, and slow: for checking, not for long braids.

References:

  • Friction as a tangential spring, capped by Coulomb’s law: P. A. Cundall and O. D. L. Strack, “A discrete numerical model for granular assemblies”, Géotechnique 29, 47 (1979), https://doi.org/10.1680/geot.1979.29.1.47 (not free to read). The same tangential spring, among other contact models, free to read: “Review of contact models used in Discrete Element Method (DEM)”, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07461.

  • FIRE, and the contact geometry: see braidpy.rope.

braidpy.form.friction_force(grips: dict[int, list[float]], key: int, v: Sequence[float], i: int, j: int, u: float, w: float, nx: float, ny: float, nz: float, push: float, dt: float, mu: float, kt: float) → tuple[float, float, float]

Friction at a contact: the tangential spring between the segments at offsets i and j of the beads’ velocities v, at u and w along them, stretched by how the contact points slid past each other this step — kept in the contact’s tangent plane, normal (nx, ny, nz) — and given way to what friction holds, mu times the push, when it pulls harder: the contact slips. The springs are kept in grips by the pair’s key.

Returns:

The friction force on the first segment.

A braid made by its carriers: each yarn drawn by its carrier going round the machine, through a forming ring, into the braid taken off above.

Nothing here is laid in advance. The carriers go round their tracks (carrier_trajectories()), and the yarns follow:

  • To scale. Lengths are in yarn diameters, the machine at its real size: a gear some 5.5 cm across is GEAR_DIAMETER of 1100 dtex yarn, about 0.4 mm thick; the forming ring stands RING_HEIGHT above the carriers’ eyes, 3 cm.

  • Pulled by the carriers. Each yarn runs straight from its carrier’s eye up to BELOW under the ring; from there to the braid it is a chain of beads. Its carrier pulls it with a steady tension, as a carrier’s spring tensioner does: the lowest bead is pulled towards the eye, and yarn is paid out — a bead added at the bottom — when the braid draws it up, or taken back when it slackens. No bead is ever renamed, so a contact remembers its friction for as long as it lasts.

  • The forming ring, a torus of wire round the braid’s axis, the yarns passing inside it: it brings them together where the braid forms.

  • Friction holds the yarns where they cross, as on a real machine: a crossing is beaten up at the fell and carried up with the braid. With none, two taut yarns slide to wherever they touch, and the braid taken off would have no crossings at all.

  • The braid taken off: ABOVE over the ring, the yarns are made — frozen — and drawn up at a steady rate, TAKE_OFF a step of the machine.

Between moves of the carriers, the beads settle by FIRE, with the mechanics of braidpy.rope — stretching, bending, contact — and the friction of braidpy.form. Pure Python, and slow: a reference, for checking, and for a few steps of a small machine.

Braid Studio

What the web page asks of braidpy.

Package: braidpy.web Description: Braids as plain data, for a page to draw Authors: Baptiste Labat Created: 2026-10-04 Repository: https://github.com/baptistelabat/braidpy License: Mozilla Public License 2.0

The braidpy web page runs braidpy itself, in the browser, through Pyodide, and draws what it computes with three.js. This package is everything the page asks of braidpy: what can be made (catalog()), and the braid a description makes (build()), both as plain JSON-ready data — lists, numbers and strings — so the page needs nothing of Python’s to draw it.

A description says where the braid comes from — by default, the first source offered:

{"source": "word", "word": "1 -2", "n_strands": 3, "repeat": 6}

A braid word: signed generator indices (1 -2), s1 s2^-1, or letters (aB, a for σ₁ and A its inverse). With "layout": "ring", a ring word, the strands round a circle: n crosses the last strand and the first, across the seam, and n + 1 turns them all one place round. With "layout": "band", a band word (braidpy.band_canonical_form): 4:1 crosses strands 4 and 1 in front of those between, 1:4 the other way.

{"source": "kumihimo", "pattern": "SR", "n_strands": 8, "repeat": 8}

Kumihimo’s own moves: swap top and bottom, rotate a quarter.

{"source": "mobidai", "name": "KONGO_8", "cycles": 8}

A disk braid from the catalogue (braidpy.mobidai_catalog).

{"source": "sinnet", "name": "abok_3042", "cycles": 4}

An Ashley solid sinnet (braidpy.solid_sinnets_catalog).

{"source": "machine", "name": "tubular_8", "cycles": 3}

A horn gear braiding machine (braidpy.horn_gear.examples).

Every description may also give yarn_diameter and iterations, the tightening steps; 0 lays the yarns without tightening them.

what differs from the source’s defaults is left to them.

Return type:

Their descriptions, as short as they can be

Disk braids: kumihimo’s own S/R moves, a mobidai braid, an Ashley solid sinnet. Each is laid round a ring with its rows in the order the disk makes their crossings, so the page can show the disk and the braid in step, and comes with its moves, for the page to make it move by move as on a marudai.

braidpy.web.disks.from_b3d(text: str) → Spec

A design saved by braid3d, as your own mobidai braid’s description (mobidai_from_b3d()): its disk, where each yarn starts, in its colour, a cycle’s moves and how many cycles.

Parameters:

text – The .b3d file’s text.

Returns:

The description, for the page to fill its fields with and make.

Raises:

ValueError – If the file holds no design, or one not read here.

Horn gear braiding machines: the braid a machine makes, loaded as it loads itself or by hand, stopped where carriers meet; and the machine as the page draws it from above, to load it by hand.

braidpy.web.machines.machine_geometry(name: str) → MachineGeometry

A machine as the page draws it from above, to load it by hand: its gears — where, how big, the circle their carriers ride, their slots, the way they turn and where each slot is at step 0, drawn as braidpy draws it (GearAngles) — the contacts between them, the machine’s own loading, every place it could feed an axial yarn (axial_spots()), those it does, in the colour cores are drawn in, and, for a machine of gears geared together, the machine written as the gears that mesh (graph_of()), for your own to start from.

braidpy.web.machines.tracks(machine: Any, layout: Any = None) → list[tuple[str, Any]]

A machine’s carrier tracks, seen from above as the demo draws them (coloured_tracks()), each in its colour, with fewer points: none for a machine driven by a programme.

Parameters:

  • machine – The machine.

  • layout – Where its gears are; worked out if None.

Returns:

Per track, its colour and its points, shape (n, 2), in the layout’s plane — the carriers’ too.

braidpy.web.machines.machine_turned(name: str, loading: list[list[Any]], time: int, frames: int = 8) → MachineTurned

A machine’s handle turned time steps by hand, as the page shows it (see braidpy.horn_gear.handle): stopped where carriers meet, and drawn through the next step, for the page to turn it smoothly.

Parameters:

  • name – The machine.

  • loading – The carriers at step 0, as (gear, slot).

  • time – How many steps to turn.

  • frames – Pictures of the next step.

Returns:

time, the step reached; carriers there, in the loading’s order; met, where carriers met, if they did; slots, every slot gear by gear; and frames, the slots’ and carriers’ places through the next step, the first at the step reached.

braidpy.web.machines.machine_origin(name: str, place: list[Any], time: int) → list[Any] | None

The slot at step 0 whose carrier is at place at step time: where a carrier put on the machine there goes in its loading.

Parameters:

  • name – The machine.

  • place – As (gear, slot), at step time.

  • time – The step.

Returns:

(gear, slot) at step 0; None if no slot leads there.

Braid words, flat or round a ring: laid as braidpy draws them, and as moves on a ring of bobbins, for the page to make the braid move by move as on a marudai.

braidpy.web.words.place_program(program: RingProgram, slots: int = 12) → DiskProgram

A ring program (braidpy.ring_program.RingProgram) as a disk program for the page: each place slots slots on from the last, each swap made as _swapped() makes it, the braid hanging free. An empty place holds no bobbin: a strand beside it moves into it.

Parameters:

  • program – The ring program.

  • slots – Slots between neighbouring places.

Returns:

What the disk does, strands by index.

braidpy.utils.lazy_module(name: str) → Any

A module that is only imported when first used.

Drawing libraries — plotly, matplotlib — are heavy, and most of braidpy computes without them: in a browser, through Pyodide, not loading them is the difference between a page that opens and one that downloads tens of megabytes first. Modules that draw import them this way, and keep the real import under TYPE_CHECKING for the type checker.

Parameters:

name – The module’s dotted name.

Returns:

A stand-in that imports the module on first attribute access.

Bases: Exception

A braid computation that ran but did not give what it must: a bug in braidpy rather than in what it was asked.

braidpy.utils.play_controls(frame_duration_ms: float, marks: Sequence[tuple[str, str]]) → dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]]

Play and pause buttons, and a slider, for a Plotly animation.

Parameters:

  • frame_duration_ms – How long each frame is shown while playing.

  • marks – The slider’s notches, as (frame name, label).

Returns:

updatemenus and sliders, for Figure.update_layout. The slider’s read-out is hidden: Plotly’s repeats the active notch’s label, and notches between two labelled ones have none to repeat, so it would blank out while the animation ran.
